The Swedish Government maintained that the deportation would not violate Article 3. They argued that the applicants lacked credibility, had failed to establish their identities, and had submitted documents of low evidentiary value. The Government contended that the Uzbek Embassy had not been informed of the applicants' asylum status and that there was no substantiated individual risk to the applicants upon return.

case_name: CASE OF USTYANTSEV v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### 1. The Parties
The case of *Ustyantsev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 3299/05) involves the applicant, Mr. Sergey Vladimirovich Ustyantsev, a Ukrainian national born in 1972, and the respondent State, Ukraine, represented by its Agent, Mr. Y. Zaytsev. ### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 12 September 2001, the applicant was arrested and subsequently charged with car theft. His pre-trial detention was authorized on 14 September 2001. In January 2002, the domestic court ordered that the car theft case be joined with a separate burglary case dating from September 2001. In protest of these joined proceedings, the applicant made several suicide attempts and went on hunger strikes. On 3 March 2003, the District Court convicted the applicant on both charges, sentencing him to nine years’ imprisonment. On 31 July 2003, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed the burglary conviction and remitted it for a retrial, while upholding the car theft conviction and reducing that sentence to five years and six months. The Supreme Court of Ukraine dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal regarding the car theft conviction on 22 March 2005. During the retrial on the burglary charge, numerous hearings were rescheduled due to the absence of defense lawyers and witnesses. On 1 June 2005, the court found that the investigator had forged the applicant’s signature on key procedural documents and remitted the case for additional investigation. On 4 October 2005, the investigator discontinued the burglary proceedings against the applicant due to a lack of proof. The applicant was held in various detention facilities, including the Odessa Remand Centre (SIZO), temporary detention centers, and correctional colonies, between September 2001 and January 2007, when he was released on parole. He was re-arrested in August 2007 on new suspicions. In March 2006, the applicant brought a civil action against the SIZO seeking compensation for poor detention conditions, but domestic courts dismissed the claim on procedural grounds. ### 3. The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant alleged that the conditions of his detention in the temporary detention centre, the SIZO, the court's detainees' room, and during transportation in prison vans violated Article 3 of the Convention. Specifically, he complained of severe overcrowding (alleging space was limited to approximately one square metre per person in his SIZO cell), constant night lighting, concrete floors, poor hygiene, and inadequate medical treatment for his deteriorating health, which included chronic prostatitis and venereal disease. He also alleged that his pre-trial detention and trial were excessively long and that he was unable to obtain compensation for his lengthy detention. ### 4. The Government's Position
The Government contested the applicant's claims regarding the SIZO conditions. They maintained that the cells met domestic standards, providing at least 2.5 square metres of space per person, basic furniture, separated toilets, adequate lighting, ventilation, and regular access to walks and baths. They also submitted medical records indicating that the applicant received appropriate medical examinations and treatment for his health conditions. ### 5. Procedural History before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his application with the Court on 1 November 2004. On 16 March 2009, the President of the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaints to the Ukrainian Government and to examine the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.

case_name: CASE OF HRISTOZOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: Hristozov and Others v. Bulgaria

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicants were ten Bulgarian nationals (Mr. Zapryan Hristozov, Ms. Anna Staykova-Petermann, Ms. Boyanka Tsvetkova Misheva, Mr. Petar Dimitrov Petrov, Ms. Krastinka Marinova Pencheva, Ms. Tana Tankova Gavadinova, Ms. Blagovesta Veselinova Stoyanova, Mr. Shefka Syuleymanov Gyuzelev, Mr. Yordan Borisov Tenekev, and Mr. David Sabbatai Behar) who suffered from various terminal cancers. During the course of the proceedings, four of the applicants passed away, and their legal heirs expressed their wish to pursue the applications in their stead. The respondent party was the Government of the Republic of Bulgaria. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicants, having either exhausted conventional cancer treatments or been advised that such treatments would not be effective or available in Bulgaria, sought access to an experimental anti-cancer product known as "MBVax Coley Fluid." The product, developed by a Canadian company, was not authorized in any country but was permitted for "compassionate use" in several other jurisdictions. The manufacturer offered to supply the product free of charge to a private clinic in Sofia for use on these patients in exchange for clinical data. However, the Bulgarian Medicines Executive Agency and the Ministry of Health refused to authorize the import or use of the product. The authorities stated that Bulgarian law made no provision for the compassionate use of unauthorized medicines outside of clinical trials, and that the product did not meet the regulatory requirements for any domestic exceptions. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants alleged that the domestic authorities' refusal to permit the compassionate use of the experimental treatment violated their right to life under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights and constituted inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3. They also argued that the ban infringed upon their right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. Additionally, they claimed under Article 13 that they lacked an effective domestic remedy to challenge the authorities' decisions, noting that they did not seek domestic judicial review of the individual refusals because the administrative authorities maintained there was no legal framework for such requests. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Bulgarian Government contended that MBVax Coley Fluid did not qualify as a "medicinal product" under applicable European Union and domestic legislation. They disputed the applicants' assertion that the product was undergoing active clinical trials in Germany. The Government maintained that domestic regulations strictly prohibited the use of unauthorized medicines outside clinical trials to protect public health and safety, and emphasized that EU law did not mandate a harmonized approach to compassionate use. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 July and 5 December 2011. Following the deaths of four applicants, the Court permitted their legal heirs to continue the proceedings. On 9 February 2012, the President of the Fourth Section granted priority to the applications. On 21 February 2012, the Court joined the applications, declared them partly inadmissible, and gave notice to the Government of the complaints concerning the refusal of authorization and the alleged lack of effective remedies, deciding to examine the admissibility and merits of these remaining complaints together.

case_name: CASE OF BAJSULTANOV v. AUSTRIA
step1_summary:
### Summary

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case of *Bajsultanov v. Austria* (Application no. 54131/10) involves Mr. Ruslan Bajsultanov, a Russian national of Chechen origin born in 1980, and the Republic of Austria. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Mr. Bajsultanov arrived in Austria with his family in July 2003 and applied for asylum. He claimed that he had supported Chechen fighters during the first Chechen war (1994–1996) and that, in 2003, security forces had searched for him, beaten his father, and burned down his family's home. In July 2005, the Austrian Independent Federal Asylum Panel granted him asylum, finding his claims credible and concluding that he faced a real risk of ill-treatment if returned to Russia. His wife and two children were subsequently granted independent asylum status in Austria in 2007. Between 2005 and 2008, the applicant was convicted of several criminal offenses in Austria. These included a 2005 conviction for attempted theft (suspended sentence), a 2006 conviction for attempted resistance to public authority, aggravated damage to property, and aggravated bodily harm (eight-month sentence, six months suspended), and a 2008 conviction for aggravated bodily harm (twelve-month sentence). He was released from prison in August 2009. In October 2008, the Federal Asylum Office lifted the applicant’s asylum status and ordered his expulsion to the Russian Federation. The office determined that his repeated violent offenses constituted "particularly serious crimes" under the 2005 Asylum Act and that the security situation in Chechnya had sufficiently improved. The Asylum Court dismissed his appeal in August 2009, and the Constitutional Court declined to review the matter in March 2010. In September 2010, the Graz Federal Police Authority issued a ten-year exclusion order against the applicant. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that his planned expulsion to the Russian Federation would violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by exposing him to a real risk of torture, disappearance, or ill-treatment. He also alleged a violation of Article 8, arguing that his expulsion would separate him from his wife and children. He emphasized that because his family members held independent asylum status in Austria, they could not reasonably be expected to follow him to Russia, thereby permanently disrupting their family life. Additionally, he argued that his domestic convictions did not meet the legal threshold of "particularly serious offences" required to lift his asylum status. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Austrian Government contested the applicant's claims. They argued that the domestic authorities had conducted a thorough, individualized assessment of the security situation in Chechnya and the applicant's personal circumstances. The Government maintained that due to the passage of time, the applicant was no longer at risk of persecution for his past activities. They further asserted that his repeated violent offenses justified the revocation of his asylum status and that the public interest in preventing crime and maintaining public order outweighed his right to family life in Austria, particularly given his lack of social and linguistic integration. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 September 2010. On 23 September 2010, the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, directing the Austrian Government to stay the applicant's expulsion until further notice. The application was communicated to the Austrian Government on 28 January 2011. On 25 May 2011, the Russian Government informed the Court that they would not exercise their right to intervene in the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF GAS AND DUBOIS v. FRANCE
step1_summary:
### Summary

**1. The Main Parties**
The case of *Gas and Dubois v. France* was brought by two French nationals, Ms Valérie Gas and Ms Nathalie Dubois (the applicants), against the Republic of France (the respondent Government). **2. Key Factual Circumstances**
The applicants are two women who have cohabited since 1989. In September 2000, Ms Dubois gave birth to a daughter, A., who was conceived in Belgium via anonymous donor insemination. The child has no legally established paternal tie and has lived with both applicants since birth. In April 2002, the applicants registered a civil partnership agreement (*pacte civil de solidarité* or PACS). In March 2006, Ms Gas applied to the domestic courts for a "simple adoption" order of A., with Ms Dubois’s formal consent. Under Article 365 of the French Civil Code, a simple adoption transfers all parental responsibility to the adoptive parent, unless the adopter is married to the child’s biological parent, in which case parental responsibility is shared. Because French law at the time restricted marriage to opposite-sex couples, the applicants, as civil partners, could not share parental responsibility. Consequently, granting the adoption would have legally stripped Ms Dubois of her parental rights over her biological daughter. **3. Domestic Procedural History**
In July 2006, the Nanterre *tribunal de grande instance* rejected the adoption application. Although the court acknowledged that the applicants jointly provided the child with care and affection, it ruled that the adoption would run counter to the child’s interests by depriving the biological mother of her parental rights. The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld this decision in December 2006, confirming that the statutory exception allowing for shared parental responsibility applied strictly to married spouses. The applicants appealed to the Court of Cassation, but the appeal was declared forfeit in September 2007 after they did not pursue the proceedings to their conclusion. **4. The Applicants’ Allegations**
Before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), the applicants alleged that they had been subjected to discriminatory treatment based on their sexual orientation. They argued that, unlike heterosexual couples, same-sex couples in France had no legal avenue to access second-parent adoption. They relied on Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken in conjunction with Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life). **5. The Government’s Position**
The French Government raised a preliminary objection regarding the applicability of the Convention. They argued that Article 8 does not guarantee a right to adopt or to establish a legal parent-child relationship. Because the Convention does not cover a right to adopt, the Government contended that Article 14 was inapplicable, as it has no independent existence outside the ambit of other Convention rights. **6. Procedural History before the European Court**
The application was lodged on 15 June 2007. On 31 August 2010, the Court declared the application admissible. In doing so, the Court dismissed the Government’s preliminary objection, finding that the applicants’ relationship fell within the definition of "family life" under Article 8, thereby making Article 14 applicable in conjunction with it. Several non-governmental organizations, including ILGA-Europe and the International Commission of Jurists, submitted third-party comments. A public hearing on the merits of the case was held in Strasbourg on 12 April 2011.

case_name: CASE OF KHONIAKINA v. GEORGIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Khoniakina v. Georgia* (Application no. 17767/08)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mrs. Adelina Khoniakina, a Georgian national born in 1926 and a retired judge of the Supreme Court of Georgia. *   **Respondent State:** Georgia, represented by the Ministry of Justice. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Mrs. Khoniakina served as a Supreme Court judge from 1956 until her retirement on age grounds in May 2000. Under the original version of Section 36 of the Act on the Supreme Court of Georgia, she was granted a life-long pension equal to her final salary (GEL 1,073). This provision included an "adjustment clause" stipulating that her pension would increase in line with any future salary rises of active Supreme Court judges. Between 2001 and 2005, Section 36 was amended multiple times. The adjustment clause was removed in March 2001, reintroduced in a modified form in March 2005, and ultimately replaced by an amendment on December 23, 2005 (effective January 1, 2006). This final amendment replaced the adjustable pension with a flat-rate State compensation of GEL 1,200 for retired Supreme Court judges and was explicitly given retroactive effect. #### 3. Procedural History
The applicant initiated two separate sets of domestic proceedings:
*   **First Pension Dispute (2004–2006):** The applicant sued the State Social Insurance Fund, challenging the retroactive application of the 2001 amendment that had removed her adjustment rights. In February 2006, the Supreme Court of Georgia ruled in her favor, ordering the Fund to pay her pension arrears up to December 2005 based on the original adjustable scheme. One member of the bench, Judge S., dissented, arguing that the retroactive legislative changes did not violate legal certainty. *   **Second Pension Dispute (2006–2007):** Following the implementation of the December 2005 amendment capping her pension at GEL 1,200, the applicant filed a new lawsuit. The Tbilisi City Court and the Tbilisi Regional Court dismissed her claims, holding that Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 does not guarantee a pension of a specific amount. In October 2007, a Supreme Court bench—which included Judge S.—declared her cassation appeal inadmissible. The applicant challenged the decision, arguing Judge S. should have been disqualified for bias due to his prior dissenting opinion. In December 2007, the Supreme Court rejected her challenge, finding no evidence of bias. #### 4. Applicant's Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained of:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Fair Trial):** She alleged that the participation of Judge S. in the examination of her second pension dispute violated the requirement of tribunal impartiality, given that he had already expressed an unfavorable opinion on the core legal issue in his previous dissent. *   **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of Property):** She argued that the retroactive application of the December 2005 amendment arbitrarily deprived her of her vested proprietary right to an adjustable pension, violated the principle of legal certainty, and forced her to bear an individual and excessive burden. #### 5. Government's Position
The Government contested the applicant's claims:
*   **Regarding Article 6 § 1:** They argued that the two pension disputes were distinct legal matters involving different facts and statutory provisions. They maintained that Judge S.'s participation complied with domestic law and did not objectively justify any apprehension of bias. *   **Regarding Article 1 of Protocol No. 1:** They asserted that the state enjoys a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy. The 2005 reform aimed to ensure the sustainability of the public budget and rationalize public spending during a period of significant public-sector salary increases. They emphasized that the applicant's capped pension of GEL 1,200 preserved the essence of her entitlement, exceeded her final active salary, and remained nearly twelve times higher than the average national retirement pension, thereby maintaining a fair balance.

case_name: CASE OF KESKINEN AND VELJEKSET KESKINEN OY v. FINLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Keskinen and Veljekset Keskinen Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 34721/09)

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicants:** Mr. Vesa Petteri Keskinen (a Finnish national born in 1967) and Veljekset Keskinen Oy (a Finnish limited liability company). Both are based in Töysä, Finland, and were represented by lawyer Mr. Esa Mäntynen. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Finland, represented by its Agent, Mr. Arto Kosonen of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In February 2005, the applicants organized an ice fishing competition, charging an entrance fee of 20 euros. This was the seventh time they had run the event. For the 2005 competition, the applicants rented a lake and stocked it with 5,551 marked salmon of varying weights (ranging from one to five kilograms). While the primary tournament winners were determined by the volume of fish caught, participants who caught any of the marked salmon won specific prizes corresponding to the fish's weight. The prizes ranged from 200-euro gift certificates for a one-kilogram salmon, up to a grand prize of one million euros for the single five-kilogram salmon. The mass event attracted 27,731 participants, and 2,188 marked salmon were caught, resulting in the distribution of numerous gift certificates. Prior to the event, the Ministry of the Interior had raised concerns. Regarding a previous iteration of the competition in 2003, the Ministry concluded the event was partially an illegal lottery under the Lotteries Act, though no legal action was taken. In January 2005, the Ministry again warned the applicants and local police that the upcoming competition might constitute an unauthorized lottery because the distribution of marked fish prizes was heavily dependent on chance. Although the applicants informed the police of the event in advance, the authorities did not exercise their right to prohibit it. #### 3. Procedural History (Domestic Courts)
In 2006, the public prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings. The first applicant was charged with organizing an illegal lottery without a permit, and the prosecutor requested that the profits gained by the applicant company from the event be forfeited to the State. On June 5, 2006, the Seinäjoki District Court held an oral hearing and dismissed all charges and the forfeiture request. The court agreed that the event constituted an illegal lottery, but concluded that the first applicant’s mistake of law was excusable given the lack of clarity in the legislation, the history of the event, and the fact that authorities had not intervened to stop it. The public prosecutor appealed to the Vaasa Appeal Court, requesting an oral hearing to examine Ministry officials regarding the applicants' intent and to assess evidence concerning the forfeiture of profits. The applicants also appealed regarding legal costs and requested an oral hearing to present witnesses on the organization of the competition and the company's financial outcomes. On August 8, 2007, the Vaasa Appeal Court rejected the requests for an oral hearing, determining that the facts and written evidence were already sufficiently clear. Without holding a hearing, the Appeal Court convicted the first applicant of breaching lottery provisions, sentencing him to 50 day-fines (13,300 euros), and ordered the forfeiture of the company's profits. #### 4. Applicants' Allegations and Proceedings before the ECtHR
The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on June 30, 2009. They alleged under Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) that their rights were violated because the Vaasa Appeal Court convicted the first applicant and ordered the forfeiture of the company's profits without holding an oral hearing. The application was communicated to the Finnish Government on June 28, 2010. (The provided text does not detail the Government's specific substantive arguments on the merits of the Article 6 complaint).

case_name: CASE OF X v. FINLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: X v. Finland

#### Parties
The applicant, X, is a retired Finnish paediatrician born in 1943. The respondent party is the Republic of Finland. #### Key Factual Circumstances
In 1995, X examined a child, V, and suspected she had been sexually abused by her father. In June 2000, V was taken into public care. In December 2000, V’s mother failed to return V to her care centre and brought her to X’s practice. V remained missing until April 2001. X was subsequently arrested and charged with aiding and abetting the aggravated deprivation of V’s liberty, having allegedly assisted the mother and helped secure accommodation for them. During the criminal proceedings, the District Court ordered X to undergo a psychiatric assessment. X went into hiding to avoid the assessment but was arrested in October 2004 and placed in Vanha Vaasa Hospital. The assessment concluded that X suffered from a delusional disorder, lacked criminal responsibility at the time of the alleged offense, and required a guardian for the trial. In February 2005, the Forensic Psychiatry Board ordered X’s involuntary hospital care. While hospitalized, X was subjected to the forcible administration of antipsychotic medication despite her physical and verbal resistance. She was discharged in January 2006, and her involuntary care was officially terminated in June 2006. #### Procedural History
In March 2005, the District Court appointed X's public defender as her guardian for the criminal proceedings against her will. In April 2005, the District Court found X responsible for aiding and abetting but refrained from sentencing her due to her lack of criminal responsibility. X’s guardian appealed, and X filed her own appeal requesting an oral hearing and the examination of 18 witnesses. The Court of Appeal rejected her requests as manifestly unnecessary and upheld the judgment. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in February 2006. Regarding her involuntary care, X appealed the initial confinement order. In October 2005, the Supreme Administrative Court held an oral hearing and dismissed her appeal, finding the diagnosis of delusional disorder reliable and involuntary care justified. Subsequent hospital decisions to continue her involuntary care were also upheld on appeal. #### The Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, X alleged under Article 6 of the Convention that she did not receive a fair hearing because she was denied an oral hearing regarding the appointment of her guardian and was unable to examine witnesses on her behalf. Under Articles 5 and 8, she argued that her involuntary confinement and the forcible administration of medication were unlawful and unnecessary. Under Article 13, she claimed she lacked an effective remedy to challenge the forced medication. #### The Government’s Position
The Government contested the allegations, arguing that X’s involuntary confinement was lawful, necessary, and proportionate under the Mental Health Act. They maintained that her delusional disorder was a serious psychosis that endangered her health and potentially the health of others, and that outpatient treatment was inadequate. #### European Court of Human Rights Proceedings
The application was lodged on 30 September 2004. In May 2009, the Court notified the Government of the application. The Court declared the complaint concerning X's psychiatric assessment inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, while declaring the complaints concerning her involuntary care, forced medication, and the fairness of the domestic proceedings admissible.

case_name: CASE OF HARDY AND MAILE v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicants are Ms. Alison Hardy and Mr. Rodney Maile, British nationals residing in Milford Haven, Wales, who were members of "Safe Haven," a local resident group opposed to the development of liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals. The respondent is the Government of the United Kingdom. ### Factual Circumstances
The case concerns the authorization, construction, and operation of two major LNG terminals at Milford Haven harbour: the Dragon and South Hook sites. Operating these terminals required planning permissions, hazardous substances consents, and compliance with major accident hazard regulations. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE), a statutory consultee, assessed the land-based and jetty-based risks of the projects but did not evaluate marine-based risks, such as those from LNG ships transiting the harbour or moored but not attached to the jetty. The Milford Haven Port Authority (MHPA) held statutory responsibility for marine safety and navigation within the harbour. While MHPA participated in various risk assessments and simulation exercises with the developers and advised local planning authorities that the operations could be conducted safely, it refused to publicly disclose several of its technical safety reports, citing commercial confidentiality. ### Applicants' Allegations
The applicants alleged that the United Kingdom had failed in its duties under Articles 2 (right to life) and 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, they argued that the authorities failed to properly assess the marine risks of the LNG operations—particularly the potential consequences of a major LNG release from a delivery ship, which they argued could form a flammable gas cloud threatening the local population. They also complained under Article 8 about the lack of public dissemination of the safety and risk assessment reports. Additionally, under Article 6 § 1, they alleged that their right to a fair trial was violated by the domestic courts' refusal to make disclosure orders and by a Court of Appeal panel's failure to recuse itself during reopening proceedings. ### Government's Position
The Government argued that Article 8 was inapplicable because no environmental pollution had occurred and the probability of a major marine accident was extremely small. They maintained that a robust, multi-layered regulatory framework was in place and that the planning authorities had properly relied on the expert advice of the HSE and MHPA. They contended that sufficient safety information had been made public through environmental statements and public exhibitions. Finally, they argued the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, as they brought their judicial review challenges out of time and did not seek to have the consents revoked through available administrative channels. ### Procedural History
In March 2005, the applicants sought judicial review of the planning permissions and hazardous substances consents. The High Court refused leave due to undue delay and potential prejudice to the operators. In March 2006, the Court of Appeal upheld this refusal. However, the Court of Appeal's judgment contained a factual error, mistakenly stating that the HSE had assessed ship-based releases. Although the HSE subsequently corrected this statement, the Court of Appeal refused the applicants' application to reopen the appeal under CPR Part 52.17, ruling that the error was not material to its decision on delay. Separately, the applicants requested safety reports from MHPA under the Environmental Information Regulations. Following a complaint, the Information Commissioner ordered the disclosure of two key reports in March 2007, and MHPA subsequently provided redacted copies. The first applicant's subsequent judicial review challenge regarding MHPA's refusal to disclose further documents was dismissed by the domestic courts in late 2007. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 July 2007.

case_name: CASE OF H. v. FINLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *H. v. Finland* (Application no. 37359/09)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Ms H., a Finnish national born in 1963. Born male, she underwent gender reassignment surgery in 2009 and lives as a woman. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Finland. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant married a woman in 1996, and the couple had a child in 2002. In 2006, the applicant was diagnosed as transgender and has lived as a woman since that time. Although she successfully changed her first names, passport, and driver’s license in 2006, her official identity number continued to indicate that she was male. In June 2007, the applicant requested the local Register Office to change her male identity number to a female one. The Register Office refused the request, citing the Act on Confirmation of the Gender of a Transsexual. Under this Act, gender confirmation is conditional on the applicant being unmarried or, if married, obtaining the spouse's consent to convert the marriage into a civil partnership. The applicant’s wife did not consent to this conversion, as both spouses wished to remain married. They argued that a divorce or conversion to a civil partnership was contrary to their religious convictions and that a civil partnership would not provide the same security as marriage, potentially affecting their child's legal status. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
The applicant appealed the Register Office's refusal to the Helsinki Administrative Court, which rejected the appeal in May 2008. The applicant then appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, arguing that the state was violating her right to privacy by forcing her to choose between maintaining her marriage and obtaining an accurate identity number. In February 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected her appeal, ruling that Finnish law reserved marriage for opposite-sex couples and that the legal and economic consequences of a civil partnership were essentially comparable to marriage. Following her gender reassignment surgery, the applicant filed an extraordinary appeal, which the Supreme Administrative Court refused in August 2010. #### 4. The Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that her rights under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention had been violated. The Court also decided *ex officio* to examine the application under Article 12 (right to marry). The applicant argued that making the legal recognition of her gender conditional on converting her marriage into a civil partnership was an unnecessary and disproportionate interference with her private and family life. She contended that she should not be forced to end her marriage to secure her right to privacy, and that the difference in treatment between married and unmarried transgender individuals lacked objective and reasonable justification. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Finnish Government contested the applicant's claims. They argued that the domestic measures were prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aims of protecting health, morals, and the rights and freedoms of others. The Government maintained that the system was not disproportionate, as the applicant could obtain a female identity number without divorcing if her spouse consented to converting the marriage into a civil partnership. They emphasized that civil partnerships in Finland provided legal protections almost identical to marriage, and that the applicant's parental rights and obligations toward her child would remain unaffected by the conversion.

case_name: CASE OF KAPERZYNSKI v. POLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Kaperzyński v. Poland* (Application no. 43206/07)

#### 1. The Main Parties
* **The Applicant:** Mr. Przemysław Kaperzyński, a Polish national who, at the material time, was the editor-in-chief of the local weekly newspaper *Iławski Tydzień*. * **The Respondent:** The Republic of Poland, represented by the Polish Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 17 October 2005, *Iławski Tydzień* published an article co-authored by the applicant entitled "Municipality in danger; authorities fail to see problem." The article criticized the state of the sewage system in the Iława municipality, alleging that the sanitary situation posed significant public health risks, that municipal authorities were dealing with the issues incompetently, and that the mayor had failed to properly manage the situation. On the same day, the mayor of Iława sent a letter to the newspaper. The letter criticized the article's tone, questioned the applicant's professional motives, and requested the publication of a rectification under the Press Act of 1984, detailing the municipality's ongoing and planned infrastructure projects. The applicant did not reply to the mayor's letter and did not publish it. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
The municipality of Iława initiated private criminal proceedings against the applicant, accusing him of failing to publish a rectification or reply as required by section 46 § 1 of the Press Act. The applicant argued that the mayor's letter did not meet the statutory requirements of a "rectification" because it lacked objectivity, contained personal attacks, and exceeded the permissible length. On 13 December 2006, the Elbląg District Court convicted the applicant. The court sentenced him to a suspended four-month restriction of liberty (involving twenty hours of community service per month), banned him from practicing journalism for two years, and ordered the judgment to be publicly displayed at the municipal office. The court found that the applicant had a clear statutory obligation to either publish the response or formally notify the mayor of the reasons for his refusal, neither of which he did. The applicant appealed the decision, but on 29 March 2007, the Elbląg Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. #### 4. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that his criminal conviction breached his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. He argued that:
* Enforcing journalistic obligations through criminal sanctions is incompatible with a free press in a democratic society. * The decision not to publish the mayor's letter was a matter of editorial policy protected by Article 10. * The domestic courts failed to assess whether the mayor's letter actually met the legal definition of a rectification. * The sanctions imposed—particularly the community service and the two-year ban on practicing journalism—were highly disproportionate, lacked a pressing social need, and forced him to leave his profession. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Polish Government contested the application on both procedural and substantive grounds:
* **Admissibility:** They argued the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he did not file a constitutional complaint challenging the Press Act provisions, nor did he lodge a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. * **Merits:** They contended that the interference was prescribed by law and served the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others and the freedom of the press. They argued that the applicant's refusal to publish the response prevented a balanced public debate and blocked the mayor from presenting factual information to the local community. The Government maintained that the interference was necessary and that the suspended sentence and professional ban were proportionate.

case_name: CASE OF BALOGUN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Balogun v. the United Kingdom* involves Mr. Moshood Abiola Balogun, a Nigerian national born in 1986, and the Government of the United Kingdom. ### Factual Circumstances
The applicant claims to have arrived in the United Kingdom at the age of three, though official records first document his presence in 1994 when he was eight. Following allegations of physical abuse by his aunt, he was placed in foster care in 2002 and was subsequently granted indefinite leave to remain in December 2003. Between 2004 and 2005, the applicant accumulated several criminal convictions, including drug possession and handling stolen goods. In February 2007, at age twenty, he was convicted of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply and was sentenced to three years' imprisonment. In October 2007, the Home Office notified him of its intention to deport him. Following the rejection of his subsequent human rights appeals, the applicant attempted suicide in August 2009 and was treated for moderate depression. He was taken into immigration detention in November 2009, during which he made a further minor self-harm attempt. ### Domestic Procedural History
The applicant appealed the deportation decision, but the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal dismissed his appeal in March 2008. The Tribunal found that he did not have a protected family life in the UK, as his relationships with his girlfriend, aunts, and half-brother did not establish the requisite elements of dependence. It also concluded that his deportation was a proportionate interference with his private life when balanced against the public interest. A deportation order was signed in October 2008. The applicant’s subsequent request to revoke the order was rejected by the Secretary of State, and his application for judicial review was refused by the High Court on October 30, 2009. He was detained on November 10, 2009, and removal directions were set for November 19, 2009. ### Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on November 13, 2009. On November 18, 2009, the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that the applicant should not be expelled to Nigeria pending the Court’s decision. ### The Parties' Submissions

#### The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant alleged that his deportation to Nigeria would violate Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. Under Article 3, he argued that the deportation would pose a severe risk to his life due to his mental health history and suicidal ideation. Under Article 8, he contended that deportation would disproportionately interfere with his private and family life, emphasizing his residence in the UK since early childhood, his lack of ties to Nigeria, and his established relationships, education, and social ties in the UK. #### The Government's Position
The Government argued that the Article 3 complaint was inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies, as the applicant had not raised his suicide risk during his domestic appeals or judicial review proceedings. On the merits, they asserted that adequate protective measures would be implemented during detention and transit to mitigate any self-harm risk, and that sufficient psychiatric care was available in Nigeria. Regarding Article 8, the Government maintained that the applicant did not have a family life in the UK and that the interference with his private life was proportionate to the legitimate aim of preventing crime, given the gravity of his adult drug offenses.

case_name: CASE OF SOLOMAKHIN v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Solomakhin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24429/03)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicant was Mr. Sergey Dmitriyevich Solomakhin, a Ukrainian national born in 1964 who lived in Donetsk. Following his death in September 2010, his mother, Mrs. Vera Petrovna Solomakhina, was permitted by the Court to pursue the application on his behalf. The respondent party was the Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 23 November 1998, the applicant sought medical assistance at Donetsk City Hospital No. 16 and was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease. On 27 November, he was tested for susceptibility to diphtheria antigens, showing no susceptibility. The following day, 28 November 1998, he was vaccinated against diphtheria. From late December 1998 onward, the applicant spent more than six months in various medical institutions receiving treatment for several chronic diseases, including pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis, and colitis. On 4 February 1999, the hospital’s Chief Doctor reprimanded the attending doctor and nurse for vaccinating the applicant despite his objections and while he was being treated for an acute respiratory infection, ordering them to retake a test on vaccination regulations. #### 3. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
On 26 April 1999, the applicant instituted civil proceedings in the Budyonnovskiy District Court in Donetsk against the local public health department and the hospital, seeking compensation for damage to his health. Between May 2000 and February 2003, four separate medical expert examinations were conducted regarding his allegations. On 2 June 2003, the District Court ruled against the applicant. Relying on the medical expert reports, the court established that there was no causal link between the vaccination and the applicant's chronic diseases. It also found that the applicant had no acute symptoms of disease at the time of vaccination, that the regional epidemiological situation required the vaccination, and that no physical force had been used. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court upheld this judgment on 19 March 2008 and 22 August 2008, respectively. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 22 July 2003. On 6 May 2008, the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to examine the remaining complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. #### 4. The Applicant's Main Allegations
Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, the applicant complained that the domestic court proceedings, which lasted over nine years across three levels of jurisdiction, exceeded a "reasonable time." 

Under Article 8, the applicant alleged that the vaccination constituted an unjustified interference with his physical integrity. He claimed he was vaccinated against his will during an acute illness, that the vaccine used was expired and of poor quality, and that this medical intervention directly caused his chronic health conditions. He also alleged that medical staff and domestic authorities had falsified his medical records to conceal the malpractice. #### 5. The Government's Position
Regarding Article 6 § 1, the Government contended that the length of the proceedings was justified by the particular complexity of the case, which required extensive forensic medical examinations of the applicant's health and medical files. Regarding Article 8, the Government acknowledged that the compulsory vaccination constituted an interference with the applicant's private life but argued it was justified. They submitted that the vaccination was compulsory under domestic law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting public health during a diphtheria epidemic. They emphasized that the applicant's suitability for the vaccine had been checked beforehand, no physical coercion was used, and subsequent domestic medical and judicial reviews confirmed that the vaccine had no causal link to the applicant's chronic illnesses.

case_name: CASE OF ALEKSEJEVA  v. LATVIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: Aleksejeva v. Latvia (Application no. 21780/07)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicant is Ms. Jeļena Aleksejeva, a Latvian national born in 1984. The respondent party is the Republic of Latvia, represented by its Government Agent. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In October 2006, the applicant was detained in Iļģuciema Prison, the only female correctional facility in Latvia. Her mother had worked at the prison for approximately twenty-five years and was serving as an assistant to the prison governor at the time of the applicant's arrival, retiring immediately thereafter. Upon her admission, prison staff advised the applicant to conceal her mother's identity from other inmates and staff due to potential safety risks. A photograph of her mother was confiscated to prevent her family ties from being discovered. The applicant was initially placed in a two-person cell with a former bailiff but interacted with the general prison population during daily activities. She claimed to live in constant fear of exposure and later alleged that an inmate had made veiled threats after learning of her family background. In December 2006, a domestic court rejected the applicant's request to postpone her sentence. In February 2007, she petitioned the Ombudsman for a transfer to an open prison to ensure her safety. Prison management indicated that complete isolation was the only way to guarantee separation, which both parties agreed was undesirable. In April 2007, the applicant signed a form agreeing to share a cell in a medium-security regime, where she was subsequently placed with first-time offenders. The Ombudsman later concluded that the prison's security measures were sufficient. Regarding visitation, the applicant was initially denied long-term visits from her partner because her divorce from her husband was not yet finalized. Following her divorce in April 2007, these visits were permitted. Additionally, her mother did not visit her in prison because staff warned that such visits would expose their relationship; instead, they communicated via telephone, and the applicant was later granted temporary leave to visit her mother. The applicant was transferred to an open prison in January 2008 and subsequently released. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged a violation of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), arguing that the prison administration failed to adequately separate vulnerable inmates like herself from the general population, leaving her in constant fear for her safety. She also alleged a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) due to the restrictions and practical obstacles that prevented her from receiving visits from her partner and her mother. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government contested the allegations. Regarding Article 3, they argued that the prison administration was fully aware of the applicant's situation and took proactive measures to ensure her safety, such as housing her with a former bailiff and first-time prisoners. They also noted that she had consented in writing to sharing a cell. The Government maintained that her fears were hypothetical and lacked evidence of actual ill-treatment meeting the minimum severity threshold required by the Convention. #### 5. Procedural History
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on April 13, 2007. On June 21, 2007, the Court communicated the application to the Latvian Government and decided to examine the admissibility and merits of the case concurrently.

case_name: CASE OF VIDGEN v. THE NETHERLANDS
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Vidgen v. the Netherlands*

**Parties**  
The case involves Mr. Nicholas Otto Vidgen, a British national born in 1958, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands. **Key Factual Circumstances**  
On 5 September 2003, the Utrecht Regional Court found the applicant guilty of co-perpetrating the illegal transport of MDMA (ecstasy) from the Netherlands to Germany, with the ultimate intention of shipping the substances to Australia. The drugs were hidden inside the cylinders and crankcases of motor car engines destined for "H. Autosport," a Sydney-based business established by the applicant. Throughout the domestic proceedings, the applicant admitted his involvement in shipping the car engines but denied any knowledge of the hidden drugs, focusing his defense on his lack of criminal intent. The prosecution’s evidence regarding the applicant's intent relied heavily on pre-trial statements made by a co-suspect, M., to German prosecutors and Dutch police. M. had linked the applicant to the smuggling scheme and to a handwritten note containing the Sydney business address. Although the applicant repeatedly requested to question M., M. refused to answer substantive questions during the pre-trial phase and at subsequent hearings, invoking his right to remain silent. **Procedural History**  
Following his conviction and five-year prison sentence by the Utrecht Regional Court, the applicant appealed to the Amsterdam Court of Appeal. In August 2004, the Court of Appeal held a hearing where M. was summoned as a witness. M. again refused to answer substantive questions, invoking his right not to self-incriminate due to pending extradition proceedings. In December 2004, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal, ruling that M.'s refusal to testify did not violate the defense's rights because his prior statements were sufficiently corroborated by other evidence, including intercepted communications and the confessions of another co-suspect, A. The applicant subsequently appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands. The Procurator General issued an advisory opinion recommending that the appeal be upheld, arguing that the conviction was based decisively on M.'s untested pre-trial statements in violation of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, on 6 June 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the conviction, though it reduced the applicant's sentence by six months due to the excessive length of the domestic proceedings. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 17 July 2006. **Applicant’s Allegations**  
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention. He argued that his criminal conviction was based solely, or at least to a decisive extent, on the statements of a witness (M.) whom he had not been able to examine or cross-examine at any stage of the proceedings. **Government’s Position**  
The Dutch Government denied any violation of the Convention, maintaining that the proceedings as a whole were fair. They argued that the domestic courts had provided the applicant with every reasonable opportunity to question M. The Government emphasized that M.'s silence was a legitimate exercise of his privilege against self-incrimination, which the courts had to respect. Furthermore, they asserted that the conviction did not rely solely on M.'s statements, as there was sufficient corroborating evidence—such as intercepted communications and observations—to support the domestic courts' findings.

case_name: CASE OF J.M. v. DENMARK
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *J.M. v. Denmark* (Application no. 34421/09)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. J.M., a Danish national born in 1991 who was fifteen years old at the time of his arrest. *   **Respondent Government:** The Kingdom of Denmark. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 13 September 2007, the applicant was arrested in Greenland and charged with the rape and homicide of an eighty-five-year-old woman in Aalborg, Denmark. Upon his arrest, the applicant admitted to both charges. He was subsequently transferred to Denmark and placed in "Grenen," a secure residential institution for young offenders, which provided structured daily routines and educational support as an alternative to standard prison. The applicant’s pre-trial detention was extended by the domestic courts approximately every four weeks. The primary factor driving the length of the detention was the preparation of forensic psychiatric evaluations to determine the most appropriate legal sanction, given his status as a minor and potential mental development issues. This process became complex due to differing medical opinions. Over the course of the proceedings, the authorities obtained two forensic psychiatric reports, two assessments from the Medico-Legal Council, and an opinion from the Joint Council for the Mentally Disabled to resolve whether the applicant should face ordinary imprisonment or specialized socio-psychiatric care. On 1 July 2008, while the applicant was in custody, Section 768a of the Danish Administration of Justice Act came into effect. This statute limited the pre-trial detention of juveniles to a maximum of eight months unless "very special circumstances" applied. On 11 September 2008, the applicant objected to any further extension of his detention, citing this new statutory limit. The Aalborg City Court extended the detention nonetheless, ruling that "very special circumstances" existed because of the extreme gravity of the crimes and the necessity of resolving the appropriate sanction. This decision was upheld on appeal. On 27 January 2009, the City Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The court rejected the applicant's request for a sentence reduction based on the length of the proceedings, concluding that the psychiatric evaluations were of vital significance and that the prosecution had acted with due diligence. The High Court of Western Denmark upheld the conviction and sentence on 4 June 2009. In total, the applicant’s pre-trial detention lasted one year, four months, and fourteen days. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that the length of his pre-trial detention was excessive and routinely extended in violation of Article 5 § 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He argued that the Danish authorities failed to demonstrate a concrete, ongoing threat to public order that would justify detaining a minor. He further contended that the fourteen-month psychiatric evaluation process was unnecessarily prolonged and that the resulting delays and disagreements among medical experts were entirely attributable to the State. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Danish Government contested the applicant's allegations, maintaining that the pre-trial detention was necessary and compliant with the Convention. They argued that the extreme gravity of the offenses, coupled with the applicant's confession, meant that his release pending trial would have severely offended the public sense of justice. The Government emphasized that the domestic courts had actively utilized a less restrictive alternative to standard prison by placing him in a specialized youth facility. Finally, they asserted that the complex psychiatric evaluations were indispensable for determining the correct sanction for a juvenile and were pursued with continuous diligence and no significant periods of inactivity. #### 5. Procedural History
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 June 2009. On 22 March 2010, the Court communicated the application to the Danish Government and decided to examine the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The Court subsequently declared the applicant's separate complaints under Article 5 § 1 inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies, while declaring the complaint under Article 5 § 3 admissible.

case_name: CASE OF BOUKROUROU AND OTHERS v. FRANCE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Boukrourou and Others v. France*

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicants are six French nationals: Abdelkader Boukrourou, Samira Mehigueni, Fatiha Hassioui, Karim Boukrourou, Lahoucin Boukrourou, and Yamina Boukrourou. They are the brother, sister, widow, brother, father, and mother of the deceased, M.B. The respondent party is the Government of France. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 12 November 2009, M.B., a 41-year-old man with a history of psychiatric disorders, entered a pharmacy in Valentigney to exchange medication. He became highly agitated and incoherent, prompting the pharmacy staff to call the police. Four police officers arrived at 4:53 p.m. When M.B. refused to leave, the officers physically forced him out. During the struggle outside, M.B. fell to the ground, was punched twice in the abdomen by an officer using "diversionary blows," and was handcuffed. M.B. was then forced into a police van, where he continued to resist. To immobilize him, one officer positioned himself across M.B.’s shoulders, another stood on his buttocks, and a third held his legs. At 4:58 p.m., five minutes after their arrival, the officers requested emergency medical assistance. By the time the fire brigade arrived, M.B. had calmed down, but his heart had stopped. Despite resuscitation efforts, he was pronounced dead at 6:02 p.m. Subsequent medical and autopsy reports concluded that M.B. died of sudden cardiac arrest caused by a coronary spasm, triggered by intense physical and emotional stress acting on a pre-existing, asymptomatic heart condition (70% arterial stenosis). The reports ruled out mechanical asphyxiation. Conversely, a report by the national Ombudsman criticized the police intervention, describing the immobilization techniques in the van as dangerous, disproportionate, and a serious infringement of human dignity, and recommended disciplinary action against the officers. #### 3. Procedural History
A domestic judicial investigation for manslaughter was opened in December 2009, and the applicants joined the proceedings as civil parties. In March 2012, the four officers were charged with manslaughter. However, in December 2012, the investigating judges dismissed the charges, finding no case to answer. They ruled that the force used was necessary and proportionate, and that M.B.'s death was unforeseeable. The Investigation Division of the Besançon Court of Appeal upheld this decision in October 2013, and the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants' appeal on points of law in November 2014. The applicants subsequently lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 May 2015. #### 4. Applicants' Allegations
Before the European Court, the applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) of the Convention. They argued that the police acted negligently, lacked training for dealing with vulnerable individuals, and used disproportionate force. They asserted that this physical coercion directly generated the intense stress that triggered M.B.'s fatal heart failure. #### 5. Government's Position
The French Government contested these allegations, maintaining that the use of force was absolutely necessary and proportionate to manage M.B.'s dangerous and highly agitated behavior. They emphasized that medical experts ruled out a direct causal link between the physical restraint and the death, and argued that the officers fulfilled their positive obligations by promptly summoning emergency medical services within five minutes of their arrival.

case_name: CASE OF EGILL EINARSSON v. ICELAND
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Egill Einarsson v. Iceland* (Application no. 24703/15)

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Egill Einarsson, a well-known Icelandic media personality, blogger, and author. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Iceland. *   **Other Key Party:** "X," an individual who posted the controversial content about the applicant on social media. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant, a prominent public figure in Iceland, was accused of sexual offences, including rape, by two women in late 2011 and early 2012. Following police investigations, the Public Prosecutor dismissed both cases in 2012 on the grounds that the evidence was insufficient to secure a conviction. On November 22, 2012, a leading Icelandic magazine published a front-page interview with the applicant. In the interview, the applicant discussed the rape allegations, asserted his innocence, and claimed the accusations were part of a conspiracy. On the same day, X posted an altered version of the applicant’s front-page photograph on Instagram. X drew an upside-down cross on the applicant’s forehead, wrote the word "loser" across his face, and added the caption: "Fuck you rapist bastard." Although X claimed he believed the post was restricted to a private circle of followers, the account was public, and the image was subsequently featured in an online newspaper article the following day. #### 3. Procedural History (Domestic Courts)
In December 2012, the applicant initiated civil defamation proceedings against X in the District Court of Reykjavík, seeking to have the statement declared null and void and requesting non-pecuniary damages. On November 1, 2013, the District Court ruled against the applicant. The court found that because the applicant was a well-known public figure who actively participated in controversial public debates, he had to tolerate a higher degree of criticism. It concluded that X’s post, taken as a whole, was a value judgment expressing personal dislike rather than a factual statement. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court of Iceland. On November 20, 2014, the Supreme Court upheld the District Court’s decision in a 2-1 majority ruling. The majority agreed that the phrase "rapist bastard" in this context constituted a value judgment and a form of "invective" within a ruthless public debate that the applicant himself had helped instigate. A dissenting minority judge, however, argued that the term was a grave factual insinuation of a serious criminal offence which the applicant should not have to tolerate, particularly since the criminal investigation against him had been dismissed. #### 4. The Applicant’s Allegations before the ECtHR
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the Supreme Court’s judgment violated his right to respect for his private life under Article 8 of the Convention. He argued that calling someone a "rapist" is a factual allegation capable of proof, not a value judgment. He maintained that because the criminal charges against him had been officially dismissed, the public dissemination of this statement severely damaged his reputation and moral integrity, and that the domestic courts had failed to protect his rights. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Icelandic Government contested the applicant's claims. They argued that the domestic courts had carefully balanced the applicant's Article 8 rights against X’s right to freedom of expression under Article 10, in accordance with the criteria established in the Court's case-law. The Government emphasized that the applicant was a highly controversial public figure who frequently provoked public debate regarding women and sexual freedom. They contended that X’s post was an individual's value judgment on a matter of intense public interest—the justice system's handling of sexual violence—and argued that the domestic courts should be afforded a wide margin of appreciation in resolving such disputes between private parties.

case_name: CASE OF MAŽUKNA v. LITHUANIA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Mažukna v. Lithuania* (Application no. 72092/12)

**1. The Main Parties**
*   **Applicant:** Mr Aleksandras Mažukna, a Lithuanian national born in 1959. Following his death on 9 January 2016, his son and legal heir, Mr Marius Mažukna, expressed the wish to pursue the proceedings on his father's behalf. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Lithuania, represented by its Agent, Ms K. Bubnytė. **2. Key Factual Circumstances**
On 17 April 2007, the applicant was working as a welder for a company at a factory construction site in Klaipėda. While he and two other workers were standing on scaffolding approximately two metres above the ground, the scaffolding collapsed, causing them to fall. The applicant suffered severe injuries, including multiple facial bone fractures and a deep head wound that left permanent facial scarring and disfigurement. The State Labour Inspectorate initially declined to investigate, but later issued conflicting conclusions. While one inspector initially blamed the applicant's own recklessness, the Inspectorate ultimately concluded in June 2009 that the scaffolding had not complied with safety requirements, the workers had not been properly instructed, and the employer had breached safety regulations. **3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations**
The applicant alleged that the Lithuanian authorities had failed to carry out an effective and prompt investigation into the circumstances of the workplace accident in which he was seriously injured. In his application to the European Court of Human Rights, he relied on Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention. The application was also communicated to the Government under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment). **4. The Government’s Position**
The Lithuanian Government was represented by their Agent. Their specific arguments regarding the merits of the investigation's effectiveness are not detailed in the provided text. **5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment**
*   **Pre-trial Investigation:** The applicant requested a pre-trial investigation in September 2007. Over the next three years, the prosecutor discontinued the investigation three separate times (in October 2008, July 2009, and May 2010), repeatedly finding that the accident was caused by the workers' own recklessness. *   **Court Interventions:** Following each discontinuance, the Klaipėda District Court overruled the prosecutor’s decisions and ordered the investigation to be reopened, noting that the employer had a legal duty to ensure safe working conditions. A forensic expert report in February 2010 confirmed that the scaffolding was unsuitable for the weight of the platform being handled. *   **Indictment and Trial:** In October 2010, the construction manager, V.J.S., was declared a suspect. An indictment was issued in April 2011 for violating work safety requirements under Article 176 § 1 of the Criminal Code. *   **Statute of Limitations:** The trial before the Klaipėda District Court faced numerous delays due to absent witnesses and the prolonged illness of the accused. On 14 May 2012, the court terminated the criminal case against V.J.S. because the five-year statute of limitations had expired. The court did not rule on the applicant's civil claim for damages. The applicant's subsequent appeal was rejected on procedural grounds. *   **Proceedings before the ECtHR:** The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 November 2012. The case was communicated to the Lithuanian Government on 10 September 2014.

case_name: CASE OF HAARDE v. ICELAND
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Haarde v. Iceland* (Application no. 66847/12)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Geir Hilmar Haarde, an Icelandic national born in 1951, who served as the Prime Minister of Iceland from 2006 to 2009. The respondent party is the Government of the Republic of Iceland. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In October 2008, the Icelandic banking system collapsed, leading to the state seizing control of the country’s three largest banks. In December 2008, the Icelandic Parliament (*Althingi*) established a Special Investigation Commission (SIC) to investigate the causes of the collapse. Released in April 2010, the SIC’s report criticized several public officials, including the applicant and three other cabinet ministers, for negligence in responding to the impending financial crisis. In response, Parliament established an ad hoc Parliamentary Review Committee (PRC) to assess ministerial accountability under the Ministerial Accountability Act. In September 2010, the PRC proposed commencing impeachment proceedings against all four ministers. However, following individual parliamentary votes, Parliament decided to impeach only the applicant. #### 3. Procedural History Up to the European Court
The applicant was formally indicted in May 2011 before the Court of Impeachment (*Landsdómur*), a specialized constitutional court. The indictment consisted of two main sections:
* **Count 1 (subdivided into 1.1–1.5):** Alleged various omissions and neglect of ministerial duties to reduce the financial risk to the state. * **Count 2:** Alleged a failure to implement Article 17 of the Constitution, which mandates holding ministerial meetings on "important government matters."

The applicant requested a dismissal of the entire case. On October 3, 2011, the Court of Impeachment dismissed Counts 1.1 and 1.2 due to a lack of specificity but allowed the remaining charges to proceed. On April 23, 2012, following a public trial featuring testimony from the applicant and 40 witnesses, the Court of Impeachment delivered its judgment. The court unanimously acquitted the applicant of Counts 1.3, 1.4, and 1.5. However, by a 9-to-6 majority, the court found him guilty under Count 2, ruling that he had failed to hold cabinet meetings on the critical situation of the banking system. The court did not impose any punishment, and the Icelandic State was ordered to pay all of the applicant's legal costs. The judgment was final and not subject to appeal. #### 4. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 7 (no punishment without law). Under Article 6, the applicant argued that:
* The pre-trial stage was deficient because neither the PRC nor the prosecutor conducted an independent criminal investigation or interviewed him. * Parliament’s decision to prosecute him alone was arbitrary and politically motivated. * The charges and the applicable legal provisions (Article 17 of the Constitution and section 8(c) of the Ministerial Accountability Act) were too vague and unpredictable to formulate a proper defense. * His defense counsel was appointed too late in the process. * The prosecutor lacked impartiality because she had previously advised the PRC on the draft indictment. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Government contested the applicant's claims. They first argued that the applicant lacked victim status under Article 34 of the Convention because he was acquitted of the majority of the charges, received no criminal penalty, and had his legal fees fully covered by the state. On the merits, the Government maintained that the proceedings as a whole were fair. They asserted that any pre-trial investigative limitations did not prejudice the trial, as the applicant was able to testify twice and fully present his defense before the Court of Impeachment. They denied that the prosecution was political, noting that the vote did not strictly follow party lines. Finally, they argued that the constitutional requirement to hold meetings on "important government matters" was sufficiently clear and foreseeable to a person in the applicant's position.

case_name: CASE OF TURAL HAJIBEYLI v. AZERBAIJAN
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Tural Hajibeyli v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 69180/11)

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Tural Vagif oglu Hajibeyli, an Azerbaijani national born in 1992 and residing in Baku. He was represented by lawyers Mr. I. Aliyev and Mr. K. Bagirov. *   **Respondent Government:** The Republic of Azerbaijan, represented by its Agent, Mr. Ç. Asgarov. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 12 March 2011, an opposition demonstration was held in central Baku to protest corruption and demand the resignation of the President. Although organizers had notified the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA), the BCEA refused to authorize the central location, proposing an alternative on the outskirts of the city. The organizers proceeded with the demonstration in the center. The applicant attended the event. Shortly after it began, police dispersed the crowd and arrested the applicant. He was charged under the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) with violating rules on holding public assemblies (Article 298) and failing to comply with a lawful order of a police officer (Article 310.1). In August 2014, during unrelated criminal proceedings against the applicant’s representative, Mr. I. Aliyev, domestic authorities searched Mr. Aliyev's office and seized his case files, including the applicant's complete file for the pending European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) application. Following unsuccessful domestic appeals by Mr. Aliyev against the search and seizure, the investigating authorities returned the applicant's file to Mr. Aliyev’s lawyer on 25 October 2014. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that:
*   His arrest and conviction violated his right to freedom of assembly, maintaining that the demonstration was peaceful. *   He was denied access to a lawyer of his choosing and was not served with copies of the administrative-offence report or other case documents. *   The domestic court proceedings were unfair. He claimed that his name was added to the police arrest report later in different handwriting, and that the courts failed to address his requests to conduct a handwriting analysis, examine video and photographic evidence of his arrest, or summon defense witnesses. *   The State-funded lawyers appointed to represent him did not provide active or effective legal assistance. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government’s substantive arguments on the merits of the arrest and trial are not detailed in the provided text. Procedurally, the Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee of the Court. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
*   **First Domestic Trial (12 March 2011):** The Sabail District Court convicted the applicant under Article 310.1 of the CAO and sentenced him to eight days’ administrative detention. *   **First Appeal (18 March 2011):** The Baku Court of Appeal partially granted the applicant's appeal and remitted the case for re-examination, finding that the first-instance court had failed to examine the original police report. *   **Second Domestic Trial (12 April 2011):** The Sabail District Court re-examined the case, heard testimony from two police officers, and sentenced the applicant to seven days’ administrative detention. *   **Second Appeal (28 April 2011):** The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal and upheld the lower court's decision, without addressing his requests to examine video evidence or summon witnesses. *   **Proceedings before the ECtHR:** The applicant lodged his application with the ECtHR on 5 November 2011. On 22 June 2015, the Court communicated the complaints concerning Articles 5, 6, 11, and 13 of the Convention to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Court also rejected the Government's objection to the case being examined by a Committee.

case_name: CASE OF THUO v. CYPRUS
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Thuo v. Cyprus* (Application no. 3869/07) involves Mr. David William Thuo, a Kenyan national (the applicant), and the Republic of Cyprus (the respondent Government). ### Factual Background
The applicant entered Cyprus unlawfully in April 2005. He was arrested shortly thereafter at Larnaca Airport while attempting to travel on a forged passport and was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment. While serving his sentence, he applied for asylum. Upon his release from criminal custody on 14 November 2005, he was immediately re-arrested under immigration detention and deportation orders. He was subsequently held in the immigration detention facilities in Block 10 of Nicosia Central Prisons. His asylum application and subsequent administrative appeal were rejected, and he was deported to Kenya on 9 March 2007. ### The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights were violated. Regarding his deportation on 9 March 2007, he claimed that immigration officers and prison guards verbally abused him with racial slurs and physically assaulted him, including hitting him and pinching his testicles. He further alleged that at Larnaca Airport, officers beat him, stuffed brown paper into his mouth, applied adhesive tape over his mouth and neck, and wrapped bandages around his head, keeping him bound and gagged during the initial part of his flight. He claimed this treatment caused him severe pain and left several of his teeth loose.
