In response, the applicant acknowledged that he had not appealed every single decision but contended that such appeals would have had no realistic prospect of success. ### 5. Procedural History
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on October 7, 2015. On February 9, 2017, the Polish Government was formally given notice of the application. The case was assigned to a Committee of the First Section of the Court, which held private deliberations on the matter on June 16, 2020.

case_name: CASE OF MUGEMANGANGO v. BELGIUM
step1_summary:
### Parties and Background
The case of *Mugemangango v. Belgium* concerns an application lodged against the Kingdom of Belgium by Mr. Germain Mugemangango, a Belgian national and chairman of the Hainaut Province branch of the Workers’ Party of Belgium (PTB). ### Factual Circumstances
In May 2014, the applicant stood as the leading candidate on the PTB-GO! electoral list for the Charleroi constituency in the elections to the Parliament of the Walloon Region (the Walloon Parliament). The list received 16,554 votes, falling fourteen votes short of the quota required to secure a seat under the "related lists" system. Had the list obtained these additional votes, the seat would have been allocated to the applicant. In the same constituency, 21,385 ballot papers were declared blank, spoiled, or disputed. The day after the elections, the applicant requested a recount of the blank, spoiled, and disputed ballots from the local electoral boards. The boards declined jurisdiction and referred him to the Walloon Parliament. The applicant then lodged a formal complaint with the Walloon Parliament, alleging various irregularities during the vote-counting process, including counter fatigue, poor physical conditions, inadequate training of polling officers, and the improper invalidation of valid ballot papers. The Walloon Parliament’s Credentials Committee examined the complaint. After holding a public hearing, the committee voted three-to-one to declare the complaint well-founded and proposed a full recount of the constituency's ballots. However, during a plenary session of the Walloon Parliament, the members voted forty-three to thirty-two to reject the committee's findings. All members of parliament, including those elected in the applicant's constituency whose seats could have been affected by a recount, participated in this vote. The Parliament subsequently approved the credentials of the elected representatives and issued a reasoned decision rejecting the applicant's complaint, finding that the alleged irregularities were either unproven or inherent to the electoral system. ### The Applicant's Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to stand for election) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He argued that the Walloon Parliament lacked the necessary impartiality to examine his complaint, acting as both "judge and party" because its members had direct political interests in the outcome. He further complained of a lack of adequate procedural safeguards, noting the absence of a judicial remedy and the fact that the decision-making plenary body did not grant him a hearing or an adversarial procedure. ### The Government's Position
The Belgian Government contested these allegations, arguing that the electoral process was reliable and that the alleged errors did not affect the outcome. They maintained that the system of parliamentary self-scrutiny is a cornerstone of the separation of powers and parliamentary independence. The Government also asserted that the applicant was afforded sufficient safeguards in practice, as he was heard by the Credentials Committee with legal representation, and the Parliament provided a detailed, reasoned decision. ### Procedural History
The application was lodged on 22 December 2014. It was initially allocated to the Second Section of the Court, which relinquished jurisdiction in favor of the Grand Chamber on 11 June 2019. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission) and the Government of Denmark submitted third-party comments. A public hearing was held before the Grand Chamber on 4 December 2019, after which the Court deliberated on the case.

case_name: CASE OF PROJECT-TRADE D.O.O. v. CROATIA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Project-Trade d.o.o., a commercial company incorporated under Croatian law. The respondent is the Government of the Republic of Croatia. ### Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant company was a shareholder in Croatia Bank (*Croatia banka d.d.*), a privately owned joint-stock company, holding 1,251 shares. Following an expert report indicating that the bank's debts outweighed its share capital, the Croatian National Bank proposed a recovery and restructuring process. On 23 September 1999, the Croatian Government adopted a Decision on the recovery and restructuring of the bank. Under this Decision, all existing shares were revoked and cancelled, and the bank was ordered to issue new shares entirely owned by the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). Between 1999 and 2000, several other shareholders (excluding the applicant) petitioned the Constitutional Court to review the constitutionality of the Government Decision. In January 2003, the Constitutional Court discontinued these proceedings because the underlying legislation had been repealed. However, the court's majority stated that affected shareholders could seek individual judicial protection through civil proceedings. Two dissenting judges contested this, arguing that no effective domestic remedy existed to challenge the Decision. ### The Applicant’s Allegations
The applicant company alleged that the revocation and cancellation of its shares constituted an unjustified deprivation of property. It argued that the bank had been in good standing, that potential losses were incorrectly treated as actual losses, and that the Government Decision was arbitrary. Furthermore, the applicant alleged a violation of its right of access to a court, asserting that domestic courts could not effectively review the validity of the Government Decision, and complained about the excessive length of the domestic proceedings. ### The Government’s Position
The Government, represented by their Agent, participated in the proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights and submitted observations in response to the applicant's complaints. ### Procedural History
On 12 September 2003, the applicant company initiated civil proceedings in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and the DAB, seeking a declaration that it remained the holder of the shares and requesting their return. On 21 February 2006, the Zagreb Commercial Court dismissed the action, finding that the shares had been legally extinguished by the Government Decision. On 18 June 2008, the High Commercial Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, confirming that the shares no longer existed and that the first-instance court could not override the Government Decision. On 20 December 2013, the applicant company lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. The Court subsequently gave notice to the Croatian Government of the complaints concerning access to court, the reasoning of the Constitutional Court’s decision, the length of the proceedings, and the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

case_name: CASE OF STAVROPOULOS AND OTHERS v. GREECE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Stavropoulos and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 52484/18)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicants in this case are Mr. Nikolaos Stavropoulos, Ms. Ioanna Kravari, and their daughter, Ms. Stavroula-Dorothea Stavropoulou, who are Greek nationals residing in the United Kingdom. The respondent party is the Government of Greece. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In August 2007, Mr. Stavropoulos registered the birth of his daughter at the Amarousio registry office in Greece. During the registration process, the registry official entered the child's forename into the birth register and added the abbreviated word for "naming" (*ονοματοδοσία*) in parentheses next to her name. Under the domestic legal framework, specifically Law no. 344/1976, "naming" is designated as the statutory procedure for declaring a newborn's name, whereas a separate provision exists for recording a subsequent christening in the side section of the birth registry. #### 3. Procedural History Prior to the European Court of Human Rights
In October 2007, the applicants filed an application with the Supreme Administrative Court of Greece, seeking to annul the registration of the word "naming" next to their daughter's name. They argued that the inclusion of this term indicated that the child had not been christened, thereby revealing their religious beliefs. In March 2018, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the application as inadmissible, ruling that the applicants lacked a legal interest to act. The court held that under Law no. 344/1976, "naming" by parental declaration is the sole legal method for a child to acquire a name, regardless of whether a christening occurs later. Consequently, the court concluded that the term merely reflected the statutory terminology and could not serve as a basis for discrimination or cause the alleged harm. #### 4. The Applicants' Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that the inclusion of the term "naming" on the birth registration act violated Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the negative aspect of the freedom to manifest one's religion or belief. They argued that because registry offices in practice only appended this note to children who were not christened, the entry effectively disclosed their choice not to baptize their child, thereby revealing their personal religious convictions. They also contended that this practice violated Article 8 of the Convention by exposing sensitive personal data on public documents, which could subject them to administrative discrimination. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Greek Government argued that the application was inadmissible. First, they contended that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, as they could have applied for a simple correction of the birth registry entry through a public prosecutor or a Magistrates' Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Second, the Government argued that the applicants had not suffered any significant disadvantage. They asserted that the birth register is not publicly accessible and that the disputed note does not appear on the standard birth certificate extracts used for school enrollment or other public services, meaning there was no risk of discriminatory treatment.

case_name: CASE OF KLOPCOVS v. LATVIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Klopcovs v. Latvia* (Application no. 26902/13)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Boriss Klopcovs, a Latvian national born in 1951 and residing in Riga. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Latvia, represented by its Agent, Ms. K. Līce. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In 2005, the applicant was held in pre-trial detention at Riga Central Prison. Throughout June, July, and August of 2005, the prison administration monitored and intercepted the applicant’s correspondence addressed to private individuals and various institutions. In September 2005, the applicant submitted complaints to the Prisons Administration regarding these actions. The Prisons Administration rejected his complaints in October 2005. Subsequently, the Ministry of Justice reviewed the matter and deemed the actions of the prison administration, as well as the decisions of the Prisons Administration, to be lawful. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
On 22 September 2006, the applicant initiated administrative court proceedings against the Ministry of Justice, and the Prisons Administration subsequently joined the litigation. The domestic proceedings spanned several years and involved multiple levels of jurisdiction:
*   **First-Instance Court (21 October 2008):** The Administrative District Court ruled that the actions of the Riga Central Prison administration were unlawful but rejected the applicant’s claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages totaling 5,406 Latvian lats (approximately 7,692 euros). *   **Appellate Court (3 December 2009):** The Administrative Regional Court quashed the initial judgment and remitted the case to the first-instance court. *   **First-Instance Court (27 April 2010):** The District Court again found the prison's actions unlawful and denied the damages claim. The applicant’s appeal regarding the damages was rejected as out of time, but the opposing parties' appeals were accepted, moving the case forward. *   **Appellate Court (15 February 2012):** The Administrative Regional Court partially ruled in the applicant's favor, finding the prison's actions unlawful because the applicant had not been informed of the reasons for stopping his letters, and because one specific letter had been stopped unlawfully. The rest of his claims were dismissed. *   **Supreme Court (26 October 2012):** In a final decision, the Senate of the Supreme Court upheld the Regional Court's judgment and dismissed the cassation complaints of both the applicant and the Prisons Administration. During the domestic proceedings, ten hearings were scheduled. At least one hearing was adjourned because the applicant failed to return 77 pages of case documents to the file between February and September 2008, explaining later that he believed they were for his personal use. The applicant also initiated several ancillary procedural challenges. #### 4. The Applicant’s Allegations before the ECtHR
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 April 2013. He alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, complaining that the total length of the domestic administrative proceedings (from September 2006 to October 2012) failed to comply with the "reasonable time" requirement. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Latvian Government contested the applicant's allegations and raised two primary admissibility objections:
1. **Incompatibility *ratione materiae*:** The Government argued that Article 6 § 1 under its civil head was inapplicable because the core dispute concerned public law prison administration actions rather than civil or pecuniary rights, and the applicant had failed to properly maintain his damages claim on appeal. 2. **Non-exhaustion of domestic remedies:** The Government contended that the applicant should have filed a civil claim under Article 92 of the Latvian Constitution to seek compensation for the length of the proceedings, citing a domestic court precedent from April 2013. #### 6. Admissibility Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights
The Court declared the remainder of the application inadmissible and gave notice of the length-of-proceedings complaint to the Government. In its admissibility assessment, the Court rejected the Government’s *ratione materiae* objection, finding that the right to respect for correspondence falls within the sphere of personal rights and is civil in nature, thereby making Article 6 § 1 applicable. The Court also rejected the non-exhaustion objection, noting that the domestic precedent cited by the Government was established after the final domestic decision in the applicant's case and was not sufficiently certain at the material time. Consequently, the Court declared the complaint under Article 6 § 1 admissible.

case_name: CASE OF MIRGADIROV v. AZERBAIJAN AND TURKEY
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Mirgadirov v. Azerbaijan and Turkey*

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Rauf Habibula oglu Mirgadirov, an Azerbaijani national born in 1961. He is a well-known journalist, political analyst, and recipient of several national and international press awards. *   **Respondent States:** The Republic of Azerbaijan and the Republic of Turkey. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In July 2010, the applicant relocated to Turkey, where he worked as a correspondent for the Azerbaijani newspaper *Zerkalo*. In April 2014, the Turkish Directorate General of Press and Information annulled his press card, which led to the revocation of his Turkish residence permit. On April 18, 2014, while traveling by bus toward Georgia with his family, the applicant was detained by Turkish police during an identity check. The following day, April 19, he was placed on a flight and deported to Baku, Azerbaijan. Upon his arrival at Baku Airport on April 19, 2014, the applicant was immediately arrested by agents of the Azerbaijani Ministry of National Security. He was suspected of high treason (Article 274 of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan) for allegedly collaborating with Armenian intelligence services and providing them with state secrets. On April 21, 2014, the Nasimi District Court in Baku ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody for a period of three months, citing the severity of the charges and the risk of him absconding. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
*   **Against Turkey:** The applicant alleged that his detention on April 19, 2014, was unlawful and that he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest. He claimed he was denied access to a lawyer, was unable to challenge the lawfulness of his detention, and that the actions of the Turkish authorities violated his right to freedom of expression as a journalist. *   **Against Azerbaijan:** The applicant alleged that his arrest and detention lacked "reasonable suspicion" of a criminal offense and that he was held for 16 hours without a judicial order. He argued that his pre-trial detention was unjustified, that the domestic courts failed to adequately review his arguments for release, and that his lawyers were excluded from a key detention hearing. He also claimed that public statements by the investigating authorities violated his right to the presumption of innocence, that restrictions on his correspondence and family visits during detention were unlawful, and that his prosecution was politically motivated, serving an ulterior purpose. #### 4. The Governments' Positions
*   **The Turkish Government** maintained that the applicant’s residence permit was lawfully revoked following the annulment of his press card. They submitted that the applicant was notified of the deportation and administrative detention procedures but refused to sign the relevant information documents. *   **The Azerbaijani Government** contended that the criminal proceedings and the applicant's subsequent detention were fully justified. They argued that there was sufficient evidence to suspect the applicant of high treason, pointing to his admitted meetings with Armenian nationals, and asserted that the domestic courts properly assessed the necessity of his pre-trial detention. #### 5. Procedural History
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on September 11, 2014. On January 11, 2016, the Court gave notice of the complaints to both the Azerbaijani and Turkish Governments. The application was granted priority treatment. Written observations were submitted by the applicant, both respondent Governments, and three intervening non-governmental organizations: the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Human Rights House Foundation, and Freedom Now.

case_name: CASE OF ŁABUDEK v. POLAND
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case

#### 1. The Parties
The case of *Łabudek v. Poland* (Application no. 37245/13) involves Mr. Zdzisław Łabudek, a Polish national born in 1961 (the applicant), and the Republic of Poland, represented by its Agent from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (the respondent Government). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant was arrested on 18 January 1999 on charges of participating in an organised armed criminal group and committing several violent offences, including two murders. In February 2008, the Katowice Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to life imprisonment. However, in February 2010, the Katowice Court of Appeal partly quashed this judgment and remitted the case back to the first-instance court. Although the applicant’s detention on remand was lifted in May 2010, he remained incarcerated until 22 July 2011 to serve a prison sentence imposed in a separate set of criminal proceedings. On 27 June 2011, the Katowice Regional Court again ordered his detention on remand within the remitted proceedings. The court justified this measure based on the high probability of guilt, the severity of the potential sentence, and a significant risk of obstruction. It noted that the applicant had a history of threatening and attempting to influence witnesses, and had allegedly made preparations to murder a witness in another case. The applicant’s detention on remand was subsequently extended on numerous occasions. The domestic courts consistently cited the original grounds, the complexity of the multi-defendant case, and the pending testimony of a key "crown witness." The applicant lodged several unsuccessful appeals against these extensions. Between 11 June 2015 and 6 April 2016, his detention on remand was temporarily interrupted while he served another prison sentence. On 12 October 2016, the Katowice Regional Court again convicted the applicant and sentenced him to life imprisonment. During the retrial proceedings, which involved a 75,000-page case file, the court scheduled 276 hearings, of which 174 were held and 102 were adjourned. #### 3. The Applicant’s Allegations
The applicant complained under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that the length of his detention on remand after 23 July 2011 had been excessive and unreasonable. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Polish Government contested the applicant's allegations, arguing that the duration of the detention was compatible with Article 5 § 3 standards. They asserted that the domestic courts provided "relevant" and "sufficient" grounds to justify the entire period. Specifically, they pointed to the persistent reasonable suspicion of guilt, the severity of the anticipated penalty, the risk of collusion, and the applicant's specific role within the criminal group. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 April 2013. The Court subsequently declared the applicant's complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention admissible, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Court calculated the relevant period of detention on remand to be considered under Article 5 § 3 as four years, four months, and twenty-five days, excluding the periods during which the applicant was serving other prison sentences.

case_name: CASE OF SIGRÍÐUR ELÍN SIGFÚSDÓTTIR v. ICELAND
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Sigríður Elín Sigfúsdóttir v. Iceland* (Application no. 41382/17)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Ms. Sigríður Elín Sigfúsdóttir, an Icelandic national and the former director of corporate banking at Landsbanki. *   **Respondent Government:** The Republic of Iceland. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In October 2008, the global liquidity crisis severely impacted the Icelandic financial sector, leading to the collapse of Landsbanki, one of the country's largest banks. Prior to the collapse, the applicant, in her capacity as a member of Landsbanki’s credit committee, approved a loan to a private company (Imon ehf.) to purchase shares in Landsbanki. Following the bank's collapse, the office of a Special Prosecutor was established to investigate financial irregularities. In March 2013, the applicant was indicted on charges of fraud by abuse of position and market manipulation related to the Imon transaction. In December 2016, media reports revealed that several Supreme Court Justices had personally owned shares in Icelandic banks prior to the 2008 crash, and that these holdings had resulted in significant financial losses when the banks collapsed. Regarding the five-judge Supreme Court panel that adjudicated the applicant's case:
*   **Justice V.M.M.** had owned Landsbanki shares with a purchase price of approximately ISK 14.7 million (valued at ISK 8.5 million just before the collapse), which became worthless. *   **Justice E.T.** had owned Landsbanki shares valued at approximately ISK 1.7 million at the time of the collapse, which also became worthless. *   **Justice M.S.** had owned shares in a different collapsed bank (Glitnir) and suffered losses in other domestic investment funds. #### 3. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
On 5 June 2014, the District Court of Reykjavik acquitted the applicant of the charges. On 8 October 2015, the Supreme Court of Iceland overturned the acquittal, convicting the applicant of fraud by abuse of position and aiding and abetting in market manipulation. She was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment. Following the December 2016 media disclosures regarding the judges' financial interests, the applicant requested the Committee on Reopening of Judicial Proceedings to reopen her case. On 12 May 2019, the Committee accepted her request, concluding that Justice V.M.M.’s financial losses in Landsbanki were substantial enough to justify objective doubts regarding the panel's impartiality. The reopening proceedings were pending before the Supreme Court of Iceland when the applicant's case was being examined by the European Court of Human Rights. #### 4. The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to an independent and impartial tribunal) of the European Convention on Human Rights. She argued that the substantial financial losses suffered by Justices V.M.M., E.T., and M.S. in the banking collapse created a conflict of interest, as they were effectively victims of the broader events surrounding her prosecution. She asserted that these undisclosed interests raised legitimate doubts about the panel's objective and subjective impartiality. She also alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), claiming that the Supreme Court held a preconceived idea of her guilt, shifted the burden of proof to the defence, and interpreted a lack of evidence to her disadvantage. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Government contested the applicant's claims. On admissibility, they argued that the application was lodged outside the six-month time-limit and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted because the reopening proceedings were still pending. On the merits of Article 6 § 1, the Government maintained that the judges were impartial. They argued that the financial losses had occurred seven years prior to the trial, the judges held no personal animosity toward the applicant, and the shareholdings of Justices E.T. and M.S. were either minor or entirely unrelated to Landsbanki. Regarding Article 6 § 2, the Government denied that the burden of proof had been shifted, asserting that the Supreme Court’s conviction was based on a comprehensive and objective evaluation of the evidence.

case_name: CASE OF SHEBALDINA v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Main Parties
The applicant is Ms. Alla Petrivna Shebaldina, a Ukrainian national born in 1959 who worked as a teacher. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine. ### Key Factual Circumstances
From 1988 until 2006, the applicant was employed as a teacher at a state-run specialized child-care center. Under Article 57 of the 1991 Education Act, she was entitled to seniority and recreation allowances. However, she did not receive these allowances for the period between 1997 and 2002. ### Procedural History
In December 2007, the applicant filed a lawsuit in the domestic courts against the child-care center and the regional department of the State Treasury to recover the unpaid arrears (amounting to 2,244.30 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH)), along with an index-linked adjustment, compensation for non-pecuniary damage, and legal costs. In October 2010, the Bilgorod-Dnistrovskyy Town Court partly ruled in her favor. It ordered the center to pay the arrears and the index-linked adjustment, finding that the applicant was entitled to the allowances. The court noted that because the center's failure to pay resulted from a lack of state funding, the center could subsequently seek recovery of these funds from the State budget. In April 2011, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed the lower court's judgment and dismissed the applicant's claims. While acknowledging the unpaid arrears, the Court of Appeal held that under the 2004 Act on the Restructuring of Indebtedness, such payments were recognized as a debt to be paid directly from the State budget rather than by the center itself. It also found that the State Treasury was not a proper defendant and dismissed the claims for index-linking and non-pecuniary damages. In July 2011, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to examine the applicant’s appeal on points of law. To support her case, the applicant provided copies of domestic court decisions from 2004 and 2011, in which the Court of Appeal had upheld similar allowance claims against the same center for other employees, ruling that payments were not conditional on budget availability. ### The Applicant's Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). She argued that her statutory right to the allowances constituted a "possession" under domestic law. She asserted that both domestic courts had confirmed the existence of the debt and that the State could not rely on a lack of budgetary funds to avoid its financial obligations. She also maintained that the unpaid allowances, representing 30% of her monthly salary, had a significant financial impact on her. ### The Government's Position
The Ukrainian Government raised several objections. First, they argued the application was inadmissible because the disputed amount (equivalent to approximately EUR 204) did not meet the threshold of "significant disadvantage." Second, they claimed the application was submitted past the six-month deadline. Finally, they argued on the merits that because the child-care center had a dual status as a healthcare institution, the applicant was not legally entitled to the allowances, meaning she had no "legitimate expectation" or "possession" under the Convention.

case_name: CASE OF BAZ v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Baz v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40962/13)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves Mr. Mekhmet Takhır Dıno Baz, a Turkish national born in 1976 who resides in Ukraine, and the Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant arrived in Ukraine in 2004 and was granted refugee status on 23 March 2011. On 18 October 2012, the State Migration Service revoked his refugee status on the grounds that he had concealed the fact that he was wanted by Turkish law-enforcement authorities. The applicant challenged this revocation in the Ukrainian courts, which ultimately rejected his claims, culminating in a final decision by the High Administrative Court on 3 April 2013. While those proceedings were ongoing, the applicant applied for subsidiary protection on 14 March 2013. This application was initially rejected as inadmissible, but on 27 February 2014, the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court quashed that rejection and ordered the migration authorities to review the application on its merits. In parallel, on 3 October 2012, the Turkish authorities requested the applicant’s extradition to Turkey on charges of participation in terrorist and separatist activities in 1998. The Turkish request specified that the criminal charges would become time-barred on 15 August 2013. On 14 November 2012, the applicant was detained by Ukrainian authorities with a view to his extradition, and a domestic court formally ordered his detention pending extradition on 16 November 2012. During his detention, the applicant was also prosecuted and sentenced in Ukraine to two months' imprisonment for using forged documents, a conviction he subsequently appealed. On 17 July 2013, a domestic court upheld his continued detention pending extradition. However, on 30 August 2013, the court ordered the applicant's release, noting that the limitation period for the Turkish prosecution had expired on 15 August 2013, which legally barred extradition under the European Convention on Extradition. On 23 September 2013, the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine formally rejected the Turkish extradition request. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant complained that his detention pending extradition violated Article 5 § 1 (f) of the Convention. He raised three primary arguments:
* His detention was unlawful prior to 3 April 2013 because his appeals against the revocation of his refugee status were still pending, during which time he could not legally be extradited. * He could not be extradited while his application for subsidiary protection (filed on 14 March 2013) was pending. * His detention after 15 August 2013 was unlawful because the prosecution against him in Turkey had become time-barred, rendering extradition legally impossible. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Ukrainian Government did not submit observations on the admissibility or the merits of the case within the time-limits established by the Court. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 June 2013. The Court subsequently gave notice to the Ukrainian Government of the complaint under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Turkish Government chose not to exercise their right to intervene in the proceedings. The Court subsequently declared the complaint under Article 5 § 1 admissible, noting that it was not manifestly ill-founded or inadmissible on any other grounds, and proceeded to examine the merits.

case_name: CASE OF SMBAT AYVAZYAN v. ARMENIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Smbat Ayvazyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 49021/08)

#### 1. Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Mr. Smbat Ayvazyan, an Armenian national, former Member of Parliament, and former government minister. Following his death in 2014, his widow informed the Court of her wish to pursue the application. * **Respondent Government:** The Republic of Armenia, represented by its Agent. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Following the Armenian presidential election on 19 February 2008, supporters of the main opposition candidate, Mr. Ter-Petrosyan, held daily protest rallies in Yerevan to protest alleged election irregularities. The applicant, an active opposition supporter, regularly attended these demonstrations. On 24 February 2008, police stopped the applicant's car and took him into custody on suspicion of carrying illegal weapons. During a search at the police station, officers recorded finding a spring baton in his coat pocket. The applicant initially signed a statement admitting the baton belonged to him, but later claimed he was coerced into doing so under threats that his companions would otherwise be prosecuted. A pistol was also found in his car but was later deemed ineffective by experts. Later that night, after undergoing a drug test (which returned negative), police officers reported that the applicant disobeyed orders, insulted them, and punched an officer in the chest outside the Kentron Police Station. The applicant denied that any such incident occurred, asserting that he entered the station peacefully and that several relatives, friends, and a journalist standing outside could verify this. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights of several violations of the European Convention on Human Rights:
* **Article 5 § 1:** He argued that a portion of his detention was unlawful because his court-authorized detention expired on 15 July 2008, and the trial judge failed to formally rule on its continuation until later, retroactively correcting the omission as a "typographical error."
* **Article 5 § 3:** He claimed the domestic courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for his continued pre-trial detention. * **Article 5 § 4:** He alleged a violation because the Court of Appeal refused to examine his appeal against his extended detention on the sole ground that his case had already been referred for trial. * **Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d):** He argued his trial was unfair because his conviction relied almost exclusively on the testimonies of the police officers involved. He further complained that the domestic court refused to summon his proposed defense witnesses (who were outside the station or in nearby cells) and denied him adequate opportunity to question certain prosecution witnesses. * **Articles 10, 11, and 14:** He maintained that his arrest, prosecution, and conviction were politically motivated, aimed at punishing him for his political activism and restricting his right to freedom of peaceful assembly. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Armenian Government, represented by their Agent, participated in the proceedings and filed observations in response to the applicant's complaints, contesting his allegations regarding the unlawfulness of his detention, the unfairness of the trial, and the alleged political motivation behind his prosecution. #### 5. Procedural History
On 27 February 2008, the District Court ordered the applicant's pre-trial detention, which was subsequently extended. On 7 July 2008, the investigation concluded, and the case was sent to trial. On 19 November 2008, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found the applicant guilty of assaulting a police officer (Article 316 § 1 of the Criminal Code) and illegally carrying a cold weapon (Article 235 § 4). He was sentenced to two years' imprisonment and a fine. The District Court relied on police testimony and the applicant's initial statement, dismissing his defense arguments and written witness statements as biased. The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 27 January 2009, and the Court of Cassation declared the applicant's appeal on points of law inadmissible on 15 June 2009. The applicant was released under an amnesty in June 2009 after serving more than half of his sentence. He had previously lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 September 2008.

case_name: CASE OF M.A. AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *M.A. and Others v. Bulgaria* originally involved five Chinese nationals of Uighur Muslim origin from the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region (XUAR). Following the withdrawal of two applicants who left Bulgaria, the remaining three applicants are Mr. A.N., Mr. Y.M., and Mr. S.H. The respondent State is the Republic of Bulgaria. ### Factual Background
The applicants fled China on various dates, alleging individual persecution by Chinese authorities in the XUAR. Their accounts included harassment by security agents, detention and torture following internet discussions, and penalties for violating family planning policies or teaching the Uighur language. After traveling through Southeast Asia, they resided in Turkey. In 2017, fearing potential deportation from Turkey to China due to changing bilateral relations, they crossed into Bulgaria unlawfully. They were apprehended, received suspended sentences for illegal entry, and were detained. The Chinese embassy subsequently issued travel documents for them. ### Procedural History
In December 2017, the applicants applied for asylum in Bulgaria. The State Refugees Agency rejected their applications, and the Haskovo Administrative Court upheld these decisions in January 2018. The court concluded that the applicants had not demonstrated a specific, individualized risk of persecution or ill-treatment in China, characterizing their fears as assumptions based on general country conditions. In parallel, the State Agency for National Security ordered the applicants' expulsion on national security grounds in January 2018. The agency asserted that the applicants had traveled to Syria, trained with the East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM), and maintained contacts with individuals linked to terrorist organizations. In May 2019, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicants' appeals, finding that confidential intelligence data sufficiently demonstrated they posed a national security threat. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) on January 26, 2018. The ECtHR applied an interim measure under Rule 39, directing Bulgaria not to remove the applicants to China. The ECtHR subsequently declared the complaints under Articles 2 and 3 admissible, dismissing the Government's objection that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies regarding their initial repatriation orders. ### Applicants' Allegations
Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that their forced return to China would violate Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the Convention. They argued that as Uighurs returned from abroad, they would face arbitrary detention, torture, and potential execution. They maintained that the human rights situation in the XUAR was highly repressive and that they faced a real, personal risk of harm. ### Government's Position
The Bulgarian Government argued that the general situation in the XUAR did not amount to a systemic exposure of Uighurs to ill-treatment. They contended that the applicants' personal accounts lacked corroborating evidence and did not establish a specific, individualized risk of persecution, as they were not high-profile activists, intellectuals, or religious leaders. The Government also noted that the Chinese authorities' actions in the region were aimed at countering terrorism and extremism, and stated that alternative removal options to third countries remained open.

case_name: CASE OF MIRGADIROV v. AZERBAIJAN AND TURKEY
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Mirgadirov v. Azerbaijan and Turkey* (Application no. 62775/14)

#### 1. Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Mr. Rauf Habibula oglu Mirgadirov, an Azerbaijani national, prominent journalist, and political analyst. * **Respondent States:** The Republic of Azerbaijan and the Republic of Turkey. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In July 2010, Mr. Mirgadirov relocated to Turkey, where he worked as a correspondent for the Azerbaijani newspaper *Zerkalo*, writing primarily on regional foreign policy. In April 2014, the Turkish Directorate General of Press and Information revoked his press card, which led to the cancellation of his Turkish residence permit. On April 18, 2014, while traveling by bus toward Georgia with his family, Mr. Mirgadirov was detained by Turkish police. He was held in administrative custody and deported to Azerbaijan on April 19, 2014. Upon his arrival at Baku Airport on April 19, 2014, Mr. Mirgadirov was immediately arrested by agents of the Azerbaijani Ministry of National Security. He was suspected of high treason under Article 274 of the Azerbaijani Criminal Code. The prosecution alleged that he had been recruited by Armenian intelligence services to collect and transmit state secrets, including information regarding Azerbaijan's military, socio-political, and economic situations. Mr. Mirgadirov denied the espionage charges, maintaining that his contacts with Armenian nationals were strictly limited to public discussions at international conferences. On April 21, 2014, the Nasimi District Court in Azerbaijan formally charged him and ordered his pre-trial detention for a period of three months, citing the severity of the charges and the risk of flight. #### 3. The Applicant’s Allegations
Mr. Mirgadirov raised multiple complaints under the European Convention on Human Rights against both respondent states:
* **Against Turkey:** He alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 2, 3, and 4, asserting that his detention was unlawful, that he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest, that he was not brought before a judicial authority, and that he was unable to challenge the lawfulness of his detention. He also alleged a violation of his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. * **Against Azerbaijan:** He alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 3, and 4, arguing that his arrest lacked "reasonable suspicion," that his subsequent detention was unjustified, and that the domestic courts failed to conduct an adequate judicial review of his detention. He also claimed violations of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence regarding public statements by authorities), Article 8 (unlawful restrictions on his correspondence, telephone calls, and family visits during detention), and Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5 (alleging his prosecution was driven by an ulterior, politically motivated purpose). #### 4. The Governments' Positions
Both the Azerbaijani and Turkish Governments contested the applicant's allegations. They submitted written observations to the Court defending the lawfulness of their respective administrative and judicial procedures, maintaining that their authorities acted in accordance with domestic legislation and national security requirements. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on September 11, 2014. On January 11, 2016, the Court gave notice of the complaints to both respondent Governments and granted the case priority treatment under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. Written interventions were subsequently received from three non-governmental organizations: the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Human Rights House Foundation, and Freedom Now.

case_name: CASE OF KEANEY v. IRELAND
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Mr. Vincent Keaney, an Irish national born in 1955. The respondent party is the Government of Ireland. ### Factual Background
In 1996, Mr. Keaney purchased the Scotts Building in Cobh, Ireland, with the intention of renovating and operating it as "The Titanic Bar and Restaurant." Due to unexpected structural defects, he ran out of funds and subsequently entered into a series of business agreements with an investor, M.N., and a financial consultant, J.S., which included transferring shares and leasing the premises to a newly incorporated company. Relations between the parties deteriorated, the business failed, and subsequent agreements to separate their commercial interests broke down, resulting in M.N. taking possession of the premises. ### Domestic Procedural History
On 8 February 2006, Mr. Keaney commenced High Court proceedings against eighteen defendants, claiming deceit, fraud, misrepresentation, and undue influence. The case was admitted to the fast-track Commercial List. Between 2006 and 2008, the litigation was marked by extensive procedural disputes regarding the applicant's pleadings. In January 2007, the High Court struck out the claims against eleven defendants and limited the claims against others. By early 2007, claims against fourteen of the eighteen defendants had been dismissed. The applicant was repeatedly ordered to reformulate his remaining claims due to poor particularization, ultimately amending his statement of claim eight times. On 19 December 2008, the High Court dismissed the remaining claims on their merits, noting that aspects of the applicant's case bordered on an abuse of process. Between February 2007 and February 2009, Mr. Keaney appealed various High Court orders and judgments to the Supreme Court. The appeal process experienced substantial delays. The respondents brought motions to dismiss the appeals due to the applicant's failure to lodge the required documentation. After the Supreme Court issued peremptory orders, the applicant filed the necessary books of appeal and legal submissions, though the respondents contested their completeness and compliance. On 23 July 2015, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against the first High Court judgment, characterizing the applicant's unsubstantiated allegations as an abuse of process. On 5 April 2017, the Supreme Court delivered its final judgment, dismissing the remaining appeals. ### The Applicant’s Complaints
Mr. Keaney lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, complaining under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the eleven-year duration of the civil proceedings was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement. He argued that the primary responsibility for controlling the pace of proceedings rests on the judicial system. He alleged that the delays were caused by systemic deficiencies, including shortages of judges, staff, and court resources, as well as the administrative complication of having multiple different judges handle his case at various stages. ### The Government’s Position
The Irish Government contested the applicant's claims, arguing that no violation of Article 6 § 1 had occurred. They submitted that the litigation was highly complex and had been actively case-managed by the High Court. The Government asserted that the delays were directly attributable to the applicant's conduct, highlighting his repeated failure to deliver proper pleadings, his failure to submit complete appeal documentation and legal submissions within the prescribed time limits, and his non-compliance with court directions. They emphasized that both the High Court and the Supreme Court had identified the applicant's conduct as an abuse of process, and argued that finding a violation would create a perverse incentive for litigants to pursue abusive proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF IVASHCHENKO v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Ivashchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 41303/11)

#### 1. Main Parties
* **The Applicant:** Mr. Valeriy Volodymyrovych Ivashchenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1956. He served as the Deputy Minister of Defence of Ukraine from October 2007 to June 2009, and as the acting Minister of Defence from June 2009 to May 2010. * **The Respondent State:** Ukraine, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In August 2010, the General Prosecutor’s Office of Ukraine initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant on suspicion of abuse of power and exceeding his authority, stemming from his signing of a financial rehabilitation plan for a State-owned enterprise in November 2009. The applicant was arrested on August 21, 2010. The Pechersk District Court of Kyiv ordered his pre-trial detention, citing risks of absconding and hindering the investigation. This detention was subsequently extended multiple times by domestic courts. The applicant had a history of chronic medical conditions dating back to 1995, including spinal osteochondritis, cervical spine instability, and arthritis, which had historically required bi-annual inpatient treatment at the Main Military Clinical Hospital (MMCH). Following his placement in the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (SIZO), the applicant’s health deteriorated, and he was diagnosed with additional conditions, including coronary heart disease and hypertension. Multiple medical panels recommended that he undergo inpatient neurological treatment, noting that the SIZO lacked a neurological department and a staff neurologist. Although the trial court eventually stated in December 2011 that it did not object to the applicant receiving inpatient treatment at the MMCH, the prison escort service refused to transport him there. Throughout his trial, the applicant was systematically confined in a metal cage during court hearings. His requests to be released from the cage during proceedings were denied by the trial court, which stated that the confinement complied with domestic legislation. On April 12, 2012, the District Court found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. On August 14, 2012, the Kyiv Court of Appeal quashed this judgment, replacing it with a suspended sentence and a one-year probation period, resulting in the applicant's release from custody. #### 3. The Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant raised complaints under two main articles of the European Convention on Human Rights:
* **Article 3 (Prohibition of degrading treatment):** He alleged that he was denied access to adequate medical treatment and assistance while in detention, and that his systematic confinement in a metal cage during public court hearings constituted degrading treatment. * **Article 5 (Right to liberty and security):** He complained that his pre-trial detention was unlawful, excessively lengthy, and lacked sufficient justification, and that he lacked an effective procedure under domestic law to challenge its lawfulness. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government of Ukraine contested the applicant's allegations:
* **Regarding Medical Care:** They argued that the medical treatment, regular examinations, and supervision provided to the applicant while in custody were adequate and compatible with the requirements of Article 3. * **Regarding the Metal Cage:** The Government maintained that the applicant's confinement in a metal cage during the trial hearings was carried out in accordance with the domestic legislation in force at the time. #### 5. Procedural History
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on June 27, 2011. The Government was given formal notice of the application on October 23, 2014.

case_name: CASE OF PASQUINI v. SAN MARINO (No. 2)
step1_summary:
### Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Enrico Maria Pasquini, an Italian national born in 1948 who resides in San Marino. At the material time, he was the chairman and sole shareholder of S.M.I., a fiduciary company operating in San Marino. The respondent State is the Republic of San Marino. S.M.I., represented by its liquidators after entering compulsory liquidation, participated in the domestic proceedings as a civil party. ### Key Factual Circumstances
In June 2011, following an inspection of S.M.I.’s headquarters, the Central Bank of San Marino submitted a report to an investigating judge alleging suspicious financial operations. Consequently, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. He was charged with exercising fiduciary activity without a licence, three counts of obstruction of surveillance, misreporting to shareholders and supervisory boards, and continuing aggravated embezzlement. The prosecution alleged that between April 2009 and March 2010, the applicant had misappropriated EUR 2,633,055.77 from a fiduciary account administered by S.M.I. The prosecution asserted that these funds were withdrawn to pay invoices for non-existent services issued by foreign broker companies located in tax havens, which were ultimately traceable back to bank accounts controlled by the applicant. ### Procedural History
On 8 April 2014, the first-instance judge found the applicant guilty of all charges, sentencing him to four years’ imprisonment and a fine, and ordering an interim compensation payment of EUR 2,633,055.77 to S.M.I. The judge concluded that the applicant had established a complex system of simulated business operations to manipulate the company's patrimony for his personal benefit. The applicant appealed, arguing that the statutory limitation period for the embezzlement charge had expired. While the appeal was pending, the Judge of Criminal Appeals referred a constitutional question regarding the court's jurisdiction to decide civil claims when a criminal offence becomes time-barred. Consequently, the legislature enacted Article 196 bis of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which empowered appeal judges to decide on civil obligations deriving from an offence even after declaring the criminal charge discontinued due to the statute of limitations. On 19 September 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals applied this new provision. The judge acquitted the applicant of certain charges for lack of evidence, declared the remaining charges (including aggravated embezzlement) discontinued as time-barred, but upheld the civil compensation order. To justify the compensation, the judge reviewed the elements of the embezzlement charge, noting that the first-instance reasoning did not indicate that the alleged facts had not occurred or that the accused had not committed them. ### Applicant's Allegations and ECtHR Proceedings
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 March 2017. Under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention (presumption of innocence), the applicant alleged that, in the absence of a formal finding of guilt, the judgment of the Judge of Criminal Appeals nevertheless reflected the judge's conviction that he was guilty. He further complained that he was ordered to pay damages precisely on the basis of this declaration of criminal responsibility, without his guilt having been established in the criminal proceedings. On 4 September 2017, the Court gave notice of the Article 6 § 2 complaint to the Government of San Marino, which was represented by its Agent, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Italian Government did not exercise its right to intervene in the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF PILETIĆ v. MONTENEGRO
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Piletić v. Montenegro* (Application no. 53044/13)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The original applicant in this case was Ms. Piletić, a Montenegrin national, who was represented by Ms. A. Đukanović, a lawyer practicing in Podgorica. Following the applicant's death during the course of the proceedings, her daughters, Ms. Nina Đikanović and Ms. Jelka Tomašević, acting as her legal heirs, sought to pursue the application. The respondent party is the Government of Montenegro. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The case concerns the duration of domestic civil proceedings in Montenegro to which the applicant was a party. The proceedings progressed through the domestic court system, and the primary dispute centered on the total time elapsed during the determination of the applicant's civil rights and obligations. #### 3. The Applicant's Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that the length of the domestic civil proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement. She claimed a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which provides that everyone is entitled to a hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal in the determination of their civil rights and obligations. Following the applicant's death on 22 December 2015, her daughters asserted that they had a legitimate interest in obtaining a finding regarding the alleged breach of Article 6 § 1 and requested to maintain the application before the Court. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Government of Montenegro was formally given notice of the application. In such proceedings, the Government's role involves addressing the admissibility and merits of the applicant's complaints, typically by submitting observations on the complexity of the domestic case, the conduct of both the applicant and the relevant administrative and judicial authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant in the dispute. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The application was officially lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 July 2013 under Article 34 of the Convention. While the application was pending, the applicant passed away on 22 December 2015. On 25 May 2016, the applicant’s daughters, Ms. Nina Đikanović and Ms. Jelka Tomašević, submitted a formal request to the Court expressing their intention to pursue the application as her legal heirs. Before evaluating the core complaint regarding the length of the civil proceedings, the Court was required to address the preliminary procedural question of *locus standi* (standing)—specifically, whether the daughters possessed a legitimate interest under the Convention to continue the application in place of the deceased applicant.

case_name: CASE OF D. v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *D. v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 25397/09)

#### 1. The Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Ms. D., a Moldovan national born in 1990. * **Respondent State:** The Republic of Moldova. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Following the Moldovan general elections in April 2009, public protests erupted in Chișinău over alleged electoral fraud. On the night of 7–8 April 2009, public order forces and special units conducted a large-scale operation to clear the central square. The applicant, alongside her roommate and a relative, Mr. V. Boboc, was present at the Great National Assembly Square. The applicant states that police and special forces surrounded their group, ordered them to the ground, and subjected them to physical violence. During the arrest, she witnessed police beating Mr. Boboc while he was unconscious; he died shortly thereafter. The applicant was subsequently transported to the Buiucani police station, where she claims she and other detainees were subjected to further abuse, threats, and insults before being released without explanation. Fearing reprisal, the applicant initially told a medical specialist that her injuries resulted from an attack by an unknown person on the street. A subsequent examination by a specialized rehabilitation center for torture victims diagnosed her with post-traumatic stress disorder and physical consequences consistent with cranial trauma. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that:
* She was subjected to severe physical ill-treatment by police officers during her arrest and detention, and that the state failed to conduct an effective investigation into her complaints (violating Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention). * She was unlawfully detained for over five hours without explanation (violating Article 5). * Her life was placed at serious risk after she witnessed the fatal beating of Mr. Boboc, and the state failed to protect her by refusing her request for witness protection (violating Articles 2 and 13). #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government contested the application on several grounds:
* They argued the application was politically motivated and constituted an *actio popularis*. * They asserted the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and had lost her victim status after receiving MDL 7,000 (approximately EUR 447) under a state compensation scheme. * Regarding the ill-treatment claims, they argued there was no reliable evidence of her detention or physical abuse, pointing to inconsistencies and delays in her medical reports. * Regarding the threat to her life, they maintained that no immediate danger existed and that concealing her identity during domestic testimonies was sufficient protection. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant filed a formal complaint with the Prosecutor General on 4 May 2009. A military prosecutor opened a criminal investigation in July 2009. This investigation was joined with other cases in 2010 and suspended in January 2013 because authorities could not identify the specific officers responsible. In parallel domestic proceedings, a police officer on duty at the Buiucani police station was convicted of negligence by the Chișinău Court of Appeal in 2015 (upheld by the Supreme Court of Justice in 2016) for failing to intervene while detainees, including the applicant, were being ill-treated. The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 May 2009. During the proceedings, the Court struck out two other initial co-applicants due to a loss of contact with their representative. In its admissibility assessment, the Court declared the applicant's complaints under Articles 2 and 13 regarding the threat to her life inadmissible. However, the Court dismissed the Government's preliminary objections regarding victim status and domestic remedies, declaring the applicant's complaints under Article 3 (concerning the alleged ill-treatment and the effectiveness of the investigation) admissible.

case_name: CASE OF MIRGADIROV v. AZERBAIJAN AND TURKEY
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Mr. Rauf Habibula oglu Mirgadirov, an Azerbaijani national and a prominent journalist and political analyst. The respondent states are the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Republic of Turkey. ### Factual Background
In July 2010, the applicant relocated to Turkey, where he worked as an Ankara-based correspondent for the Azerbaijani newspaper *Zerkalo*. In April 2014, the Turkish Directorate General of Press and Information revoked his press card, which subsequently led to the revocation of his residence permit. On April 18, 2014, while traveling by bus toward Georgia, the applicant was detained by Turkish police during an identity check. He was informed that his residence permit was invalid, and administrative deportation proceedings were initiated. On April 19, 2014, he was placed on a flight to Baku, Azerbaijan, under police supervision. Upon his arrival at Baku Airport on April 19, 2014, the applicant was immediately arrested by agents of the Azerbaijani Ministry of National Security. He was detained as a suspect and subsequently charged with high treason under Article 274 of the Azerbaijani Criminal Code. The prosecution alleged that the applicant had been recruited by Armenian intelligence services and had provided them with state secrets, including information on the socio-political, economic, and military situation in Azerbaijan. The applicant denied the accusations of high treason, maintaining that his contacts with Armenian individuals occurred within the framework of legitimate international conferences. On April 21, 2014, the Nasimi District Court in Azerbaijan ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention for a period of three months, citing the seriousness of the charges and the risk of him absconding. ### The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant lodged complaints against both respondent states under the European Convention on Human Rights. Against Turkey, he alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 2, 3, and 4, asserting that his detention on April 19, 2014, was unlawful, that he was not informed of the reasons for his detention, that he was not brought before a judge, and that he was unable to challenge the lawfulness of his detention. He also alleged a violation of his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. Against Azerbaijan, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 3, and 4, claiming there was no reasonable suspicion that he had committed a crime, that his detention from November 19 to 20, 2014, was unlawful, that his pre-trial detention lacked justification, and that the domestic courts failed to properly review his detention or allow his lawyers to attend a key hearing. He further alleged a violation of the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2), unlawful restrictions on his correspondence and family visits during his detention (Article 8), and that his arrest and detention served an ulterior, unauthorized purpose (Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5). ### Government Positions and Procedural History
The Turkish and Azerbaijani Governments both submitted observations contesting the applicant's allegations. The Turkish authorities maintained that the applicant's deportation and detention followed standard administrative procedures due to the revocation of his residence permit. The Azerbaijani authorities relied on the criminal charges of high treason and the domestic judicial orders authorizing his detention. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on September 11, 2014. On January 11, 2016, the Court gave notice of the application to both respondent governments. Several non-governmental organizations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, Human Rights House Foundation, and Freedom Now, were granted leave to intervene as third parties.

case_name: CASE OF STAFEYEV v. RUSSIA
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case: Stafeyev v. Russia

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Vyacheslav Vladimirovich Stafeyev, a Russian national born in 1978, who was represented by Mr. E. Markov, a lawyer practicing in Strasbourg. *   **Respondent Government:** The Russian Federation, represented initially by Mr. G. Matyushkin and subsequently by Mr. M. Galperin, Representatives of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In February 2001, three members of the Sh. family were murdered in their flat. In November 2004, the applicant was detained on unrelated charges, and his fingerprints were entered into a database. In December 2004, police matched his fingerprints to those found at the murder scene. A subsequent search of the applicant’s flat uncovered items belonging to the victims. Between December 8 and 10, 2004, police questioned the applicant. He confessed to the murders, though the parties dispute the nature of this confession: the applicant claimed it was made under duress, while the Government maintained it was spontaneous and voluntary. On December 10 and 16, 2004, the applicant waived his right to counsel and repeated his confessions during formal interviews. On January 20, 2005, during a detention hearing where he was assisted by a lawyer, the applicant retracted his confessions. #### 3. Procedural History
*   **First-Instance Trial:** During the trial before the Sverdlovsk Regional Court, the applicant maintained his innocence. On December 15, 2005, the court declared the confessions of December 10 and 16 inadmissible because they were obtained without counsel and subsequently retracted. However, the court admitted the initial confession from December 8. On December 14, 2005, the court convicted the applicant of murder, robbery, and destruction of property, sentencing him to life imprisonment. *   **Appeal Stage:** The applicant’s trial lawyer appealed. At the scheduled appeal hearing on May 15, 2006, the lawyer failed to appear. The Supreme Court of Russia appointed a new lawyer, R., and adjourned the hearing to May 29, 2006. *   **Consultation and Appeal Hearing:** On May 23, 2006, lawyer R. visited the applicant in detention. The applicant alleged that detention facility staff limited their meeting to 15 minutes and that guards repeatedly interrupted them. On May 25, the applicant drafted a request for an additional consultation. This request was registered by the detention facility on May 26 but was not received by the Supreme Court until June 5. On May 29, 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. Lawyer R. was present at the hearing, and the applicant participated via video link. #### 4. The Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 in conjunction with Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention. He alleged that he was denied effective legal assistance on appeal because he was granted only 15 minutes to consult with his newly appointed lawyer. He further alleged that the Supreme Court refused to admit his request for an additional consultation into the case file during the hearing, and complained about the poor quality of the video link during the appeal. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, asserting that he did not raise his complaints about the consultation time in a timely manner. They submitted that the Supreme Court did not receive his written complaints until after the appeal hearing had concluded. Regarding the video link, the Government presented a certificate from the Supreme Court’s IT department stating that no technical failures had been recorded during the hearing on May 29, 2006.

case_name: CASE OF TALALIKHINA v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Talalikhina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 13919/12) involves the applicant, Ms. Olga Vasilyevna Talalikhina, a Ukrainian national born in 1954, and the respondent State, Ukraine. ### Factual Background
In September 2007, criminal proceedings for theft were initiated against the applicant, who signed an undertaking not to abscond. In April 2009, while those proceedings were still pending, the applicant was involved in a domestic dispute that resulted in the death of her cohabitant. She was arrested on April 17, 2009, and on April 20, 2009, the Leninskyy District Court of Sevastopol ordered her pre-trial detention. On June 15, 2009, the prosecutor approved an indictment charging her with aggravated serious bodily harm resulting in death and referred the case to the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol. The applicant remained in custody. On July 6, 2009, the Nakhimovskiy District Court committed her for trial and ruled that her detention should continue. The court subsequently rejected her applications for release in August 2011 and May 2012. On June 20, 2012, the court ordered her release under the guarantee of her relatives. In September 2012, the theft charge against the applicant was dropped. In February 2013, the Nakhimovskiy District Court convicted her of unintentional homicide and sentenced her to two years' imprisonment. ### The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) raising multiple complaints. Under Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, she alleged that her pre-trial detention between the end of the investigation in June 2009 and the court order of July 6, 2009, lacked a legal basis. She further argued that the July 6, 2009 court order authorising her continued detention was arbitrary. Additionally, the applicant raised complaints regarding the overall length of her pre-trial detention, the length of the criminal proceedings against her, and the lack of effective domestic remedies in that regard. ### The Government's Position
The Ukrainian Government stated they were unable to provide detailed comments on the application because the physical case files remained at the Nakhimovskiy District Court in Sevastopol, a territory over which Ukraine did not exercise control at the time of notification. Regarding admissibility, the Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because she had not appealed the initial detention order of April 20, 2009. The Government did not submit observations on the merits of the Article 5 § 1 complaint. ### Procedural History
The application was lodged with the ECHR on February 20, 2012. On May 2, 2019, the Court gave notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government. In addressing the Government's procedural difficulties regarding the unavailable physical files, the Court decided to proceed using the existing case file, noting that the applicant had provided the necessary documentation and that electronic copies of the domestic court decisions were accessible in Ukraine's official state register. Regarding admissibility, the Court dismissed the Government's objection of non-exhaustion, finding that an appeal against the initial April 2009 order did not address the specific subsequent periods of detention challenged by the applicant. The Court subsequently declared the Article 5 § 1 complaint admissible.

case_name: CASE OF YELNIK v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Yelnik v. Ukraine* (Application no. 10444/13)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The proceedings involve the applicant, Mr. Yelnik, a Ukrainian national, and the respondent State of Ukraine, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The case arises from domestic criminal proceedings initiated against the applicant by the Ukrainian authorities. In connection with these criminal charges, the applicant was placed into pre-trial detention. The specific dates of the applicant's arrest, the exact duration of his confinement, and the underlying criminal charges are set out in the case's appended records. The factual background centers on the timeline of the applicant's deprivation of liberty prior to his trial and the overall timeframe of the criminal prosecution. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant raised two primary complaints under the European Convention on Human Rights:
*   **Article 5 § 3 (Right to liberty and security):** The applicant complained principally that the duration of his pre-trial detention was excessive and unreasonable. He alleged that the domestic authorities failed to release him pending trial or to bring his case to trial within a reasonable time, in violation of the guarantees set forth in Article 5 § 3. *   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a fair trial):** The applicant also submitted a complaint regarding the overall length of the criminal proceedings against him. He alleged that the duration of the criminal process failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement mandated for the determination of criminal charges. #### 4. The Government’s Position
Following the introduction of the application, the Ukrainian Government was formally given notice of the complaints. Under the Court's standard procedures, the Government was afforded the opportunity to submit its observations concerning the admissibility and merits of the applicant's allegations regarding both the length of his pre-trial detention and the duration of the criminal proceedings. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant lodged his application (no. 10444/13) with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 January 2013, invoking Article 34 of the Convention. Following notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government, the case was assigned to the Fifth Section of the Court. It was configured to be examined by a Committee composed of Judges Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer (President), Mārtiņš Mits, and Lәtif Hüseynov, with the assistance of Liv Tigerstedt, the Acting Deputy Section Registrar. During the preparation of the case, the procedural framework drew upon established European Court jurisprudence. This included general principles regarding the right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial (referencing cases such as *Kudła v. Poland* and *McKay v. the United Kingdom*), as well as prior judgments concerning similar detention issues in Ukraine (such as *Kharchenko v. Ukraine* and *Ignatov v. Ukraine*). The Committee met in private to deliberate on the admissibility and merits of the application on 16 January 2020.

case_name: CASE OF CHERNOV v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Mr. Oleksandr Gennadiyovych Chernov, a Ukrainian national. The respondent State is Ukraine. ### Key Factual Circumstances and Procedural History
On 20 June 2007, the applicant was arrested in Sumy, Ukraine. On 21 June 2007, the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found him guilty of the administrative offence of "minor disorderly acts" under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
