Following the legislature's failure to act, the Constitutional Court ruled in January 2012 that the unconstitutional provisions would lose legal validity, which occurred on 28 February 2012. Consequently, local elections could not be held in Mostar during the 2012 and 2016 election cycles. The mayor of Mostar, who was elected by the city council in 2009, has operated under a "technical mandate" since 2012. In the absence of an elected city council, the mayor has repeatedly adopted the city budget through exceptional legislative workarounds enacted by the Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Various international bodies, including the United Nations High Representative and the Council of Europe, have repeatedly called on domestic political actors to resolve the legislative deadlock. ### The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant complained about her prolonged inability to vote or stand in local elections in Mostar. She alleged that this situation amounted to discrimination based on her place of residence, relying on Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which provides a general prohibition of discrimination. ### The Government's Position
The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina raised objections regarding the admissibility of the application. They argued that the application was an *actio popularis*, asserting that the applicant had not been directly disenfranchised by any specific and individual measure of interference. Additionally, the Government contended that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies as required by Article 35 § 1 of the Convention, noting that she had not utilized any domestic legal remedies for the alleged violation of her rights. ### Procedural History
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 4 June 2018. On 15 January 2019, the Court gave notice to the Government of the complaint concerning Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the Convention, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court subsequently deliberated on the case in private on 8 October 2019.

case_name: CASE OF KOPYTETS AND SHTOPKO v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Kopytets and Shtopko v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 9706/19 and 9709/19)

#### 1. Main Parties
The case involves two individual applicants, Mr. Kopytets (application no. 9706/19) and Mr. Shtopko (application no. 9709/19), both of whom are Ukrainian nationals. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applications stem from separate domestic criminal proceedings initiated by Ukrainian authorities against each of the applicants. In both instances, the criminal prosecutions remained pending before the domestic authorities and courts for an extended period. In addition to the ongoing criminal proceedings, the applicant in application no. 9709/19 was subjected to domestic legal measures that restricted his freedom of movement, a common occurrence for defendants undergoing active criminal prosecution or investigation. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants brought several complaints before the European Court of Human Rights, relying on the following provisions of the Convention:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** Both applicants alleged that the total duration of the criminal proceedings against them was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement. They argued that the delays were unreasonable under the circumstances of their cases and were primarily attributable to the conduct of the domestic authorities. *   **Article 13 (Right to an Effective Remedy):** The applicants asserted that Ukrainian domestic law did not provide them with an effective remedy. Specifically, they argued that they had no accessible legal mechanism to either accelerate the delayed criminal proceedings or obtain adequate compensation for the protracted duration of the trial. *   **Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (Freedom of Movement):** The applicant in application no. 9709/19 raised an additional complaint concerning the restrictions placed on his liberty of movement during the criminal process, alleging that the travel restrictions imposed on him were unjustified or disproportionate. #### 4. The Government's Position
Following the introduction of the applications, the Ukrainian Government was formally notified of the complaints. The available text does not outline the specific factual or legal arguments submitted by the Government in defense of the domestic proceedings, noting only that they were given notice of the applications as the respondent state. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the Court's Judgment
The applicants lodged their applications with the European Court of Human Rights in early 2019. Recognizing that both applications shared a similar factual and legal subject matter—namely, the length of criminal proceedings in Ukraine and the availability of domestic remedies—the Court deemed it appropriate to join the applications to examine them together in a single proceeding. The Court subsequently proceeded to deliberate on the admissibility and merits of the complaints.

case_name: CASE OF YAKUBA v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Yakuba v. Ukraine* (Application no. 1452/09)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Vasyl Ivanovych Yakuba, a Ukrainian national born in 1971. The respondent state is Ukraine, represented before the European Court of Human Rights by its Government Agent. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In early 2007, Ukrainian police targeted the applicant—who had prior drug-related convictions—in an undercover test purchase operation. An undercover agent, P., allegedly purchased opium from the applicant on three occasions: February 26, March 6, and March 9, 2007. The first transaction was video-recorded using a hidden camera. On March 9, 2007, the applicant was arrested. Police officers used physical force and handcuffed him. The applicant admitted that he had a drug-filled syringe at the moment of his arrest and had attempted to eject the liquid to destroy the evidence. However, he alleged that after he was immobilized on the ground, officers continued to drag him around, causing him pain and humiliation. A medical examination conducted on March 15, 2007, revealed abrasions on the applicant’s hand, shin, and knees, which the medical expert noted could have been sustained on the day of his arrest. During the investigation, the police investigator reviewed the video recording of the first transaction but denied the defense's request to view it, citing the need to protect the undercover agent's identity. The investigator also reported that police were unable to locate a witness, B., whom the applicant claimed could verify he only possessed drugs for personal use. #### 3. Procedural History (Domestic)
In May 2007, prosecutors declined to initiate criminal proceedings against the arresting officers. The applicant did not appeal this decision but raised his ill-treatment complaints during his subsequent criminal trial. At trial before the Kirovograd Kirov District Court, the applicant maintained he possessed drugs only for personal use and denied selling them. The court denied his requests to view the video recording, to summon the undercover agent P., to locate witness B., and to examine the forensic expert. On June 26, 2007, the court convicted the applicant of drug trafficking and sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment. The conviction relied on pre-trial statements by P., testimony from a police officer and an attesting witness, a marked banknote found on the applicant, and forensic analysis. The Kirovograd Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on March 25, 2008, additionally citing the investigator's written report of the video recording. On September 4, 2008, a Supreme Court judge refused cassation review. Following his conviction, the applicant’s requests to obtain copies of court records to prepare an application to the European Court of Human Rights were repeatedly denied by domestic courts, which stated that domestic law did not allow convicts to access case files after proceedings concluded. #### 4. The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging:
*   **Article 3:** That he was ill-treated by police during his arrest. *   **Article 6:** That his trial was unfair because he was denied access to the video recording of the test purchase and was unable to cross-examine the undercover agent P. *   **Article 34:** That the domestic authorities' refusal to provide copies of case documents hindered his right of individual petition. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Ukrainian Government contested the applicant's claims. Regarding Article 3, they argued the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not appealing the prosecutor's decision, and that the force used during the arrest was proportionate and necessary to prevent the destruction of evidence. Regarding Article 6, the Government maintained that the applicant had been given sufficient time to prepare his defense and that all relevant witnesses had been examined.

case_name: CASE OF BURLAKOV AND LYSENKO v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Main Parties
The applicants are Mr. Yevgeniy Aleksandrovich Burlakov and Mr. Ilya Vladimirovich Lysenko, both Ukrainian nationals. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine. ### Key Factual Circumstances
At approximately 11:30 p.m. on June 25, 2010, the applicants were arrested by officers of the State Security Service on suspicion of drug trafficking. Following their arrest, both applicants underwent medical examinations. On June 26 and during a subsequent expert examination from June 29 to July 2, 2010, Mr. Burlakov was found to have minor bruises on his arms, trunk, right thigh, and legs, which experts concluded were caused by blunt solid objects. Mr. Lysenko was examined on June 29, 2010, and was found to have minor bruises on his head, right arm, and right leg, also attributed to blunt solid objects. The applicants were placed in pre-trial detention, which was repeatedly extended by domestic courts. In July 2011, they were committed for trial. On August 15, 2014, the Kominternovskyy District Court of Kharkiv convicted them of drug trafficking and sentenced them to over nine years' imprisonment. During their detention and transport to court hearings, the applicants experienced conditions involving prison vans and transit cells with poor ventilation, high temperatures, exposure to tobacco smoke, and a lack of food. On two occasions, Mr. Burlakov was transported alongside inmates suffering from tuberculosis. Mr. Lysenko also required medical attention during his detention for spinal disc herniation and a gall bladder polyp. ### Applicants' Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), the applicants alleged that they were beaten and ill-treated by security officers during and after their arrest, and that the state failed to conduct an effective investigation into these events (Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention). They also complained about the poor conditions of their transport and detention on hearing days, inadequate medical assistance for Mr. Lysenko, the length and justification of their pre-trial detention (Article 5), and the alleged hindrance of their communication with the ECHR (Article 34). ### Government's Position
The Ukrainian Government did not submit comments regarding the merits of the applicants' allegations of ill-treatment and the lack of an effective domestic investigation. ### Procedural History
At the domestic level, prosecutors repeatedly refused to initiate criminal proceedings regarding the alleged ill-treatment. For Mr. Burlakov, an investigator's refusal in August 2010 was upheld by the Chervonozavodskyy District Court in April 2011 and the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal in July 2011, on the basis that the injuries were minor and officers were authorized to use force to overcome resistance. For Mr. Lysenko, a similar refusal in September 2010 was upheld by the District Court in December 2010 and the Court of Appeal in July 2011, which noted that his injuries appeared to predate the arrest. Regarding detention conditions, the Kharkiv regional prosecutor's office dismissed Mr. Burlakov's complaints in 2012 and 2013, though they acknowledged the tuberculosis exposure. In October 2013, the Ombudsman's office informed Mr. Lysenko that his complaints about transit cell conditions were partly substantiated, prompting a remedial plan. The applicants lodged their application with the ECHR on March 17, 2011. On December 7, 2016, the Government was officially notified of the complaints, while other portions of the application were declared inadmissible.

case_name: CASE OF ANTONOV AND OTHERS v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA AND RUSSIA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Antonov and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*

#### 1. Main Parties
The case involves six individual applicants: 
*   **Evghenii Antonov** (a Russian national) and **Iryna Antonova** (a Ukrainian national)
*   **Alexandru Băluţă** and **Tamara Băluţă** (both Moldovan nationals)
*   **Oleksandr Bezrodnii** (a Ukrainian national) and **Liudmila Bezrodnyaya** (a Russian national)

The respondent states are the **Republic of Moldova** and the **Russian Federation**. #### 2. Procedural History (Up to the Court's Judgment)
The applicants lodged three separate applications with the European Court of Human Rights on December 23, 2009. The Court officially communicated these applications to both respondent governments on May 3, 2010. Given the closely related factual and legal issues, the Court subsequently decided to join the three applications into a single proceeding. #### 3. Key Factual Circumstances and Applicants' Allegations
The applications stem from the arrest and detention of three of the applicants—Evghenii Antonov, Alexandru Băluţă, and Oleksandr Bezrodnii—by the authorities of the self-proclaimed "Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria" (MRT) between 2004 and 2009. *   **Evghenii Antonov** was arrested in August 2009 on drug and weapon charges. He and Iryna Antonova alleged that he was held in dark, damp, and unhygienic cells. They also reported that he participated in a mass hunger strike with approximately 90 other detainees to protest these conditions, during which independent observers, including the OSCE, were barred from entering the facility. Antonov was convicted by a local court in November 2010. *   **Alexandru Băluţă** was arrested in 2004 on murder and arson charges, allegedly suffered physical abuse, and was rearrested in September 2009. He and Tamara Băluţă alleged that his detention conditions were inhuman, characterized by a lack of basic hygiene, no opportunities for daily exercise, and restricted family contact. They further alleged that special riot police entered the facility and assaulted prisoners during a hunger strike in October 2009. *   **Oleksandr Bezrodnii** was arrested in July 2009. He and Liudmila Bezrodnyaya alleged that local militia severely beat him to coerce a confession, resulting in visible head and body injuries. Bezrodnii described his detention conditions as highly substandard, citing extreme overcrowding, sharing cells with individuals suffering from infectious diseases, lack of clean bedding, poor sanitation, and inedible food. He also alleged a denial of necessary medical treatment. He was convicted in 2010, though his sentence was later quashed and sent for re-examination. #### 4. Governments' Positions
*   **On Jurisdiction:** The Russian Government asserted that the applicants did not fall within its jurisdiction, arguing the case was inadmissible against the Russian Federation. The Moldovan Government did not contest its territorial jurisdiction over the region but emphasized its lack of de facto control. *   **On the Merits of the Article 3 Complaints:** The Moldovan Government maintained it could not verify the allegations due to its lack of physical control over the Transdniestrian territory. The Russian Government contended that because the region is Moldovan territory and Russia exercised no control over the events, only Moldova could address the merits of the claims.

case_name: CASE OF ELČIĆ AND OTHERS v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case: *Elčić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves six individual applicants, led by the first applicant, Mr. Elčić (Application no. 34524/15 and five others). The applicants, all nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were represented in the proceedings by Mr. M. Alić, a lawyer practicing in Tešanj. The respondent party is the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The dispute arose from the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final and binding domestic decisions. The applicants had previously initiated domestic legal proceedings within Bosnia and Herzegovina, which resulted in final judicial or administrative decisions delivered in their favour. These domestic decisions ordered the state authorities or public entities to take specific actions, such as making monetary payments or providing other forms of redress. However, despite the binding nature of these domestic rulings, the state authorities either failed to execute them entirely or delayed their enforcement for an extended period. #### 3. The Applicants’ Main Allegations
The applicants alleged that the state's failure to enforce the final domestic decisions in a timely manner violated their rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, they relied on two main provisions:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** The applicants argued that the right to a fair hearing guaranteed by this Article includes the right to have final, binding judicial decisions executed. They asserted that the prolonged non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of the judgments rendered the judicial process ineffective. *   **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of Property):** The applicants contended that the final domestic decisions in their favour established legally binding pecuniary claims, which constituted "possessions" within the meaning of this Article. They argued that the state's failure to satisfy these claims in due time amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. #### 4. The Government’s Position
Following the lodgement of the applications, the European Court of Human Rights formally gave notice of the complaints to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, affording them the opportunity to submit their observations on the admissibility and merits of the cases. The available procedural text does not detail any specific arguments, justifications, or objections raised by the Government regarding the delays or the non-enforcement of the domestic decisions in question. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicants lodged six separate applications with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. Because the applications shared a virtually identical subject matter—specifically concerning the systemic issue of non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions in Bosnia and Herzegovina—the Court deemed it appropriate to join the applications to be examined together in a single proceeding. The Fourth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of three judges, subsequently deliberated on the joined applications in private to determine the admissibility and merits of the complaints.

case_name: CASE OF SAVRAN v. DENMARK
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Savran v. Denmark* (Application no. 57467/15)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Arıf Savran, a Turkish national born in 1985. *   **Respondent State:** The Kingdom of Denmark. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Mr. Savran moved from Turkey to Denmark in 1991 at the age of six under a family reunification scheme. His mother and four siblings live in Denmark, whereas he has no family or social network in Turkey, has not visited the country since 2001, and speaks Kurdish but virtually no Turkish. Mr. Savran has a history of severe mental illness and cognitive difficulties. He was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, mild intellectual disability (a diagnosis later subject to refinement), and cannabis dependence. His psychiatric treatment regimen requires daily Clozapine (Leponex) tablets and bi-weekly Risperdal Consta injections. Because Clozapine carries a risk of causing a life-threatening immune system defect, he requires regular somatic monitoring, including routine blood tests. In October 2008, the High Court of Eastern Denmark convicted Mr. Savran of assault under highly aggravating circumstances, which had resulted in the victim's death. He was sentenced to committal to a secure psychiatric unit for an indefinite period and ordered expelled from Denmark with a permanent re-entry ban. In August 2009, the Supreme Court upheld the expulsion order but modified the sentence to committal to forensic psychiatric care. #### 3. Procedural History (Domestic and European Court)
In 2012, the applicant’s guardian requested a review of his psychiatric sanction. In October 2014, the City Court of Copenhagen amended his sentence to outpatient psychiatric treatment. Under Section 50a of the Danish Aliens Act, the City Court also revoked the expulsion order, concluding that the applicant's state of health made expulsion "conclusively inappropriate" due to the high risk of relapse and violent reoffending without intensive outpatient follow-up, which it doubted he could access in Turkey. The prosecution appealed. In January 2015, the High Court of Eastern Denmark reversed the City Court's decision and upheld the expulsion. It found that the applicant could continue his medical treatment in Turkey, where psychiatric care and the necessary medications were available, and that he could apply for free or subsidized treatment. The High Court emphasized the applicant's personal awareness of his illness and the gravity of his crime. On May 20, 2015, the Appeals Permission Board refused the applicant leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. Mr. Savran subsequently lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on November 16, 2015. #### 4. Applicant's Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that his deportation to Turkey would violate Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. *   **Under Article 3:** He argued that returning him to Turkey would lead to a rapid and serious relapse of his schizophrenia due to a lack of access to necessary, highly supervised psychiatric care, regular blood monitoring, and a supportive social network. *   **Under Article 8:** He contended that expulsion would disproportionately interfere with his private and family life, given his long-term residence in Denmark since childhood, his lack of ties to Turkey, and his language difficulties. #### 5. Government's Position
The Danish Government maintained that the expulsion would not violate the Convention. They argued that the domestic courts had thoroughly assessed the applicant's health and access to care in Turkey in line with international standards. They asserted that appropriate psychiatric treatment, medications, and Kurdish-speaking staff were available and accessible in Turkey, and that the expulsion struck a fair balance between the applicant's rights and the public interest in preventing crime.

case_name: CASE OF HODŽIĆ AND SIRĆO v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Hodžić and Sirćo v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Applications nos. 34526/15 and 34530/15)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicants in this case are domestic litigants, represented by Ms. H. Kapetan, a lawyer practicing in Travnik. The respondent party is the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The case arises from domestic legal proceedings within Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants successfully obtained final and binding domestic decisions in their favor from the national authorities. These domestic decisions ordered the state authorities to take specific actions. However, the applicants faced situations where these final decisions were either not enforced at all or experienced significant delays in their enforcement by the responsible state organs. #### 3. The Applicants’ Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained about the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of the domestic decisions delivered in their favor. They relied on two primary provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** The applicants argued that the right to a fair hearing guarantees not only the process of obtaining a judgment but also its effective execution. They asserted that the state's failure to enforce the final domestic decisions in a timely manner violated this right. *   **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of Property):** The applicants contended that the final domestic decisions ordering specific action in their favor constituted "possessions" within the meaning of this Article. They alleged that the ongoing non-enforcement deprived them of the peaceful enjoyment of these possessions. #### 4. The Government’s Position
Following the lodgment of the applications, the European Court of Human Rights gave formal notice of the complaints to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, affording them the opportunity to submit their observations on the admissibility and merits of the applicants' claims. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicants lodged their respective applications with the European Court of Human Rights in 2015 (registered under application numbers 34526/15 and 34530/15). Recognizing that both applications shared a similar subject matter concerning the non-enforcement of domestic rulings, the Court deemed it appropriate to join the applications to examine them together in a single procedure. The case was assigned to the Fourth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström, Georges Ravarani, and Jolien Schukking. The Committee convened to deliberate on the joined applications on June 6, 2019.

case_name: CASE OF ROMEVA v. NORTH MACEDONIA
step1_summary:
**Parties**
The case of *Romeva v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 32141/10) was brought by Ms. Olgica Romeva, a citizen of North Macedonia born in 1947, against the Republic of North Macedonia. **Key Factual Circumstances**
In May 2000, while receiving unemployment benefits, Ms. Romeva was instructed by the state Employment Bureau to apply for a retirement pension. She submitted an application containing only basic personal details, without attaching employment records. On 23 May 2000, the Pension and Disability Fund ("the Fund") approved her application, establishing that she met the sole statutory criterion at the time: a service period of at least 35 years. Ms. Romeva began receiving monthly pension payments. Between February and July 2007, the Fund conducted an internal audit and discovered that Ms. Romeva’s physical "employment booklet" was missing. The Fund concluded that she had not actually been employed between 1963 and 1967, meaning she fell short of the 35-year requirement. Consequently, on 18 October 2007, the Fund *proprio motu* annulled its May 2000 decision and discontinued her pension. In June 2008, the Fund filed a civil lawsuit against Ms. Romeva for unjust enrichment, seeking the reimbursement of MKD 645,138—the total amount of pension benefits paid to her between 2000 and 2007. The domestic civil courts ruled in favor of the Fund, and enforcement proceedings were subsequently initiated against her. In May 2012, the Fund also filed a criminal complaint against Ms. Romeva for submitting falsified information, but the Public Prosecution rejected it because the statutory limitation period had expired. According to official records, the pension had been Ms. Romeva's sole source of income since 2006. However, following legislative changes introducing an age-based criterion, Ms. Romeva applied for and was granted a new retirement pension on 3 November 2009. **Procedural History**
Ms. Romeva challenged the Fund's October 2007 annulment decision through administrative channels. After her initial appeal received no timely response, she filed an action with the Administrative Court in February 2008. Although the Second-Instance Commission formally dismissed her administrative appeal in April 2008, the Administrative Court quashed that dismissal in November 2008, ruling that the Fund had unlawfully applied a 2006 statutory provision retroactively. In March 2009, the Second-Instance Commission issued a new decision dismissing her appeal, this time relying on provisions of the Administrative Proceedings Act regarding the reopening of cases based on erroneous documentation. Ms. Romeva challenged this decision, but the Administrative Court dismissed her action in October 2009. She then appealed to the Supreme Court, which dismissed her appeal on 26 April 2010, upholding the administrative decisions. Ms. Romeva subsequently lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights. On 8 September 2014, her complaints were communicated to the respondent Government. **The Applicant's Allegations**
Before the European Court, Ms. Romeva alleged that she had been deprived of her pension in breach of the principle of legal certainty, relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She argued that she had acted in good faith, had not submitted false documents, and that under domestic law, the responsibility for maintaining accurate employment records rested entirely with employers and the Fund. She contended that the retroactive cancellation of her pension and the subsequent demand for reimbursement of seven years of benefits imposed an individual and excessive burden on her. **The Government's Position**
The Government argued that the application was inadmissible or otherwise unfounded. They maintained that the revision of Ms. Romeva's pension was part of a legitimate, large-scale campaign to correct erroneously granted pensions and prevent the abuse of public funds. They asserted that Ms. Romeva had acted in bad faith by knowingly concealing that she did not meet the statutory criteria. The Government contended that the measures taken were lawful, in the public interest, and proportionate, particularly since she was subsequently granted a new pension under the revised legislative criteria in November 2009.

case_name: CASE OF J.D. AND A v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *J.D. and A v. the United Kingdom* (Applications nos. 32949/17 and 34614/17)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicants are two British nationals, J.D. and A. The respondent party is the Government of the United Kingdom. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In 2012, the UK Government introduced the Housing Benefit (Amendment) Regulations 2012, commonly referred to as the "bedroom tax" or the under-occupancy penalty. Under these regulations, social housing tenants deemed to have more bedrooms than permitted by the statutory criteria had their Housing Benefit reduced by 14% (for one extra bedroom) or 25% (for two or more extra bedrooms). *   **The First Applicant (J.D.):** J.D. lived with her adult, severely disabled daughter in a three-bedroom social housing property. The home had been extensively and specifically adapted to accommodate her daughter's complex physical and learning needs, featuring wheelchair access, ceiling hoists, an accessible bathroom, and an internal lift. Under the 2012 regulations, J.D.’s household was deemed to have one spare bedroom, resulting in a 14% reduction in her Housing Benefit. *   **The Second Applicant (A):** A lived with her son in a three-bedroom social housing property. Following severe domestic violence and rape by a former partner, A’s home was fortified under the police-backed "Sanctuary Scheme." The adaptations included reinforcing the property and converting the attic into a secure "panic room" to protect A and her son from potential attacks. Under the regulations, A’s household was also deemed to have one spare bedroom, resulting in a 14% reduction in her Housing Benefit. To cover the rent shortfalls, both applicants had to apply for Discretionary Housing Payments (DHPs)—a temporary, cash-limited, and discretionary fund administered by local authorities. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the reduction in their benefits constituted unlawful discrimination. They relied on Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 8 (respect for private and family life and home). *   **J.D.** alleged discrimination on the basis of her daughter's disability, arguing that the regulations failed to make reasonable accommodations for disabled individuals who have an objective, medical need for specially adapted housing. *   **A** alleged discrimination on the basis of her gender, arguing that the under-occupancy penalty disproportionately affected victims of domestic violence—who are overwhelmingly women—residing in Sanctuary Scheme homes. Both applicants argued that the discretionary and precarious nature of DHPs could not justify the discriminatory impact of the benefit reduction. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Government maintained that the regulations pursued legitimate social and economic policy aims: reducing public expenditure, encouraging social tenants to move to smaller properties, and optimizing the allocation of social housing stock. They argued that the applicants were not discriminated against because they received financial support through DHPs to cover their rent shortfalls. Furthermore, the Government contended that using a discretionary scheme like DHPs was a flexible, appropriate, and cost-effective way to address individual cases of hardship, rather than creating rigid statutory exemptions. They asserted that such socio-economic measures fell within the state's wide margin of appreciation and were not "manifestly without reasonable foundation."

#### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
Both applicants initiated domestic judicial review proceedings. *   In J.D.’s case, the Divisional Court and the Court of Appeal dismissed her claims, finding that while the regulations did discriminate against disabled persons needing extra accommodation, the difference in treatment was justified under the "manifestly without reasonable foundation" test, and that DHPs were an appropriate remedy. *   In A’s case, the High Court dismissed her claim, but the Court of Appeal subsequently ruled in her favor, concluding that the discrimination against her was unjustified because Sanctuary Scheme participants formed a small, easily identifiable class for whom statutory exemptions could easily be drafted. The Government appealed the decision in A's case, and the two cases were joined before the UK Supreme Court. In November 2016, the Supreme Court dismissed both applicants' claims. The majority held that the "manifestly without reasonable foundation" test applied to welfare benefit schemes, and that the Government’s decision to address individual needs through the DHP scheme rather than statutory exemptions was not unreasonable. The applicants subsequently lodged their applications with the European Court of Human Rights in April and May 2017. The Court joined the applications and declared them admissible.

case_name: CASE OF TSUKUR AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Tsukur and Others v. Ukraine*

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves three individual applicants, led by Mr. Tsukur (Application no. 53132/18 and two others), who lodged applications against the state of Ukraine. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicants were individuals held in state custody within Ukrainian detention facilities. During their respective periods of incarceration, they were subjected to detention conditions that they characterized as highly inadequate. The primary factual circumstances centered on the physical environment of their confinement, particularly concerning a severe lack of personal space within their prison cells, alongside other alleged material and sanitary shortcomings in the facilities. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants raised two primary complaints under the European Convention on Human Rights:
*   **Article 3 (Prohibition of Inhuman or Degrading Treatment):** The applicants alleged that the physical conditions of their detention—specifically the overcrowding, restricted living space, and general sub-standard environment—constituted degrading treatment. They argued that these conditions fell below the minimum standards of decency and respect for human dignity required under the Convention. *   **Article 13 (Right to an Effective Remedy):** The applicants further alleged that they did not have access to an effective preventive or compensatory remedy within the Ukrainian domestic legal system. They argued that there was no viable national authority or legal mechanism through which they could successfully complain about their detention conditions, secure improvements, or obtain compensation for the alleged violations. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Ukrainian Government was formally given notice of the applications by the European Court of Human Rights. Under the Court's standard procedure, the Government was represented in the proceedings and was provided the opportunity to submit its observations regarding the admissibility and merits of the applicants' complaints, as well as the availability of effective domestic remedies in Ukraine. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the Court's Judgment
The case originated from three separate applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applications were submitted on various dates, with the lead application (no. 53132/18) being filed in 2018. Following the receipt of the applications, the Court communicated the complaints to the Ukrainian Government, giving them formal notice of the proceedings. Having regard to the shared subject matter of the three applications—all of which concerned the conditions of detention in Ukraine and the alleged lack of domestic remedies—the Court decided to join the applications to examine them together in a single proceeding.

case_name: CASE OF SANCHYSHYN  v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Sanchyshyn v. Ukraine* (Application no. 81639/17)

#### 1. Main Parties
The case involves the applicant, an individual represented by Mr. O.V. Mytsyk, a lawyer practicing in Lviv, Ukraine. The respondent party is the State of Ukraine, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The application arises from domestic criminal proceedings initiated and conducted by Ukrainian authorities against the applicant. While the specific details of the underlying criminal charges are not elaborated in the main text, the proceedings spanned a duration that the applicant contested. Additionally, the circumstances of the case involved measures or restrictions that implicated the applicant's freedom of movement within the domestic jurisdiction during the course of the legal process. #### 3. The Applicant's Main Allegations
The applicant brought several complaints before the European Court of Human Rights, relying on the European Convention on Human Rights and its Protocols:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** The applicant complained that the overall length of the criminal proceedings against him was excessive and failed to comply with the "reasonable time" requirement. *   **Article 13 (Right to an Effective Remedy):** The applicant alleged that Ukrainian domestic law did not provide any effective legal remedy through which he could challenge the protracted nature of the criminal proceedings or seek redress for the delay. *   **Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (Freedom of Movement):** The applicant raised an additional complaint concerning restrictions on his liberty of movement, which arose in the context of the ongoing domestic criminal proceedings. #### 4. The Government's Position
Following the lodging of the application, the European Court of Human Rights gave official notice of the complaints to the Ukrainian Government. The provided text does not outline specific arguments, objections, or factual assertions submitted by the Government in response to the applicant's allegations. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant formally lodged the application (no. 81639/17) with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 November 2017, pursuant to Article 34 of the Convention. Following the submission, the Court communicated the application and gave notice of the complaints to the Ukrainian Government. The case was subsequently referred to the Fifth Section of the Court. It was assigned to a Committee composed of Judges Síofra O’Leary (President), Mārtiņš Mits, and Lado Chanturia, with Liv Tigerstedt serving as the Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated on the case in private on 14 February 2019, prior to issuing its judgment.

case_name: CASE OF VAN DE KOLK v. THE NETHERLANDS
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Van de Kolk v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 23192/15)

#### 1. Main Parties
The case was brought by Mr. Hugo Johannes Charles van de Kolk, a Dutch national (the applicant), against the Kingdom of the Netherlands (the Government). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 19 August 2009, the nineteen-year-old applicant was arrested on suspicion of distributing child pornography. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer. Before doing so, he participated in a "social interview" regarding his personal circumstances, during which he disclosed that he suffered from a brain disorder (cavernous hemangiomas). Once his lawyer became available, the applicant consulted him by telephone and, on his advice, declined to answer further questions. The following day, the applicant was interviewed twice regarding the suspected offense. At the start of these interviews, the applicant requested the presence of his lawyer, but was informed that this was not possible under the domestic practice at the time. During the questioning, the applicant experienced an epileptic seizure. The police suspended the interview to consult a doctor, after which the questioning resumed. The applicant made statements during these interviews that were later used as evidence against him. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
In March 2011, the Regional Court of The Hague convicted the applicant. While it found that the applicant should have been allowed to consult a lawyer before his first interview, it determined that this procedural omission did not invalidate the subsequent proceedings. On appeal in July 2013, the Court of Appeal of The Hague quashed the lower court's decision but convicted the applicant of the same offense, sentencing him to forty hours of community service. The Court of Appeal rejected the defense's argument that the applicant should have been treated as a vulnerable suspect due to his brain disorder or mental age. It held that, as an adult, he was not entitled to have a lawyer present during his interviews under the applicable *Salduz* jurisprudence. In November 2014, the Supreme Court of the Netherlands dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law with summary reasoning. #### 4. The Applicant's Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention. He alleged that he had been denied a fair trial because he was not permitted to have a lawyer present during his police interviews, a restriction he argued was particularly prejudicial given his vulnerability and medical condition. #### 5. Government's Position and Procedural History before the ECHR
The application was lodged on 8 May 2015. In 2016, the Government submitted a unilateral declaration admitting a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) and offering financial compensation, requesting the Court to strike the case out of its list. The applicant opposed this, arguing that Dutch law only permitted the reopening of domestic criminal proceedings on the basis of an ECHR judgment finding a violation, rather than a strike-out decision. In January 2018, the Court decided not to strike the case out, noting that the reopening of domestic proceedings was indeed not legally assured following a strike-out. The Court subsequently adjourned the case pending the Grand Chamber's ruling in *Beuze v. Belgium*. Regarding the merits of the application, the Government chose not to submit observations, citing subsequent domestic legislative and judicial reforms that had since aligned Dutch law with European standards regarding the right to legal assistance during police questioning.

case_name: CASE OF DOYLE v. IRELAND
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Doyle v. Ireland* (Application no. 51979/17)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Barry Doyle, an Irish national born in 1985, currently serving a life sentence for murder in Mountjoy Prison, Dublin. *   **Respondent State:** Ireland, represented by its Government Agent, Mr. Peter White of the Department of Foreign Affairs. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In the early hours of November 9, 2008, the applicant shot and killed a 28-year-old man, S.G., in Limerick. The killing was a case of mistaken identity arising from a local gang feud; the victim had no connection to criminal activity. On February 24, 2009, police arrested the applicant at his residence and brought him to a police station. He was informed of his rights, including the right of access to a solicitor. Over the course of several days, the applicant was subjected to over twenty video-recorded police interviews. While the applicant was permitted to consult with his solicitor prior to and between these interviews—both in person and via telephone—his solicitor was not permitted to be physically present inside the interrogation room during the questioning. Under police practice at the time, any request for a solicitor's physical presence during interrogation would have been denied. During his detention, police informed the applicant that his former girlfriend (the mother of his young daughter) had also been arrested and detained on suspicion of withholding information. During his fifteenth interview, following a brief telephone consultation with his solicitor, the applicant admitted to shooting the victim and provided specific details about the crime. His former girlfriend was released from custody shortly thereafter. #### 3. Procedural History
The applicant pleaded not guilty to the charge of murder. *   **First Trial (2011):** The trial was inconclusive as the jury failed to reach a verdict. *   **Second Trial (2012):** During the second trial before the Central Criminal Court, the applicant sought to exclude the admissions he had made during his police custody. The trial judge conducted a ten-day *voir dire* (a trial within a trial) to determine the admissibility of the confessions, viewing more than twenty hours of the recorded interviews. *   **Domestic Ruling:** The trial judge ruled the confessions admissible, finding beyond a reasonable doubt that they were voluntary. The judge determined that the applicant was physically and mentally strong throughout, that the interviews were professional and involved no oppression, and that any potential inducement regarding his former girlfriend's detention had been dissipated by his consultations with his solicitor. The applicant was subsequently convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. #### 4. Applicant's Main Allegations
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on July 12, 2017. He alleged a violation of Article 6 § 3 (c) (right to legal assistance of one’s own choosing) in conjunction with Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, he argued that the lack of entitlement to have his solicitor physically present during his police interrogations constituted a failure by Ireland to guarantee his right to a fair trial. #### 5. Government's Position and ECHR Proceedings
The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the application to the Irish Government on January 18, 2018, designating Ireland as the respondent State in the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF GAWLIK v. LIECHTENSTEIN
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Gawlik v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 23922/19)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Dr. Lothar Gawlik, a German national and specialist in general and internal medicine. He was employed as the deputy chief physician of the internal medicine department at the Liechtenstein National Hospital, the country's sole public hospital. *   **Respondent:** The Principality of Liechtenstein. *   **Other Key Figures:** Dr. H., the chief physician of the department and the applicant’s direct superior; and Mr. M., the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Dr. Gawlik was employed under an indefinite contract starting in June 2013. In September 2014, while conducting research in the hospital’s electronic medical database, he identified files of several deceased patients who had been treated with morphine by Dr. H. Believing the dosages and timing indicated active euthanasia, Dr. Gawlik met with Mr. M. to voice his concerns. Following Mr. M.'s advice, Dr. Gawlik bypassed the hospital's internal reporting systems—including an anonymous reporting tool—and lodged a formal criminal complaint against Dr. H. with the Public Prosecutor’s Office. He later expanded his allegations to encompass a total of ten patients. Subsequent investigations by the hospital’s foundation board and an external palliative care specialist revealed that the allegations were unfounded. The inquiries established that the patients had received appropriate palliative care, which was fully documented in their physical paper files. Dr. Gawlik had access to these paper files but had not consulted them, relying solely on the incomplete electronic records. Consequently, the hospital suspended Dr. Gawlik and dismissed him without notice in October 2014, citing an irretrievable breakdown of trust. Criminal proceedings against Dr. H. for euthanasia, as well as separate criminal proceedings against Dr. Gawlik for defamation, were ultimately discontinued. #### 3. The Applicant's Main Allegations
Before the domestic authorities and the European Court of Human Rights, Dr. Gawlik alleged that his superior had practiced active euthanasia on terminally ill patients. He further argued that his immediate dismissal violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. He maintained that he acted in good faith as a whistleblower to protect patient safety, that the electronic files provided sufficient grounds for his suspicions, and that internal reporting channels were either compromised or ineffective. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Government of Liechtenstein contended that the dismissal was a justified and proportionate measure to protect the reputation of the hospital and the accused chief physician. They argued that Dr. Gawlik had acted irresponsibly by failing to verify his serious allegations against the complete paper medical files before making external disclosures. Furthermore, the Government asserted that viable internal reporting mechanisms existed and should have been utilized before initiating external criminal proceedings. #### 5. Domestic Procedural History
*   **Regional Court:** Dismissed Dr. Gawlik's claim for compensation, ruling that the dismissal without notice was justified because he failed to verify his suspicions using the paper files and did not attempt internal resolution first. *   **Court of Appeal:** Reversed the lower decision, finding the dismissal unjustified. It held that reporting serious suspected crimes to external authorities was protected under freedom of expression and did not constitute a serious breach of the duty of loyalty. *   **Supreme Court:** Quashed the appellate judgment, reinstating the finding that the dismissal was lawful. The court emphasized that Dr. Gawlik’s failure to consult the paper files before lodging a criminal complaint constituted a severe breach of professional trust. *   **Constitutional Court:** Dismissed Dr. Gawlik's constitutional appeal. It concluded that while Article 10 was applicable, his failure to verify his suspicions against the paper files, despite knowing the electronic files were incomplete, rendered his conduct irresponsible, meaning his dismissal did not violate his right to freedom of expression. Following the exhaustion of domestic remedies, Dr. Gawlik lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights.

case_name: CASE OF M.L. v. SLOVAKIA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Ms. M.L., a Slovak national born in 1948. The respondent State is the Slovak Republic. The case also involves three domestic tabloid newspaper publishers against whom the applicant initiated civil proceedings in Slovakia. ### Factual Background
The applicant’s late son was a Roman Catholic priest. In 1999, he was convicted of sexual abuse and threatening the moral education of young people (relating to an attempt to have non-consensual oral sex with a minor). In 2002, he was convicted of disorderly conduct (relating to consensual oral sex with an adult man in public). Both convictions became legally spent in 2001 and 2003, respectively, and he died in 2006. Two years after his death, between March and May 2008, three tabloid newspapers published articles concerning his convictions, his intimate life, and his alleged suicide. The articles published his full name, details of his private life, and, in one instance, his photograph. They also alleged that he had confessed to his sexual orientation and that the Catholic Church had intervened by offering a guarantee to protect him from detention or prosecution. ### Domestic Procedural History
In August 2008, the applicant brought a civil action against the newspaper publishers under the Slovak Civil Code, seeking post-mortem protection of her son’s personal integrity and protection of her own personal integrity. She argued that the articles contained false and misleading information, used sensationalist language to increase sales, and caused her severe distress during her period of mourning. In May 2012, the Michalovce District Court partially ruled in the applicant's favor, ordering the publishers to apologize for untrue allegations regarding the Church's guarantee, but it dismissed her claims for financial compensation. In September 2013, the Košice Regional Court quashed this judgment due to insufficient reasoning. Upon remittal, the District Court issued a new judgment in February 2014 dismissing the applicant's action entirely. It concluded that as a parish priest, the son was a public figure who had to tolerate higher criticism, the publications concerned a matter of public interest, and the journalists' sources were sufficiently credible. The Regional Court upheld this dismissal in June 2015. The applicant then filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court of Slovakia, which declared it inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded in February 2017. ### Arguments Before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, complaining under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life). She alleged that the domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance between her right to respect for her private life and the publishers' right to freedom of expression. She argued that her deceased son was not a public figure, the spent convictions were old, and the sensationalist articles served no genuine public interest. She further maintained that the publications severely impacted her own well-being and privacy within her community. The Government argued that the domestic courts had properly balanced the competing rights under Articles 8 and 10 of the Convention. They contended that the moral conduct of a priest and the Church's response were matters of legitimate public interest. The Government also asserted that the journalists had acted in good faith, that the passage of time increased the public interest in open discussion, and that the applicant was not directly targeted or named in the articles.

case_name: CASE OF GRAŽULEVIČIŪTĖ v. LITHUANIA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Ms. Edita Gražulevičiūtė, a Lithuanian national, doctor, and clinical researcher. The respondent is the Government of the Republic of Lithuania, represented by the State Medicines Control Agency (SMCA). ### Factual Circumstances
In 2011, the applicant was acting as a clinical researcher in a trial of the drug tocilizumab. Following the death of a patient participating in the trial, the SMCA ordered an unscheduled inspection. The resulting inspection report identified two critical violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules: a failure to accept the patient for an unscheduled appointment and a failure to report serious side-effects. Consequently, in January 2012, the head of the SMCA suspended the applicant from the clinical trial and prohibited her from undertaking new trials. Meanwhile, a forensic expert report in separate criminal proceedings concluded that the patient had died of rapid sepsis, which was unrelated to the applicant's actions. ### Domestic Procedural History
The applicant challenged the suspension orders in court. On 6 December 2013, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court fully allowed her claim and annulled the suspension orders. This decision was not appealed and became final. The applicant subsequently lodged a claim against the State for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages resulting from her suspension. On 4 November 2015, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court partially allowed her claim, awarding her damages. The court held that, under domestic procedural law, the facts established in the final 2013 judgment did not need to be proven again, meaning the unlawfulness of the SMCA's actions was already established. Both parties appealed. On 30 January 2017, the Supreme Administrative Court of Lithuania reversed the lower court's decision and dismissed the applicant's claim in its entirety. It held that the annulment of an administrative decision does not automatically establish the "unlawfulness" required for state tort liability. The Supreme Administrative Court re-examined the factual circumstances surrounding the clinical trial and concluded that the SMCA had acted within its competence and in accordance with the law to protect patient safety, meaning there were no unlawful actions to trigger state liability. ### Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Supreme Administrative Court failed to respect the *res judicata* effect of the final 2013 judgment. She argued that the court breached the principle of legal certainty by reassessing the same factual circumstances and reaching an opposite conclusion, which rendered the first set of proceedings devoid of legal effect. She also complained under Article 8 regarding the lack of compensation for the damage caused to her professional reputation. ### Government’s Position
The Government argued that there was no breach of the principle of legal certainty. They maintained that the two sets of domestic proceedings had distinct legal scopes: the first concerned the reasonableness of the suspension, while the second concerned the legal standards for state tort liability. The Government asserted that the Supreme Administrative Court did not question the first court's factual findings but merely assessed whether the SMCA had acted within its lawful authority, which did not contradict the prior annulment of the suspension.

case_name: CASE OF M.F. v. NORWAY
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *M.F. v. Norway* (Application no. 5947/19)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves the applicant, Ms. M.F., a Norwegian national born in 1978, and the respondent State, the Kingdom of Norway. The dispute centers on the applicant’s daughter, X, who was born in December 2016. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant is a mother of four children. Her two oldest children, Y and Z, had been subject to municipal child welfare assistance measures since 2013 due to concerns regarding hygiene and school attendance. In 2016, while pregnant with X, the applicant moved in with a new partner, B. Shortly thereafter, police stopped B under suspicion of driving under the influence and discovered illegal drugs in their apartment, which was described as chaotic and unhygienic. Following X’s birth in December 2016, hospital staff and child welfare services raised concerns regarding the applicant’s hygiene, her perceived indifference to the newborn's needs, and B’s substance abuse. Although the applicant subsequently separated from B and relocated, the child welfare services applied for a public care order for X in May 2017. The services argued that the placement would likely be long-term, potentially leading to adoption, and recommended severely restricted contact to allow X to securely attach to her foster parents. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
In December 2017, the County Social Welfare Board issued a care order for X, finding that the applicant failed to comprehend X’s needs and that her caregiving deficiencies were linked to her personality. The Board set the applicant's contact rights at two hours, three times per year, under supervision. The applicant sought judicial review. In February 2018, the District Court upheld the care order and contact restrictions. Relying on an expert psychologist's report, the court concluded that the applicant suffered from a damaged ability to form relations, resulting in the emotional neglect of X. It determined that therapeutic intervention for the applicant would take years, making long-term foster care in X's best interests. The High Court refused leave to appeal in May 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's final appeal in July 2018. In subsequent domestic developments, the applicant applied to lift the care order in February 2019. While the Board initially rejected the request, the District Court ultimately ruled to lift the care order on June 22, 2020. X was returned to the applicant’s care on July 13, 2020. #### 4. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life). She alleged that the domestic proceedings resulting in the care order for X and the severe restrictions placed on her contact rights violated her right to respect for her family life. #### 5. Government Position and ECtHR Proceedings
The Norwegian Government submitted observations contesting the applicant's claims. Additionally, the Governments of the Czech and Slovak Republics, along with the Ordo Iuris Institute of Legal Culture, were granted leave to intervene as third parties. The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible.

case_name: CASE OF EFENDIĆ v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Efendić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 37130/19)

#### 1. The Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Mr. Efendić, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, represented by Mr. O. Eterović, a lawyer practicing in Sarajevo. * **Respondent State:** Bosnia and Herzegovina. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The case centers on the non-enforcement of a final domestic decision rendered by the national authorities in favor of the applicant. This domestic decision ordered the state authorities to take specific, concrete actions. Despite the binding nature of the decision, the domestic authorities failed to fully execute or enforce the ordered actions, leading to a prolonged delay. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant lodged a complaint before the European Court of Human Rights alleging that the continuous non-enforcement of the domestic decision violated his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. He relied on two specific provisions:
* **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** The applicant argued that the right to a fair hearing guarantees not only the process of obtaining a judgment but also the actual execution of that judgment. He maintained that the state's failure to enforce the final domestic decision in a timely manner deprived him of an effective judicial remedy. * **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of Property):** The applicant asserted that the domestic decision ordering specific action in his favor constituted a "possession" under the terms of the Convention. He argued that the authorities' failure to enforce this decision amounted to an unjustified interference with his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was officially given notice of the application in accordance with the Court's procedural rules. The provided text does not detail any specific arguments, justifications, or objections raised by the Government regarding the non-enforcement or the delays in executing the domestic decision. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
Following the non-enforcement of the domestic decision, the applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 June 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention. The case was assigned to the Fourth Section of the Court and was examined by a Committee composed of:
* Armen Harutyunyan (President),
* Jolien Schukking (Judge),
* Ana Maria Guerra Martins (Judge),
* and Liv Tigerstedt (Acting Deputy Section Registrar). After the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formally notified of the application, the Committee deliberated on the case in private on 21 January 2021.

case_name: CASE OF E.H. v. NORWAY
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: E.H. v. Norway

#### 1. Main Parties
The case involves Mr. E.H., a Norwegian national born in 1994 (the applicant), who lodged an application against the Kingdom of Norway (the respondent Government). The applicant is the biological father of a boy, X, born in June 2015. The other key individuals involved are B (the child’s biological mother) and X’s foster parents. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Immediately following X’s birth in June 2015, child welfare services implemented an emergency placement order due to concerns regarding both parents' caregiving abilities. In October 2015, the County Social Welfare Board issued a formal care order placing X in long-term foster care. The Board noted that B had cognitive limitations and that both parents struggled to meet the child's needs during supervised contact sessions. An expert psychological assessment in March 2016 revealed that X had extraordinary care needs, including epilepsy and severe eczema. The expert concluded that B was unable to meet these needs and that the applicant, while cooperative and showing potential for improvement, had cognitive limitations and a low tolerance for stress. Consequently, the applicant's contact rights were limited to three supervised two-hour visits per year. The applicant supported the long-term foster care arrangement but sought contact. In November 2017, when X was two and a half years old, the child welfare services applied to withdraw the biological parents' parental responsibilities and authorize his adoption by the foster parents, with whom he had lived since infancy. #### 3. Procedural History
In January 2018, the County Social Welfare Board authorized the adoption. It found that reuniting X with his biological parents was permanently unrealistic—a point the parents conceded—and that adoption was in X's best interests to ensure stability. The applicant and B challenged this decision before the City Court. In July 2018, the City Court upheld the adoption. The court declined to appoint a new expert, choosing instead to rely on general research regarding the benefits of adoption for vulnerable children. It emphasized X's vulnerability, his lack of attachment to his biological parents, and his strong bond with his foster parents. One lay judge dissented, arguing that relying on general research was insufficient to justify severing biological ties. The High Court refused the parents leave to appeal in November 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed their subsequent appeals on January 28, 2019. #### 4. Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life) that the withdrawal of his parental responsibilities and the authorization of X's adoption were unjustified. He argued that adoption was not in X's best interests and that such a decision should not have been made without an updated, case-specific expert assessment, rather than relying on general research. #### 5. Government’s Position
The Norwegian Government argued that the interference with the applicant's Article 8 rights was "necessary in a democratic society." They emphasized that the applicant had agreed he could not provide care for X and did not seek the child's return or increased contact. The Government maintained that the domestic authorities had a thorough and sufficient factual basis to conclude that adoption was in the child's best interests.

case_name: CASE OF SANCHEZ v. FRANCE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Sanchez v. France* (Application no. 45581/15)

#### 1. Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Julien Sanchez, a French national, who at the material time was a local councillor, a Front National (FN) candidate for the French parliamentary elections, and the manager of his public Facebook page. * **Respondent:** The French Republic (represented by the French Government). * **Other Key Figures:** F.P. (a Member of the European Parliament and political opponent of the applicant), L.T. (the partner of F.P. and the complainant), and S.B. and L.R. (third-party Facebook users and political supporters of the applicant). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 24 October 2011, Mr. Sanchez published a post on the publicly accessible "wall" of his Facebook account criticizing the website of his political opponent, F.P. On the same day, S.B. posted a comment on the thread associating the town of Nîmes with mosques, sharia, and drug dealers, ending with "kisses to Leila" (referring to F.P.’s partner, L.T., who has a North African-sounding name). Another user, L.R., posted three comments associating the local Muslim community with crime, drug trafficking, and insecurity. On 25 October 2011, L.T. discovered the comments, felt personally targeted by the remarks, and confronted S.B., who immediately deleted his post. On 26 October 2011, L.T. filed a criminal complaint against Mr. Sanchez, S.B., and L.R. On 27 October 2011, Mr. Sanchez posted a message asking his Facebook followers to be careful with their comments, but he did not delete L.R.’s comments. During an investigation on 6 December 2011, authorities found that L.R.’s comments were still visible on the applicant's Facebook wall. Mr. Sanchez subsequently restricted public access to his page. #### 3. Procedural History (Domestic Courts)
Mr. Sanchez, S.B., and L.R. were prosecuted for incitement to hatred or violence. On 28 February 2013, the Nîmes Criminal Court convicted all three defendants. Under section 93-3 of the Law of 29 July 1982, Mr. Sanchez was held criminally liable as the "producer" of an online public communication service for failing to act promptly to delete the illegal comments once he became aware of them. He was sentenced to a fine of EUR 4,000. Mr. Sanchez appealed. On 18 October 2013, the Nîmes Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but reduced the fine to EUR 3,000, finding that his status as a politician required heightened vigilance and that he had deliberately left L.R.’s comments online. On 17 March 2015, the Court of Cassation dismissed Mr. Sanchez's appeal, ruling that the restriction on his freedom of expression was compatible with Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Mr. Sanchez subsequently lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. #### 4. Applicant's Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mr. Sanchez alleged that his criminal conviction violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. He argued that:
* The domestic law was not foreseeable in its application, as he could not have anticipated being held criminally liable for comments written by third parties. * He had no immediate knowledge of the comments; S.B.'s post was deleted by the author within 24 hours, and L.T. had never directly requested the deletion of the remaining comments. * Political debate during election campaigns requires the highest level of protection, and the comments merely expressed views on local immigration and security. * Holding an account owner liable when the actual authors of the comments had already been identified and punished was disproportionate and would have a chilling effect, effectively forcing users to disable comment sections entirely. #### 5. Government's Position
The French Government maintained that the interference with the applicant's freedom of expression was justified under Article 10 § 2. They argued that:
* The conviction was "prescribed by law" under a foreseeable legal framework governing online "producers" of public communication services. * The measure pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation and rights of others against hate speech targeting Muslims and L.T. * The comments exceeded the limits of acceptable political debate and constituted hate speech, which does not enjoy robust protection. * As a political candidate, Mr. Sanchez had special "duties and responsibilities" to monitor his public page, and his failure to promptly delete L.R.’s comments, even after being alerted to the controversy, justified the proportionate criminal fine.

case_name: CASE OF VELICHKO v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Velichko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 22273/12)

#### 1. The Main Parties
* **The Applicant:** Mr. Vladyslav Viktorovych Velichko, a Ukrainian national born in 1973. He has a Group III disability status and was diagnosed with HIV in 1996. * **The Respondent:** The Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 22 October 2010, the applicant was placed in pre-trial detention at the Izmayil Detention Centre (Izmayil SIZO) on suspicion of theft. Over the next several months, he was diagnosed with clinical stage IV HIV, hepatitis C, and other illnesses. Because the Izmayil SIZO lacked the capacity to provide antiretroviral treatment (ART), the applicant was transferred to the Odesa SIZO in May 2011. Between June and August 2011, medical staff at the Odesa SIZO and the regional AIDS centre offered the applicant out-patient ART and tuberculosis preventative therapy. According to official records, the applicant refused this treatment on multiple occasions. Upon his transfer back to the Izmayil SIZO in August 2011, the applicant signed a statement indicating he would refuse ART in any penitentiary facility. Between late 2011 and early 2012, the applicant’s health deteriorated significantly; a February 2012 test showed his CD4 count had dropped to 79 cells/mm³. The applicant and his lawyer repeatedly petitioned the domestic court to change his detention to a non-custodial measure so he could seek specialized in-patient hospital care. In April 2012, a domestic forensic medical examination concluded that while the applicant suffered from multiple severe conditions, his illnesses were not legally incompatible with detention. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He argued that the penitentiary authorities failed to provide him with adequate medical monitoring and treatment for his life-threatening conditions between 22 October 2010 and 16 May 2012. He further asserted that he was only able to receive adequate medical care in a public hospital after the European Court of Human Rights intervened. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government maintained that the applicant had received regular medical examinations and tests while in custody. They asserted that the Izmayil SIZO was sufficiently equipped with the necessary medications for ART during the period in question. Furthermore, the Government emphasized that the applicant had repeatedly and voluntarily refused the prescribed out-patient treatments and had not filed any direct complaints with the SIZO administration regarding his medical care. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
On 16 April 2012, the applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), alongside a request for interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. On 23 April 2012, the ECtHR indicated to the Ukrainian Government that the applicant should immediately be provided with appropriate in-patient treatment in a specialized AIDS hospital. Following this indication, the applicant was admitted to a public infectious disease hospital on 14 May 2012. On 16 May 2012, the Izmayil Local Court ordered his release from detention on an undertaking not to abscond, citing his poor health. Consequently, on 6 July 2012, the ECtHR lifted the interim measure. In its admissibility decision, the ECtHR split the application into two periods:
* **22 October 2010 to 24 June 2011:** The Court declared this part of the application inadmissible. It found that the applicant's repeated refusals of treatment in June 2011 interrupted the "continuing situation" of alleged non-treatment, meaning the complaints for this period were lodged outside the six-month time limit. * **25 June 2011 to 16 May 2012:** The Court declared this part of the application admissible, as it was not manifestly ill-founded or inadmissible on any other grounds.

case_name: CASE OF CAUCHI v. MALTA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Cauchi v. Malta* (Application no. 14013/19)

**1. Main Parties**
The case involves the applicant, Ms. Catherine Cauchi, a Maltese national born in 1941, and the respondent State, the Republic of Malta. **2. Key Factual Circumstances**
Ms. Cauchi owns a residential property in Ħal Għaxaq, Malta. In February 1967, she rented the property under a temporary emphyteusis (a type of long-term lease) for seventeen years at an annual rent of approximately EUR 58.
