In December 2015, the Icelandic Parliament granted the child Icelandic citizenship, but the first two applicants remained unregistered as his parents. An earlier application for adoption had been put on hold by authorities and was ultimately withdrawn by the applicants following their divorce. #### 3. Procedural History
The applicants sought judicial review of the Ministry's decision. In March 2016, the District Court of Reykjavik rejected their claims. It held that while "family life" had been established, the refusal to register parentage was a justified interference aimed at upholding the domestic ban on surrogacy. The court noted that the authorities had mitigated the impact by granting the child citizenship and facilitating foster care. The applicants appealed to the Supreme Court of Iceland. In March 2017, the Supreme Court upheld the District Court's judgment. However, the Supreme Court departed from the lower court's reasoning regarding family life, concluding that because the applicants' bond had not been established in accordance with domestic law at the time of the registration decision, it did not enjoy constitutional protection as "family life."

#### 4. The Applicants' Allegations and Government's Position before the ECtHR
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained of a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life) due to the state's non-recognition of the parent-child relationship. The Icelandic Government argued that the application was inadmissible. They contended that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because neither the first nor the second applicant had applied to adopt the child individually or with their new spouses after their divorce. The Government also maintained that the application was manifestly ill-founded. The applicants argued that joint adoption was no longer legally possible after their divorce, and that individual adoption by one parent would have severed the child's legal ties to the other, disrupting the family structure they had established.

case_name: CASE OF SŁAWIŃSKI v. POLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Sławiński v. Poland* (Application no. 61039/16)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves Mr. Mariusz Grzegorz Sławiński, a Polish national born in 1958, as the applicant, and the Republic of Poland as the respondent State. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Domestic Procedural History
In 2001, Polish prosecutors initiated an investigation into the allegedly fraudulent activities of the applicant’s debt-collection company. On 26 February 2002, the applicant was officially charged with fraud, and an indictment was filed before the Toruń District Court on 24 June 2002. The first-instance trial began with a hearing on 4 December 2003. Over the next decade, the trial court held approximately 100 hearings and heard over 300 witnesses. On 30 October 2013, the Toruń District Court convicted the applicant of fraud, sentencing him to a suspended prison term of one year and eight months, plus a fine. Upon the applicant's appeal, the Toruń Regional Court quashed this judgment on 23 October 2014 and remitted the case for reconsideration. During the second round of proceedings, the trial court held four hearings and, on 22 June 2015, convicted the applicant of fraud within a more limited scope, issuing a suspended sentence of one year and a fine. The applicant appealed again. On 17 March 2016, the Toruń Regional Court quashed the conviction and discontinued the criminal proceedings because the prosecution of the offences had become time-barred. The written grounds for this final judgment were served on the applicant on 12 April 2016. Separately, on 6 July 2015, the applicant filed a domestic complaint under the 2004 Act concerning the excessive length of his proceedings. On 20 August 2015, the Toruń Regional Court partially allowed his complaint. It found a "flagrant lack of procedural efficiency" by the trial court, noting that very little progress had been made between 2006 and 2013. The court awarded the applicant 2,000 Polish zlotys (approximately 475 euros) in compensation. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the overall length of the criminal proceedings—which lasted approximately 14 years and one month across two levels of jurisdiction—was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement. He also alleged a lack of an effective domestic remedy to address the delay. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Polish Government contested the applicant's allegations on the merits. Additionally, they raised a preliminary objection regarding admissibility, arguing that the application had been submitted outside the six-month time-limit. The Government maintained that the six-month period began on 17 March 2016, when the final oral judgment was delivered in the presence of the applicant and his lawyer, rather than on 12 April 2016, when the written reasons were served. #### 5. Procedural History before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his application with the Court on 11 October 2016. In addressing the admissibility of the complaint, the Court examined the Government's preliminary objection regarding the six-month rule. The Court observed that the applicant was served with the detailed written grounds of the final domestic judgment on 12 April 2016. It determined that because the applicant could only fully comprehend the factual and legal reasoning of the final ruling after receiving the written text, the six-month period began running from the date of service. Consequently, because the application was submitted within six months of 12 April 2016, the Court dismissed the Government's preliminary objection and declared the applicant's complaint under Article 6 § 1 admissible.

case_name: CASE OF FEILAZOO v. MALTA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Mr. Joseph Feilazoo, a Nigerian national. The respondent State is the Republic of Malta. ### Factual Background
In February 2010, the applicant was convicted of drug-related offenses in Malta and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment, which was extended by twenty-two and a half months due to his inability to pay a fine. Upon his scheduled release on April 10, 2018, immigration authorities issued a return decision and removal order. A physical altercation occurred between the applicant and correctional officers during his transfer to immigration detention, resulting in injuries to both sides, including a fractured elbow sustained by the applicant. Consequently, the applicant was prosecuted for assaulting the officers. In February 2019, a domestic court found him guilty, sentencing him to two years' imprisonment. On appeal in May 2019, the court confirmed his guilt but suspended the sentence and ordered his immediate deportation. However, because the applicant could not pay the associated fine, the domestic court converted the fine into an additional six months' imprisonment. Following his release from prison in September 2019, he was placed in immigration detention at the Safi Detention Centre. He remained detained there until December 2020, when he was released to an open center, as his deportation to Nigeria remained unlikely due to difficulties in obtaining travel documents and a lack of mutual cooperation. ### The Applicant’s Allegations
The applicant raised several complaints under the European Convention on Human Rights:
*   **Article 3:** He alleged that his conditions of immigration detention were inadequate and amounted to degrading treatment, citing de facto isolation, poor hygiene, and exposure to health risks by being placed in COVID-19 quarantine with new arrivals. *   **Article 5 § 1:** He argued that his immigration detention was unlawful and lacked a realistic prospect of deportation, noting that the authorities failed to take active and diligent steps to deport him. *   **Article 34:** He alleged that prison authorities interfered with his correspondence with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and denied him access to his medical records. He also claimed that the domestic legal aid system provided ineffective representation, alleging that his assigned lawyer failed to communicate with him and pressured him to drop his ECHR application. ### The Government’s Position
The Maltese Government raised preliminary objections, arguing that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, such as constitutional redress proceedings or administrative complaints under the Detention Services Regulations. On the merits, they contended that the applicant's detention was lawful and that they had actively pursued his deportation by contacting Nigerian authorities, but were hindered by the applicant's lack of cooperation. Regarding legal representation, the Government maintained that the legal aid lawyer had met with the applicant, but that the applicant's behavior led the lawyer to request the revocation of her appointment. ### Procedural History before the ECHR
The applicant lodged his application with the ECHR on August 19, 2019. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government and granted it priority. Due to the complete inactivity of the applicant's domestic legal aid representative, the President of the Section decided that she should no longer represent him. The Court granted the applicant legal aid to engage a lawyer of his choice, who subsequently filed observations on his behalf.

case_name: CASE OF CAAMAÑO VALLE v. SPAIN
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Caamaño Valle v. Spain* (Application no. 43564/17)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Ms. Maria del Mar Caamaño Valle, acting on behalf of her intellectually disabled daughter, M. *   **Respondent State:** The Kingdom of Spain. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
M., born in 1996, has an intellectual disability. In December 2013, as M. approached her eighteenth birthday, her mother (the applicant) initiated domestic court proceedings to declare M. legally incapacitated in order to extend her parental guardianship. However, the applicant specifically requested that M. not be deprived of her right to vote. In September 2014, the First-Instance Judge placed M. under partial guardianship but revoked her right to vote. The judge reasoned that, based on medical expert reports and a personal examination, M. lacked the capacity to make an electoral choice, was highly influenceable, and was unaware of the consequences of voting. Under the Spanish electoral law (LOREG) in force at the time, individuals declared incapacitated by a final judicial decision could be deprived of their voting rights if the court explicitly ruled that they lacked the capacity to exercise suffrage. #### 3. Procedural History Up to the European Court
The applicant appealed the first-instance decision through several levels of domestic jurisdiction:
*   **Regional Court of A Coruña:** Dismissed the appeal in March 2015, noting that M.’s cognitive capacity was equivalent to that of a child aged six to eight and that the restriction was based on an individualized judicial review. *   **Supreme Court:** Dismissed an appeal on points of law in March 2016, finding the lower court's reasoning thorough and balanced. *   **Constitutional Court:** Dismissed an *amparo* appeal in November 2016. It held that the restriction was not an automatic ban on disabled persons as a group, but rather an individualized judicial measure based on cognitive capacity, which complied with both the Spanish Constitution and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Following the exhaustion of domestic remedies, the applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights in June 2017. #### 4. Applicant's Main Allegations
Before the European Court, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), read alone and in conjunction with Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (prohibition of discrimination). She argued that disenfranchising individuals based on intellectual disability constitutes discrimination, lacks a legitimate aim, and is disproportionate. She maintained that voting is a personal choice and that international standards, particularly the CRPD, guarantee the right to vote for persons with disabilities without exception. #### 5. Government's Position
The Spanish Government first requested that the application be struck out of the Court's list. They pointed out that a legislative reform in December 2018 (Institutional Law 2/2018) had amended the LOREG to guarantee the right to vote to all persons with disabilities, thereby automatically restoring M.'s voting rights for future elections. On the merits, the Government contended that the prior system was compatible with the Convention. They argued that the restriction was not automatic but resulted from an individualized judicial process with extensive safeguards, designed to protect vulnerable individuals. They asserted that this system fell within the State's margin of appreciation and aligned with the guidelines of the Venice Commission.

case_name: CASE OF APAP BOLOGNA v. MALTA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case involves the applicant, Mr. Louis Apap Bologna, a Maltese national, and the respondent State, the Republic of Malta. ### Factual Circumstances
In 1980, the applicant inherited a one-half undivided share of a commercial shop located at nos. 295 and 296 Republic Street in Valletta, Malta. The premises had been leased since 1922 under an agreement that was subsequently subjected to perpetual statutory protection under Chapter 69 of the Laws of Malta. This legislation forced the landlords to renew the lease indefinitely at rent rates frozen near historical levels. In 1980, the property was partitioned, and the applicant became the sole owner of the shop at no. 296. Over the years, the tenancy was transferred to other tenants whom the landlords did not formally recognize, and eviction attempts failed. The rent, which was deposited in court by the tenants from 2001 onwards, remained extremely low. Although legislative amendments in 2009 introduced minor annual increases (raising the rent from approximately EUR 401 in 2010 to EUR 818 in 2019), these amounts were far below market rates. In 2017, a court-appointed architect valued the annual market rent of the entire property (nos. 295 and 296) at EUR 86,540, whereas the legally mandated rent paid to the owners was only about EUR 743. ### Domestic Proceedings
In February 2017, the applicant initiated constitutional redress proceedings, claiming a violation of his property rights. On 4 June 2018, the Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention due to the disproportionate burden imposed on the applicant and awarded him EUR 100,000 in compensation. On 29 March 2019, the Constitutional Court confirmed the violation but reduced the compensation to EUR 55,000 (EUR 50,000 for pecuniary and EUR 5,000 for non-pecuniary damage), noting that the applicant only owned half of the physical shop valued by the architect. While it declined to order eviction, it declared that the tenants could no longer rely on Chapter 69 to occupy the premises. Following this judgment, the applicant negotiated a new private lease agreement with the tenant at a market-reflective rate. ### Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. He alleged that the EUR 55,000 compensation awarded by the Constitutional Court was grossly inadequate, as it represented only about one year of market rental value for an interference that had persisted for decades. ### Government’s Position
The Maltese Government argued that the applicant had lost his "victim status." They contended that the domestic courts had acknowledged the violation, provided sufficient redress, and enabled the applicant to evict the tenant, which he chose not to pursue, opting instead to negotiate a lucrative new lease. ### Procedural History before the ECtHR
The application was lodged on 6 September 2019. In its admissibility decision, the European Court of Human Rights rejected the Government's objection regarding victim status. The Court observed that the domestic award of EUR 55,000 was insufficient given the decades-long duration of the violation and the property's high rental value. Consequently, the Court declared the application admissible.

case_name: CASE OF SANDU AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: Sandu and Others v. Romania

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case arises from twenty individual applications lodged against the State of Romania. The lead applicant is Mr. Sandu, joined by nineteen other individuals who were held in various Romanian detention facilities. During the course of the proceedings, one of the applicants, Mr. Tudor (application no. 2673/18), passed away. His two daughters, Ms. Daniela-Loredana Tudor and Ms. Mihaela-Simona Tudor, subsequently requested to pursue the application in their late father's stead. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The factual background of the case concerns the physical conditions under which the applicants were housed during their respective periods of incarceration in Romania. While the specific dates and locations of detention varied across the twenty applications, the common factual elements centered on custodial conditions, particularly allegations of severe overcrowding, restricted personal space within prison cells, and other material deficiencies in the detention facilities. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants alleged that the conditions of their confinement amounted to a breach of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. They argued that the lack of adequate living space, combined with other custodial shortcomings, fell below the minimum standards of decency required under the Convention. Furthermore, a subset of the applicants (in applications nos. 42881/17, 44495/17, 67182/17, 81285/17, 2668/18, 2673/18, 4561/18, and 8476/18) raised additional, separate complaints under Article 3 concerning other aspects of their treatment in detention. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Romanian Government opposed the applications. In their submissions, the Government raised a preliminary objection regarding the admissibility of the complaints, asserting that the applicants had failed to exhaust the domestic remedies available to them under Romanian law. Regarding the procedural issue of Mr. Tudor’s death, the Government was notified of his daughters' request to continue the application and the supporting notary documents, but they did not submit any formal comments or objections on the matter of their legal standing. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the Court's Judgment
The twenty applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on various dates. Because the applications shared a highly similar subject matter regarding Romanian prison conditions, the Court decided to join them to be examined together in a single proceeding. Following the communication of the applications to the Romanian Government, the Court was notified of Mr. Tudor's death. His representative submitted official notary documents demonstrating that his daughters had accepted the inheritance, asserting their legitimate interest in pursuing the litigation. The Court examined this preliminary procedural question of *locus standi* to determine whether the daughters had the legal standing to continue the application. The case then proceeded to the stage where the Court evaluated the parties' arguments on the admissibility and merits of the Article 3 complaints, taking into account its existing jurisprudence on Romanian detention conditions, such as the pilot judgment in *Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania*.

case_name: CASE OF K.I. v. FRANCE
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case: *K.I. v. France* (Application no. 5560/19)

**1. Main Parties**  
The case involves Mr. K.I., a Russian national of Chechen origin born in 1994 (the applicant), and the Government of the French Republic (the respondent State). **2. Key Factual Circumstances**  
The applicant fled the Russian Federation in 2011, alleging that he had been repeatedly arrested, interrogated, and physically abused by Russian security forces due to his family’s ties to Chechen separatists and his refusal to act as an informant. After arriving in France, the French Office for the Protection of Refugees and Stateless Persons (OFPRA) granted him refugee status in January 2013. In November 2013, French authorities arrested the applicant. In April 2015, the Paris Criminal Court sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment for participating in a criminal conspiracy to commit acts of terrorism, specifically for traveling to Syria to join a jihadist group. Following his conviction, OFPRA revoked his refugee status in June 2016 under the domestic Immigration and Asylum Code, citing the serious threat his presence posed to French society. In November 2015, French administrative authorities issued a deportation order against him. **3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations**  
The applicant alleged that his deportation to the Russian Federation would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He argued that as a Chechen with family ties to former rebels, a Salafist practitioner, and an individual convicted of terrorism in France, he would face a real, personal, and systemic risk of torture, forced disappearance, or extrajudicial execution upon return. He submitted statements from relatives in Chechnya claiming that Russian security forces continued to monitor his family and inquire about his whereabouts following his French conviction. **4. The Government’s Position**  
The French Government maintained that the applicant’s deportation would not violate Article 3. They argued that the general situation in Chechnya did not preclude removal and that there was no evidence of systematic ill-treatment of returned individuals suspected of terrorism. They contended that the applicant failed to establish an individualized risk, noting that his original claims of persecution were remote and lacked credibility. The Government also pointed out that the applicant had used a Russian passport to travel to Syria, his accomplice had returned to Chechnya without facing ill-treatment, and the Russian authorities had not requested the applicant's extradition. Finally, they noted that the applicant would be returned to Moscow rather than Chechnya. **5. Procedural History**  
Following the revocation of his refugee status, the applicant appealed to the National Asylum Court (CNDA), which upheld OFPRA's decision in January 2019. In February 2019, the prefecture designated the Russian Federation as the country of destination. The applicant challenged this destination order, but the Lille Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in May 2019, finding no demonstrated personal risk of ill-treatment. In July 2020, the Conseil d’État dismissed his appeal on points of law against the CNDA's decision, though it noted that under European Union law, the revocation of "refugee status" did not strip him of his underlying status as a refugee under the Geneva Convention. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on January 25, 2019. The Court subsequently applied an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, staying his deportation to Russia pending the Court's examination of the case.

case_name: CASE OF BARSEGHYAN v. ARMENIA
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case

#### 1. The Parties
The applicant is Mr. Levon Barseghyan, an Armenian national born in 1967. He is a journalist, political activist, and the chairman of a journalists’ club based in Gyumri, Armenia. The respondent party is the Republic of Armenia. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Following the Armenian presidential election on February 19, 2008, daily protest rallies were organized in Yerevan by supporters of the main opposition candidate. On March 1, 2008, a police operation cleared the primary demonstration site in Yerevan, leading to clashes that resulted in ten deaths, numerous injuries, and property damage. In response, the President of Armenia declared a 20-day state of emergency in Yerevan, which included a ban on holding meetings, rallies, and other mass events in the capital. On March 2, 2008, the applicant arrived at Theatre Square in Gyumri, Armenia’s second-largest city, intending to hold a protest. Police officers stationed at the square denied him entry. The police alleged that the applicant began calling on bystanders to gather and hold a demonstration, and subsequently refused police orders to stop and leave the area. The applicant was taken to a police station, where administrative proceedings were initiated against him for disobeying the lawful orders of police officers. #### 3. Domestic Proceedings
On March 5, 2008, the police filed a claim with the Administrative Court seeking to penalize the applicant. The applicant filed a counter-claim, arguing that he had not intended to organize a rally, that "calling on people" was not a legally prohibited act, and that no prior notification was required under domestic law because fewer than 100 people were present. On June 10, 2008, the Administrative Court ruled in favor of the police, dismissing the applicant's counter-claim and fining him 50,000 Armenian Drams (approximately 110 euros). The court found that no prior notification had been submitted for the event. It further held that, given the state of emergency declared in Yerevan, holding a mass public event in Gyumri could have endangered public order, thereby justifying the police restrictions. The applicant appealed this decision, but on October 2, 2008, the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible. #### 4. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the domestic authorities had violated his right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the Convention. He argued that the state of emergency and Armenia's corresponding derogation under Article 15 of the Convention applied strictly to Yerevan, whereas the events involving him took place in Gyumri, where no violence or emergency situation existed. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Armenian Government contested the admissibility of the application. They argued that Armenia had derogated from its obligations under Article 11 pursuant to Article 15 of the Convention, asserting that a state of emergency effectively extended to Gyumri due to the close link and potential risks associated with the events in Yerevan. Additionally, the Government argued that the applicant could not claim victim status because he had asserted in domestic proceedings that he did not intend to organize or participate in an assembly. Alternatively, they maintained that the applicant had indeed attempted to organize an unauthorized assembly and that the police restrictions were lawful.

case_name: CASE OF ASLANIAN v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA AND RUSSIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Rostom Aslanian, a Russian national born in 1989, living in Vărăncău, Moldova. He is a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses religious community in the self-proclaimed "Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria" (the "MRT"). *   **Respondent States:** The Republic of Moldova and the Russian Federation. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Upon becoming eligible for the military draft in the "MRT," the applicant requested that the local authorities assign him to alternative civilian service rather than compulsory military service, citing his religious conscience and beliefs. In December 2010, the "MRT" authorities denied his request and initiated a criminal investigation against him on charges of draft evasion. On 29 March 2011, the "Rîbnița City and Region Court" convicted the applicant of draft evasion and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. He was placed in custody immediately in the courtroom. The applicant fully served his sentence and was released from detention on 29 March 2012. Shortly thereafter, on 7 June 2012, the "MRT" Supreme Court upheld the first-instance conviction. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that his conviction and subsequent imprisonment for refusing military service on religious grounds—despite his expressed willingness to perform alternative civilian service—constituted a breach of his freedom of conscience under Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also raised complaints under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention. #### 4. The Governments' Positions
*   **The Moldovan Government** maintained that while they had positive obligations to secure the applicant’s rights as the territorial sovereign, they lacked effective control over the Transdniestrian region. They also argued that the application should be declared inadmissible because the applicant had not notified Moldovan authorities about his situation, thereby failing to exhaust available domestic remedies in Moldova. *   **The Russian Government** argued that the applicant did not fall within their jurisdiction. They further asserted that the application should be rejected because the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies before either the Moldovan or Russian courts. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the Court's Admissibility Decision
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 November 2011. In resolving the preliminary issue of jurisdiction, the Court referred to its established case-law concerning the Transdniestrian region. It determined that the applicant fell within the jurisdiction of both respondent States. For Moldova, jurisdiction was established as the territorial state, with its responsibility limited to fulfilling positive obligations. For the Russian Federation, jurisdiction was established based on its effective control and decisive influence over the "MRT" authorities during the relevant period. Regarding admissibility, the Court dismissed the objections raised by both governments concerning the non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, noting that neither state had specified effective remedies that the applicant should have pursued. The Court subsequently declared the applicant's complaint under Article 9 of the Convention admissible.

case_name: CASE OF IBRIŠIMOVIĆ AND OTHERS v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Ibrišimović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 15634/20 and 3 others)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves several individual applicants, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who are represented in the proceedings by Mr. O. Eterović, a lawyer practicing in Sarajevo. The respondent party is the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applications stem from domestic legal proceedings within Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants had previously obtained final, binding domestic decisions delivered in their favor by national authorities or courts. These domestic decisions ordered the state or local authorities to take specific actions on behalf of the applicants. However, these final decisions were not executed, or their execution was significantly delayed, leaving the domestic rulings unenforced over an extended period. #### 3. The Applicants’ Main Allegations
The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights regarding the non-enforcement of the domestic decisions given in their favor. They relied on two main provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** The applicants alleged that the failure of the authorities to enforce final domestic judgments violated their right to a fair hearing. They asserted that the right to a court and a fair trial naturally encompasses the execution of final, binding judicial decisions, and that excessive delays or complete non-enforcement render this right illusory. *   **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of Property):** The applicants contended that the final domestic decisions ordering specific actions in their favor constituted "possessions" within the meaning of this Article. They argued that the state's failure to enforce these decisions amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formally given notice of the applications in accordance with the Court's procedural rules. The provided text does not outline any specific arguments, objections, or justifications submitted by the Government regarding the delays or the non-enforcement of the domestic decisions in question. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
Following the non-enforcement of the domestic decisions, the applicants lodged four separate applications with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The lead application (no. 15634/20) and the three subsequent applications were brought before the Fourth Section of the Court. In the preliminary stages of the proceedings, the Court noted the similarity of the subject matter across all four applications. Consequently, the Court ordered the joinder of the applications to examine them jointly in a single proceeding. The Government was notified of the complaints, and the case was subsequently referred to a three-judge Committee of the Fourth Section for deliberation on admissibility and merits.

case_name: CASE OF MILOŠEVIĆ v. CROATIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: Milošević v. Croatia (Application no. 12022/16)

#### 1. Parties
The applicant is Mr. Milan Milošević, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1966. The respondent State is the Republic of Croatia. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 29 June 2012, a joint inspection by the Vukovar Customs Office and the police revealed that a truck owned by the applicant was using red-tinted heating oil as fuel. Under the Excise Duties Act, this state-supported oil was strictly prohibited from being used to power motor vehicles. On the same day, the Customs Office issued a penalty notice finding the applicant guilty of a minor offence under the Excise Duties Act and fined him 4,800 Croatian kunas (HRK; approximately EUR 640). The applicant did not appeal, paid the fine, and the decision became final. Simultaneously, the Customs Office initiated administrative proceedings to calculate tax surcharges. On 2 July 2012, the Osijek Customs Office ordered the applicant to pay HRK 123,000 (approximately EUR 16,700) in excise duties. Pursuant to section 76(2) of the Excise Duties Act, this sum was calculated by multiplying the standard excise duty for the quantity of oil in question by a factor of one hundred due to its unauthorized use. #### 3. Procedural History
The applicant challenged the tax assessment. On 31 October 2013, the Ministry of Finance quashed the initial tax decision on the grounds that the quantity of heating oil had not been properly determined. On 15 January 2014, the Osijek Customs Office issued a fresh decision, ordering the applicant to pay a recalculated sum of HRK 83,025 (approximately EUR 11,300), which still incorporated the hundredfold increase. This decision was upheld on appeal. The applicant then initiated administrative litigation. On 20 January 2015, the Osijek Administrative Court dismissed his action, and this decision was subsequently upheld on appeal by the High Administrative Court. The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court of Croatia, explicitly alleging that he had been punished twice for the same act. On 20 January 2016, the Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, without providing a specific reply to his double jeopardy (*ne bis in idem*) complaint. #### 4. Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention (the right not to be tried or punished twice). He maintained that both the minor-offence and the subsequent administrative tax proceedings arose from the exact same event and were based on the same legal framework. He argued that the hundredfold increase in the excise duties was punitive and criminal in nature, rather than a standard administrative measure to prevent tax evasion. #### 5. Government’s Position
The Government raised a preliminary objection, arguing that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he had not raised his *ne bis in idem* complaint before the administrative authorities. On the merits, the Government contended that the two sets of proceedings formed a single, integrated, and foreseeable response to the applicant's unlawful conduct. They argued that the minor-offence proceedings aimed to protect traffic safety, whereas the tax proceedings aimed to collect unpaid duties and deter tax evasion. They further asserted that the proceedings were sufficiently connected in time and substance, and that the penalties had been integrated appropriately under domestic law.

case_name: CASE OF MONIR LOTFY v. CYPRUS
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Monir Lotfy v. Cyprus* (Application no. 37139/13) involves Mr. Nashat Monir Lotfy, an Egyptian national born in 1963, and the Republic of Cyprus. ### Factual Background
Mr. Lotfy had a protracted immigration history in Cyprus, which included two prior deportations and the revocation of his Cypriot citizenship. After unlawfully re-entering the country, he was arrested on 10 February 2013. The following day, the Cypriot authorities issued deportation and detention orders against him. He was subsequently detained in several facilities, including Block 10 of Nicosia Central Prisons, the Menoyia detention centre, and various police stations. On 11 July 2013, the applicant filed a habeas corpus application. On 30 July 2013, the Supreme Court of Cyprus ordered his immediate release, finding that the government had failed to justify his ongoing five-month detention. However, on the same day, the applicant was rearrested at the court, and new deportation and detention orders were issued based on his unlawful entry and previous deportations. The applicant filed a second habeas corpus application, which the Supreme Court rejected on 28 January 2014, ruling that his continued detention was lawful due to his lack of cooperation in obtaining travel documents. The applicant also initiated judicial review proceedings to challenge the new orders. Although the Supreme Court initially suspended his detention order on the condition of a EUR 10,000 financial guarantee, the applicant could not secure a guarantor and remained detained. His judicial review recourse was ultimately dismissed by the Administrative Court in August 2017 as moot, following his deportation to Egypt on 8 July 2014. An asylum application filed by the applicant in January 2014 was also rejected. ### The Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 3 and 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Under Article 3, he complained about the material conditions of his detention across various facilities, particularly the police stations and the Menoyia detention centre, which he argued did not meet international standards. He also alleged that he was subjected to physical ill-treatment by police officers during specific incidents in July and October 2013, that the authorities failed to investigate these incidents, that he was denied appropriate medical and psychiatric care, and that he was twice placed in solitary confinement. Under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4, he argued that his detention pending deportation was unlawful and arbitrary—especially following the first habeas corpus order—and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy to challenge it. ### The Government’s Position
The Government contested the applicant's claims. They argued that his detention was lawful, necessary, and prolonged only because of his refusal to cooperate with the authorities and the Egyptian embassy to secure travel documents. Regarding the conditions of detention, the Government maintained that the facilities met acceptable standards and that Menoyia was a specialized center designed for irregular migrants. They denied all allegations of ill-treatment, stating that the applicant's claims were unsubstantiated, that he had refused medical examinations after the alleged incidents, and that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not complaining to the Independent Authority for the Investigation of Allegations and Complaints against the Police (IAIACAP). They also submitted that the applicant received extensive medical care, with over eighty consultations or hospital visits during his detention. ### Procedural History
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 June 2013. The Court subsequently gave notice of the application to the Cypriot Government, requesting observations on the complaints under Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1 and 4, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible. Both parties subsequently submitted their written observations to the Court.

case_name: CASE OF NORWEGIAN CONFEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS (LO) AND NORWEGIAN TRANSPORT WORKERS’ UNION (NTF) v. NORWAY
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicants are two Norwegian trade unions: the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (*Landsorganisasjonen i Norge* or "LO") and the Norwegian Transport Workers’ Union (*Norsk transportarbeiderforbund* or "NTF"). The respondent state is the Kingdom of Norway. The underlying dispute also involved Holship Norge AS ("Holship"), a Norwegian subsidiary of a Danish freight forwarding group. ### Factual Background
LO and NTF were parties to a collective "Framework Agreement" with the Confederation of Norwegian Enterprise (NHO), the largest employer organization in Norway. This agreement, which dated back to the 1970s, secured benefits for dockworkers in major Norwegian ports, including the port of Drammen, in line with ILO Convention No. 137. Crucially, Clause 2(1) of the agreement granted registered dockworkers priority of engagement for loading and unloading operations. To manage these workers, an Administration Office for Dock Work was established in Drammen. Holship, which was not a member of NHO and not a party to the Framework Agreement, began using its own employees for loading and unloading operations in 2013 rather than hiring from the Administration Office. NTF demanded that Holship sign a collective agreement accepting the Framework Agreement. When Holship did not comply, NTF gave notice of a boycott (blockade) against ships involving Holship's loading and unloading activities to pressure the company into accepting the agreement. ### Procedural History
NTF initiated legal proceedings in the Drammen City Court seeking an advance declaratory judgment that the announced boycott was lawful. In March 2014, the City Court ruled the boycott lawful. This decision was upheld by the Borgarting High Court in September 2014. Holship appealed to the Supreme Court of Norway. During these proceedings, the Supreme Court requested an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court. In April 2016, the EFTA Court opined that the priority clause and the Administration Office system restricted the freedom of establishment under Article 31 of the EEA Agreement, leaving the final assessment of justification and proportionality to the national court. In December 2016, the Supreme Court of Norway, sitting in plenary, ruled 10 to 7 that the boycott was unlawful. The majority concluded that the boycott restricted Holship's EEA freedom of establishment and was not justified as a proportionate measure to protect workers. ### Applicants' Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant unions alleged that the Norwegian Supreme Court's decision declaring the boycott unlawful violated their right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention. They argued that the boycott was a primary form of industrial action aimed at protecting core trade union interests, specifically stable and organized working conditions. They further contended that the Supreme Court erred by balancing their Convention rights against an economic freedom (EEA freedom of establishment) in a manner that inappropriately subordinated fundamental human rights to economic interests. ### Government's Position
The Norwegian Government argued that the application of EEA law should benefit from a presumption of compliance with the Convention, similar to the *Bosphorus* presumption, which had not been rebutted. They also questioned whether Article 11 of the Convention protects a right to a boycott of this nature. Alternatively, the Government maintained that any interference with the applicants' Article 11 rights was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others (Holship's freedom of establishment), and was proportionate and necessary in a democratic society.

case_name: CASE OF ROVSHAN HAJIYEV v. AZERBAIJAN
step1_summary:
### Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Rovshan Bahadur oglu Hajiyev, an Azerbaijani national, journalist, and editor of the newspaper *Azadlıq*. The respondent party is the Government of the Republic of Azerbaijan. ### Key Factual Circumstances
The case centers on the Gabala Radar Station, a former Soviet military early warning radar located in the Gabala region of Azerbaijan. Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the station became the property of Azerbaijan but was operated by Russia under a lease agreement until its closure in 2012. In 2001 and 2003, the President of Azerbaijan issued orders appointing joint commissions, chaired by the Minister of Healthcare, to assess and monitor the radar station’s impact on the environment and public health. According to the applicant, independent studies indicated that the station’s operations had caused serious public health issues in the surrounding districts. ### Information Requests and Domestic Procedural History
The applicant sought to obtain the official reports concerning the station's environmental and health impacts through two separate avenues:

1. **Application no. 19925/12 (Ministry of Healthcare):** In July 2010, the applicant wrote to the Ministry of Healthcare requesting copies of the commission's reports. The Ministry replied that the report had been transmitted to the Cabinet of Ministers. The applicant filed a lawsuit to compel the Ministry to provide the document. The Nasimi District Court dismissed the claim, ruling that because the Ministry was no longer in possession of the report, it had fulfilled its statutory duty by informing the applicant of its location. This decision was upheld by the Baku Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court in 2011. 2. **Application no. 47532/13 (Cabinet of Ministers):** In December 2010, the applicant requested a copy of the report directly from the Cabinet of Ministers. Receiving no response, he initiated administrative court proceedings. The Cabinet of Ministers did not participate in the proceedings. The Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1 dismissed the claim, holding that Article 29.1 of the Law on Access to Information did not obligate information owners to disclose reports of commissions created for specific purposes. The Baku Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court upheld this interpretation and dismissed the applicant's subsequent appeals in 2012. ### Applicant's Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention. He alleged that the denial of access to the requested report violated his right to receive and impart information. He argued that the information was of significant public interest and that he required it in his capacity as a journalist. Furthermore, he contended that the domestic courts had misinterpreted the Law on Access to Information, arguing that Article 29.1 merely listed categories of information subject to proactive public disclosure, rather than limiting the scope of information that could be requested by individuals. ### Government's Position
The Government did not raise objections regarding the admissibility of the complaint, though they argued that the applicant's claims were partly substantively unmeritorious. ### Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his applications with the Court on 5 March 2012 and 10 January 2013, respectively. Having regard to the similar subject matter, the Court ordered the joinder of the two applications.

case_name: CASE OF AVCI v. DENMARK
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case

#### 1. The Parties
The applicant is Mr. Cihan Avci, a Turkish national born in Denmark in 1993. The respondent party is the Kingdom of Denmark. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Mr. Avci was born and raised in Denmark, where he lived for twenty-five years prior to his deportation. His immediate family, including his parents and three siblings, reside in Denmark. He is unmarried and has no children. His employment history included various low-skilled jobs, and he was receiving unemployment benefits at the time of his arrest. Regarding his ties to Turkey, Mr. Avci had visited the country on several holiday trips and had a maternal grandfather living there. While Danish immigration authorities initially recorded that he spoke both Turkish and Kurdish, Mr. Avci asserted during proceedings that he spoke mostly Danish, some Kurdish with his father, and virtually no Turkish. Mr. Avci’s criminal record includes a 2013 conviction for attempting to free a detainee and causing public insecurity, for which he received a 20-day suspended prison sentence. In 2018, he was prosecuted for serious drug offenses committed between January and April 2017, involving the possession and distribution of one kilogram of cocaine as part of an organized network. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
On September 12, 2018, the Glostrup District Court convicted Mr. Avci of the drug offenses, sentencing him to four years’ imprisonment and issuing a warning regarding potential expulsion. On appeal, the High Court of Eastern Denmark (*Østre Landsret*) on January 17, 2019, upheld the conviction and the four-year prison sentence. However, it overturned the District Court's decision regarding the expulsion warning, instead ordering Mr. Avci’s expulsion from Denmark with a permanent re-entry ban. The High Court found that the organized nature and gravity of the drug offenses indicated that Mr. Avci posed a serious threat to public order and carried a high risk of reoffending. While acknowledging that his ties to Denmark were stronger than those to Turkey, the High Court concluded that he possessed the necessary prerequisites to establish a life in Turkey and that his family could maintain contact with him remotely. On March 8, 2019, the Appeals Permission Board denied Mr. Avci’s request for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The deportation order was subsequently enforced, and Mr. Avci was deported to Turkey on January 24, 2020. #### 4. Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the expulsion order and the permanent re-entry ban violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention. He argued that the domestic courts had failed to properly balance the relevant factors, pointing out that he had no significant prior criminal record, had never received a prior conditional expulsion order, and possessed deep ties to Denmark with virtually no cultural or linguistic connections to Turkey. He maintained that there were no "very compelling reasons" to justify his permanent banishment. #### 5. Government’s Position
The Danish Government contended that the application should be declared inadmissible, arguing that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he had not sought a revocation of the expulsion order under section 50 of the Danish Aliens Act. On the merits, the Government argued that the expulsion was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing crime, and was proportionate. They maintained that the domestic courts had carefully balanced the applicant's personal circumstances against the gravity of his crimes in line with Article 8 and the Court's established case-law, and argued that the Court should defer to the national courts' assessment under the principle of subsidiarity. #### 6. Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his application on July 4, 2019. In its decision on admissibility, the European Court of Human Rights dismissed the Government’s preliminary objection regarding the exhaustion of domestic remedies, finding that the applicant was not required to pursue section 50 revocation proceedings after already challenging the expulsion order throughout his criminal trial. The Court subsequently declared the application admissible.

case_name: CASE OF TOŢCHI AND OTHERS v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA, RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Summary: *Toţchi and Others v. the Republic of Moldova, Russia and Ukraine*

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicants are Mr. Iurie Toțchi and Mrs. Tatiana Toțcaia (both Russian nationals) and Mr. Marc Fașcevschii (a Ukrainian national), who live in Bender. They are the parents and husband, respectively, of the deceased victim, Ms. Iana Faşcevscaia. The application was lodged against three respondent states: the Republic of Moldova, the Russian Federation, and Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In July 2001, two individuals (K.S. and K.V.) harvested wild mushrooms and sold them at a public market in Tiraspol, a city controlled by the self-proclaimed "Moldovan Republic of Transnistria" (MRT). On 8 July 2001, several people were hospitalized with mushroom poisoning. The hospital notified the local "Republican Centre for Hygiene and Epidemiology" on the morning of 9 July. Later that afternoon, Ms. Iana Faşcevscaia purchased mushrooms from the same sellers. The sellers presented her with a certificate from the market’s veterinary and sanitary laboratory declaring the mushrooms fit for consumption. After eating the mushrooms, Ms. Faşcevscaia became severely ill. She was hospitalized and subsequently transferred to a hospital in Chișinău, where she died on 15 July 2001. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
Following the death, the Tiraspol Prosecutor’s Office initiated criminal investigations against the sellers and the market's laboratory expert. In May 2002, these investigations were discontinued. It was determined that the sellers could not have known the mushrooms were poisonous, and the expert had used rudimentary visual and boiling tests because MRT laboratories lacked biochemical testing equipment. The expert was subsequently amnestied. The case against the sellers was reopened and closed multiple times before eventually being dismissed due to the expiration of the statute of limitations. The investigation was later extended to three officials from the hygiene centre for negligence in failing to act promptly on the hospital's warning. In May 2009, the Tiraspol City Court convicted two of these officials, finding that proper action would have prevented the death. They were sentenced to prison but relieved from serving the sentence due to the statute of limitations. The court also issued a decision highlighting systemic failures, including the lack of regulatory frameworks and testing equipment for laboratories, and unwarranted prosecutorial delays. This judgment was upheld by the "MRT Supreme Court" in July 2009. The Supreme Court of Moldova subsequently refused to examine the applicants' appeal on the grounds that the decisions had been issued by unconstitutional courts. #### 4. The Applicants’ Allegations
The applicants complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They alleged that the authorities failed in their positive obligation to protect the victim’s right to life by failing to establish an effective regulatory, emergency alert, and testing framework for food safety. They also argued that the domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of the death, as the delays allowed the responsible individuals to avoid criminal liability. #### 5. The Governments' Positions
* **Moldova:** The Moldovan Government submitted that they had positive obligations to secure the applicants’ rights under the Convention. * **Russia:** The Russian Government argued that the applicants did not fall within its jurisdiction and that the application should be declared inadmissible. They also contended that the application was lodged out of time, arguing the applicants were aware of the investigation's ineffectiveness by 2006 but waited until 2010 to apply to the Court. * **Ukraine:** No specific submissions on the merits or admissibility were detailed on behalf of the Ukrainian Government, though the applicants maintained that Ukraine also held jurisdiction.

case_name: CASE OF ANCIENT BALTIC RELIGIOUS ASSOCIATION “ROMUVA” v. LITHUANIA
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicant is the Ancient Baltic religious association “Romuva” (*Senovės baltų religinė bendrija „Romuva“*), a pagan religious association registered in Lithuania. The respondent is the Republic of Lithuania, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
Lithuanian law distinguishes between three categories of religious associations: traditional, non-traditional recognized by the State, and other registered religious associations. State-recognized status grants several privileges, including the right to provide religious education in public schools, perform marriages with civil effect, receive state social insurance for clergy, and obtain airtime on the national broadcaster. Under domestic law, a non-traditional religious association may request State recognition 25 years after its initial registration. The Ministry of Justice evaluates whether the association meets the statutory criteria and submits its conclusion to the Seimas (the Lithuanian Parliament), which makes the final decision by voting on a resolution. Romuva, which follows the old Baltic pagan faith, was registered as an association in 2002, though one of its constituent communities had been registered since 1992. In 2017, Romuva requested State recognition. The Ministry of Justice concluded that the association met all legal requirements, noting that it had operated for over 25 years, its teachings did not violate the law or public morals, and it possessed substantial public support, being the largest non-traditional religious group in Lithuania. In June 2019, the Seimas held debates on the draft resolution to grant Romuva recognition. Opponents raised concerns regarding the depth of Romuva's public support and questioned whether it constituted a genuine religion or rather an ethnographic heritage organization. During the legislative process, the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference (the territorial authority of the Roman Catholic Church) sent a letter to a parliamentary group opposing Romuva's recognition, arguing that the concept of an ancient Baltic faith was misleading and lacked a scientific basis. On June 27, 2019, the Seimas voted on the resolution; it failed to pass, receiving 40 votes in favor, 31 against, and 15 abstentions. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant association complained about the Seimas’ refusal to grant it State-recognized status. Romuva alleged that the refusal violated Article 9 (freedom of thought, conscience, and religion) of the European Convention on Human Rights, both taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The applicant argued that the Seimas' decision-making process was arbitrary, politically motivated, and improperly influenced by the dominant religious authority, resulting in discriminatory treatment compared to other non-traditional religious groups that had successfully obtained recognition. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Lithuanian Government contested the admissibility of the application, arguing that the applicant had failed to exhaust available domestic remedies. The Government maintained that Romuva could have lodged a complaint with the domestic administrative courts to claim damages for unlawful state action. They asserted that the administrative courts could have referred the constitutional validity of the Seimas' decision to the Constitutional Court, or that the applicant could have eventually filed an individual constitutional complaint. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on August 29, 2019. The Court subsequently gave notice of the application to the Lithuanian Government regarding complaints under Articles 9, 13, and 14 of the Convention, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible. Both parties submitted their written observations, and the Court held private deliberations on May 18, 2021, prior to preparing its judgment.

case_name: CASE OF LAMBERTNÉ BÁRSONY v. HUNGARY
step1_summary:
### 1. Main Parties
The applicant is Ms Klára Lambertné Bársony, a Hungarian national who was born in 1955 and resides in Miskolc, Hungary. The respondent party is the Republic of Hungary, represented before the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Z. Tallódi, Agent from the Ministry of Public Administration and Justice. ### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Domestic Procedural History
The case arises from a domestic civil dispute concerning the division of property. On 20 April 1998, the applicant initiated a lawsuit seeking the division of the property accumulated during her common-law partnership with a private individual, Mr. F. The litigation proceeded through three levels of domestic jurisdiction:
*   At the first instance, the case was heard and examined by the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Court. *   On appeal, the matter was brought before and reviewed by the Debrecen Court of Appeal. *   The domestic proceedings concluded when the Supreme Court of Hungary delivered its final judgment on 2 March 2010. In total, the period of the domestic proceedings began on 20 April 1998 and ended with the Supreme Court's final decision on 2 March 2010, lasting almost twelve years across three levels of jurisdiction. ### 3. The Applicant's Main Allegations
Following the conclusion of the domestic litigation, the applicant submitted an application to the European Court of Human Rights raising the following complaints and claims:
*   **Article 6 § 1 Complaint:** The applicant alleged that the overall length of the domestic civil proceedings was excessive and failed to comply with the "reasonable time" requirement guaranteed under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. *   **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 Complaint:** The applicant also raised a complaint regarding the actual outcome of the domestic litigation, alleging that the decisions of the domestic courts concerning the property division interfered with her property rights. *   **Just Satisfaction Claims:** Under Article 41 of the Convention, the applicant claimed approximately 211,000 euros (EUR) in respect of pecuniary damage, EUR 23,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage, and EUR 5,300 for the costs and expenses she incurred before both the domestic courts and the European Court. ### 4. The Government's Position
The Hungarian Government contested the applicant's arguments and claims:
*   They disputed the applicant's allegation that the length of the domestic proceedings violated the "reasonable time" requirement of Article 6 § 1. *   They also contested the applicant's claims for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, as well as her claims for the reimbursement of costs and expenses. ### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant lodged her application (no. 48689/10) with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 August 2010. On 6 March 2013, the Court communicated the application to the Hungarian Government, allowing them the opportunity to submit their observations.

case_name: CASE OF KIISA v. ESTONIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Kiisa v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 16587/10 and 34304/11)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicants are Ms. Karin Kiisa (the first applicant) and Mr. Aare Kiisa (the second applicant), both Estonian nationals. The respondent party is the Republic of Estonia, represented by its Agent from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicants were married from 1989 to 2006. In September 2002, the first applicant gave birth to a child, K., and the second applicant was registered as the father. In October 2003, the first applicant filed for divorce and the division of marital property. On October 25, 2004, the first applicant initiated civil proceedings in the Harju County Court seeking child alimony from the second applicant. In April 2005, the second applicant filed a separate action to contest his paternity (filiation proceedings). Consequently, in October 2005, the County Court suspended the alimony proceedings pending the outcome of the filiation case. Although the court ordered DNA testing, the first applicant did not present the child for analysis. The filiation action was ultimately dismissed in May 2012. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
The alimony proceedings resumed in June 2007. Over the next several years, the case underwent extensive litigation:
* **January 2008:** The Harju County Court ordered the second applicant to pay monthly alimony. Both parties appealed. * **May 2008:** The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. Both parties appealed to the Supreme Court. * **November 2008:** The Supreme Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case to the Court of Appeal. * **May 2009:** The Court of Appeal quashed the initial first-instance judgment and remitted the case back to the County Court. The Supreme Court refused the first applicant leave to appeal this remittal in September 2009. * **July 2010:** Following new evidence and amended claims, the County Court ordered monthly alimony of approximately EUR 320. Both parties appealed. * **October 2010:** The Court of Appeal reduced the monthly alimony to approximately EUR 227. Both parties appealed. * **January 26, 2011:** The Supreme Court refused the parties leave to appeal, concluding the domestic proceedings. In total, the domestic civil proceedings lasted approximately six years and three months across three levels of jurisdiction. #### 4. The Applicants’ Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), the applicants alleged that the length of the domestic civil proceedings was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also complained under Article 13 of the Convention that Estonia lacked an effective domestic remedy to address the excessive length of judicial proceedings. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Estonian Government requested the Court to strike out the applications under Article 37 of the Convention, submitting a unilateral declaration that acknowledged the domestic proceedings had exceeded a "reasonable time" and offering monetary compensation. On admissibility, the Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. They pointed to recent domestic case-law (specifically the Supreme Court's March 2011 *Osmjorkin* judgment) which established that individuals could claim compensation for excessively lengthy proceedings through the administrative courts. On the merits of the Article 6 § 1 complaint, the Government argued that the delay was primarily caused by the applicants' own conduct, including multiple requests for postponements, suspensions, and repeated appeals. #### 6. Procedural History before the European Court
The first applicant lodged her application on March 4, 2010, and the second applicant lodged his on May 31, 2011. The Court decided to join the two applications. The Court rejected the Government's request to strike out the case under Article 37, noting that the unilateral declaration did not address the Article 13 complaint. Regarding admissibility, the Court dismissed the Government's objection concerning the exhaustion of domestic remedies, finding that the administrative remedy was not sufficiently established or accessible to the applicants at the time their applications were lodged. Consequently, the Court declared both the Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 complaints admissible.

case_name: CASE OF S.J. v. BELGIUM
step1_summary:
**Parties**  
The case of *S.J. v. Belgium* (Application no. 70055/10) involves Ms. S.J., a Nigerian national (the applicant), and the Kingdom of Belgium (the respondent Government). **Key Factual Circumstances**  
The applicant arrived in Belgium in the summer of 2007 while eight months pregnant. Shortly after her arrival, she was diagnosed as HIV-positive with a serious immune system deficiency requiring antiretroviral (ARV) treatment. Between 2007 and 2012, she gave birth to three children in Belgium, all fathered by M.A., a Nigerian national who occasionally stayed in Belgium without a residence permit. While in Belgium, the applicant received specialized medical treatment and psychosocial support. Her medical condition fluctuated significantly; at various points, medical certificates indicated treatment failure, high viral loads, and low T4 counts, requiring regular adjustments to her ARV drug combinations. **Domestic Procedural History**  
In July 2007, the applicant lodged an asylum application. The Commissioner General for Refugees and Stateless Persons rejected the application in May 2010 due to inconsistencies in her account, and this decision was upheld by the Aliens Appeals Board in October 2010. In parallel, the applicant applied for leave to remain on medical grounds under Section 9ter of the Aliens Act. In September 2010, the Aliens Office rejected this request, relying on its medical adviser's opinion that appropriate ARV treatment and monitoring were available and accessible in Nigeria. Consequently, the applicant was served with an order to leave the country. The applicant applied to set aside the expulsion order and requested a stay of execution under the extremely urgent procedure. The Aliens Appeals Board rejected the stay of execution, finding that "extreme urgency" was not established because the applicant was not in detention and no repatriation date had been set. The Conseil d’État subsequently declared her appeal on points of law inadmissible. Her application to set aside the expulsion order remained pending before the domestic authorities. **Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights**  
The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on November 30, 2010. On December 17, 2010, the Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, requesting the Belgian Government not to expel the applicant and her children pending the outcome of the proceedings. The application was declared admissible on December 18, 2012. **The Applicant’s Allegations**  
The applicant alleged that her expulsion to Nigeria would violate Article 3 of the Convention, arguing that she would face a real risk of inhuman and degrading treatment due to the lack of guaranteed access to her specific, adjusted ARV treatment and specialized medical and psychosocial monitoring, which would lead to a rapid deterioration of her health and premature death. She also alleged a violation of Article 8, asserting that her expulsion would disrupt her family life, as her three young children were born and raised in Belgium and their father was also present there. Finally, she complained under Article 13 that she lacked an effective remedy with automatic suspensive effect to challenge her expulsion, as the extremely urgent procedure was practically inaccessible to her because she was not detained. **The Government’s Position**  
The Government argued that the applicant had effective domestic remedies available, asserting she could have filed an ordinary request for a stay of execution followed by a request for interim measures if enforcement became imminent. Regarding Article 3, the Government contended that appropriate ARV drugs and monitoring were available in Nigeria, the applicant was fit to travel, and her condition was stable, meaning her circumstances did not meet the high threshold of severity required to block expulsion on medical grounds. On Article 8, the Government maintained that the family would be expelled together, preventing separation, and that the children were young enough to adapt to life in Nigeria.

case_name: CASE OF MEMISHAJ v. ALBANIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: Memishaj v. Albania (Application no. 40430/08)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Enver Memishaj, an Albanian national born in 1944, residing in Tirana, and represented by lawyer Ms. Entela Memishaj. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Albania, represented by Ms. L. Mandia of the State Advocate’s Office. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant worked as an accountant for the Tirana City Hall until he was dismissed on 10 December 2001 (effective 11 January 2002). Following his legal challenge, the Civil Service Commission (CSC) quashed the dismissal on 6 February 2002 and ordered his reinstatement. This decision was upheld by a final judgment of the Supreme Court on 8 May 2003. On 15 May 2003, the Tirana District Court supplemented the CSC's decision by ordering the Tirana City Hall to pay the applicant’s salary arrears from the date of his dismissal until his reinstatement. An enforcement writ was subsequently issued on 4 June 2003. On 31 March 2006, the Constitutional Court of Albania ruled on a constitutional complaint filed by the applicant, acknowledging that his right of access to court had been breached due to the non-enforcement of the Supreme Court's decision, but it did not award any damages. Meanwhile, on 1 March 2006, the applicant took up employment with the Ministry of Tourism, Culture, Youth and Sports. Shortly thereafter, the Tirana City Hall appointed him to a position in a municipal maintenance company, which the applicant successfully challenged before the CSC. To secure his outstanding payments, the applicant initiated further domestic proceedings:
*   **2004 and 2006 Actions:** The applicant successfully sued for accrued interest due to delayed salary payments. *   **2008 Action:** On 9 April 2008, the Tirana District Court ordered the Tirana City Hall to pay ALL 774,076 in salary arrears and ALL 105,258 in accrued interest for the period up to 28 February 2006. The Supreme Court dismissed the defendant's appeal in February 2010. The Tirana City Hall paid the salary arrears on 31 March 2010, but the accrued interest remained unpaid. *   **2010 Action:** The applicant sought further accrued interest (from 9 April 2008 to 31 March 2010) and social security contributions. The Tirana District Court ruled in his favor on 30 June 2010, a decision upheld by the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court in 2011. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant complained that the prolonged non-enforcement of the final domestic decisions in his favor—specifically the Supreme Court decision of 8 May 2003, as supplemented by the decisions of 15 May 2003, 9 April 2008, and 30 June 2010—violated his rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). He also alleged under Article 14 that he was discriminated against based on his political affiliation. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government contended that the applicant could no longer claim to be a victim of a violation. They argued that the Supreme Court’s reinstatement order was effectively enforced when the applicant began working for the Ministry of Tourism on 1 March 2006. They also noted that the applicant had qualified for an old-age pension on 30 June 2007. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2008 and was communicated to the Albanian Government on 11 July 2011. In its preliminary assessment, the Court decided to join the Government's objection regarding the applicant's victim status to the merits of the case. The Court declared the applicant's complaints under Articles 6 § 1, 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 admissible. It declared the discrimination complaint under Article 14 inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded.

case_name: CASE OF TARANEKS v. LATVIA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Mr. Aivars Taraneks, a Latvian national who worked as a senior bailiff. The respondent party is the Republic of Latvia. ### Factual Circumstances
In November 2001, a Latvian court ordered the seizure of moveable property (specifically fur coats) belonging to a company, M., to secure a commercial claim by another company, R.L. The execution of the seizure was handled by a bailiff, G.P., under the applicant’s supervision. The seized property was temporarily stored by R.L.’s director, O.V. The applicant subsequently signed a document requesting an advance payment of 500 Latvian lati (LVL) from R.L. to cover potential storage and expert valuation costs. Shortly thereafter, the court quashed the seizure order. R.L. lodged an appeal, which had a suspensive effect on the return of the property. On December 14, 2001, O.V. complained to the police, alleging that the applicant and G.P. were extorting a LVL 500 bribe to prevent the property's return to M. That same day, telephone and in-person conversations between O.V., his lawyer S.Ž., G.P., and the applicant were secretly recorded. On December 18, a prosecutor approved an undercover "investigative test." O.V. went to the bailiffs' office, insisted on speaking to the applicant directly rather than receiving documents from G.P., and left LVL 500 in marked banknotes on the applicant's desk. After O.V. departed, the police detained the applicant, detected traces of a luminescent marking substance on his hands, and searched his office under a prosecutor's authorization, finding the money under some books. ### Domestic Procedural History
In March 2005, the Riga Regional Court convicted the applicant of demanding a bribe and sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The court relied on testimonies from O.V. and several witnesses, as well as the recorded conversations. It noted some pre-trial procedural "imperfections" but deemed them irrelevant to the overall weight of the evidence. In January 2006, the Supreme Court upheld the bribery conviction.
