On 25 June 2015, approximately one month after the car was impounded, the investigator applied to the Zhytomyr Bohunskyi District Court (“the Bohunskyi Court”) for the formal seizure of the vehicle. On 30 June 2015, the Bohunskyi Court granted the application during a hearing attended by the prosecutor; the applicant was not notified of the proceedings. After discovering the ruling, the applicant appealed. He argued that the seizure violated Article 171 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which mandated that if an investigator failed to apply for the seizure of temporarily withheld property within one day, the property had to be returned immediately. He also asserted that the measure was disproportionate. On 5 August 2015, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal rejected the appeal, stating that the lower court had complied with the law and noting that the legitimate owner of the car had not yet been determined. On 25 March 2016, the applicant was officially granted the status of a victim in the ongoing criminal proceedings. He repeatedly applied to have the seizure lifted. On 1 December 2016, the Bohunskyi Court partially allowed one of his applications. While maintaining the ban on the disposal or encumbrance of the vehicle, the court ordered the car transferred to the applicant for safekeeping, noting that its continued storage in an open police pound was causing it to deteriorate. On 4 November 2019, the Bohunskyi Court lifted the seizure entirely. The judge noted that no investigative measures had been carried out since September 2016, no suspects had been identified, and the applicant’s status as a bona fide owner had never been questioned. On 17 June 2020, the criminal investigation was officially discontinued because it was impossible to identify any suspects. #### 4. Applicant’s Allegations and Government’s Position
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the seizure of his car within criminal proceedings concerning third parties constituted a breach of his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). The Ukrainian Government was formally notified of the application and, alongside the applicant, submitted written observations to the Court regarding the admissibility and merits of the case.

case_name: CASE OF KOVALEVSKYY v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case: *Kovalevskyy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 712/25)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves the applicant, Mr. Kovalevskyy, a Ukrainian national who is represented in the proceedings by Mr. I. M. Serafymov, a lawyer practicing in Kyiv. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Procedural History
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 December 2024 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The background of the case concerns domestic legal proceedings in Ukraine during which the applicant was deprived of his liberty. Following his detention, domestic proceedings were conducted to review the lawfulness of his deprivation of liberty. After the conclusion of these domestic procedures, the applicant sought review before the European Court of Human Rights. The Court subsequently gave formal notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government. #### 3. The Applicant’s Allegations
The applicant’s complaints focus on the domestic proceedings concerning the review of the lawfulness of his detention. He relied on Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, which stipulates that anyone who is deprived of their liberty by arrest or detention is entitled to take proceedings by which the lawfulness of their detention is decided speedily by a court and their release ordered if the detention is not lawful. Specifically, the applicant alleged that there were critical procedural and substantive deficiencies in the way the Ukrainian courts reviewed his detention. He argued that the domestic system failed to provide him with the essential guarantees required for a fair and effective review of deprivation of liberty. In making these claims, the applicant pointed to issues similar to those previously identified by the Court in the leading case of *Kharchenko v. Ukraine* (no. 40107/02), which addressed systemic shortcomings in the Ukrainian legal framework regarding the review of detention. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Ukrainian Government was formally notified of the application. Under the Court's procedures, the Government was given the opportunity to submit its observations regarding the admissibility and merits of the applicant's complaints, specifically addressing whether the domestic proceedings complied with the procedural and substantive requirements of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention.

case_name: CASE OF STALOVIĆ v. SERBIA
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicants are Mr. Marko Stalović, a Serbian national of Roma origin, and Ms. Sandra Stalović, an Austrian national. They are a married couple residing in Belgrade and Vienna. The respondent State is the Republic of Serbia. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 21 April 2017, the applicants went to the Mladenovac Police Station to report that their car, which contained their passports, had been stolen. Following this report, they were transferred to the Belgrade Police Directorate, where they underwent a polygraph test and "informal" questioning in separate rooms. No official minutes were recorded during these informal interviews. Later that evening, the applicants were returned to the Mladenovac Police Station, where they signed formal statement minutes at approximately 9:30 p.m. The signed documents stated that they had no remarks or complaints regarding their treatment by the police. At 10:35 p.m. the same evening, Mr. Stalović underwent a medical examination at a local health centre. The examining doctor documented multiple head injuries, red spots near his left kidney, and a pressure mark on his right knee. A follow-up medical examination the next day recorded muscle pain and further head injuries, and on 26 April 2017, Mr. Stalović was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). #### 3. The Applicants’ Main Allegations
The applicants alleged that they were subjected to racially motivated physical and psychological ill-treatment by police officers during their informal questioning. * **Mr. Stalović** alleged that he was forced to kneel, slapped, kicked in the stomach, struck on his hands with a leather whip, and suffocated with a plastic bag. He also claimed officers threatened him with electrocution and shooting, insulted him with racial slurs ("Gypsy mother"), and threatened to place his children in care. * **Ms. Stalović** alleged that she was subjected to psychological abuse, including threats of detention, accusations of being "the mask of an organised criminal group," threats to take her children, and racist insults regarding her marriage to a Roma man. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The police officers involved in the questioning denied all allegations of physical or psychological ill-treatment, asserting that the informal questioning had been conducted without coercion. In the proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights, the Serbian Government was represented by their Agent and submitted observations contesting the applicants' claims. #### 5. Domestic Procedural History
The applicants pursued two distinct legal avenues at the domestic level:

* **Criminal Proceedings:** On 9 May 2017, the applicants filed a criminal complaint against eight police officers. On 17 May 2018, the First Public Prosecutor’s Office rejected the complaint. The prosecutor accepted the police officers' denials, pointed to CCTV footage showing the applicants leaving the police station without visible injuries, and noted that the applicants had signed the interview minutes without raising complaints. The prosecutor also discounted the medical reports due to identification and timing issues. This decision was upheld by the Belgrade Public Prosecutor’s Office of Second Instance. On 28 October 2021, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants' constitutional appeal, finding the criminal investigation to have been independent, thorough, and prompt. * **Civil Discrimination Proceedings:** On 1 August 2017, the applicants filed a civil discrimination claim against the State. On 1 June 2020, the Belgrade Court of Second Instance ruled in the applicants' favor. Based on medical expert opinions, the court established that police officers had applied unjustified physical and psychological pressure amounting to degrading treatment, which was motivated at least in part by Mr. Stalović's Roma origin. The court ordered the State to pay EUR 4,700 to Mr. Stalović and EUR 1,700 to Ms. Ms. Stalović in non-pecuniary damages. This judgment was upheld on appeal and became final on 17 December 2020. The applicants subsequently lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 July 2022, complaining under the European Convention on Human Rights of racially motivated police ill-treatment and the lack of an effective investigation.

case_name: CASE OF KIS AND LEVCHUK v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Kis and Levchuk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 910/18)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicants are Mr. Zoryan Romanovych Kis (born 1982) and Mr. Tymur Anzorovych Levchuk (born 1994), two Ukrainian nationals living in Kyiv. They are represented by Ms. Y.V. Naumenko, a lawyer practicing in Kyiv. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine, represented by their Agent, Ms. M. Sokorenko. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In July 2015, the applicants, a same-sex couple, agreed to participate in a social experiment organized by the online magazine *Bird in Flight* to gauge public tolerance toward same-sex couples in Kyiv. On 15 July 2015, they walked through central Kyiv holding hands while being filmed and accompanied by bodyguards. To increase the public display of affection, one applicant sat on the other’s lap on a bench on Khreshchatyk Street. Shortly after, a group of young people approached them, questioning their patriotism and making comments such as "The guys have [this place] mixed up with America" and "Europe! Europe!" The group then sprayed the applicants with pepper spray and kicked them. The bodyguards intervened immediately, limiting the physical confrontation to three to five seconds. The applicants did not seek medical assistance or undergo a forensic medical examination. On 22 July 2015, the video of the experiment, which showed the faces of some of the accosters, was published online and reported on by various news websites. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
On 29 July 2015, the first applicant filed a criminal complaint requesting an investigation under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code (violation of citizens' equality committed with violence). The second applicant filed a similar complaint and was questioned by police, where he declined to undergo a forensic medical examination. On 5 August 2015, the police opened criminal proceedings under Article 296 § 2 of the Criminal Code (hooliganism committed by a group). However, on 12 August 2015, the police closed the proceedings, citing a lack of evidence, the absence of eyewitnesses or surveillance footage, and the second applicant's refusal to undergo a medical examination. Over the next several years, the investigation followed a repetitive cycle:
* The decision to close the case was repeatedly set aside by the Shevchenkivskyi District Court of Kyiv or the local prosecutor as premature, and the case was returned to the police. * In May 2016, the applicants' lawyer requested the offense be reclassified under Article 161 (discrimination), which the police dismissed. * The police conducted minor investigative steps, such as collecting mobile phone tower data in July 2016. * In September 2017, the applicants identified a female suspect from another online video and linked her to a specific group, but no follow-up action was recorded. * Investigators issued reports in 2016, 2021, and 2022 stating they could not locate the magazine's editor or journalist, nor identify the perpetrators. * In July 2023, the police finally questioned the magazine's editor and applied for access to local mobile phone operator data. The domestic criminal proceedings remain pending. #### 4. The Applicants’ Allegations and Government Position
The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 December 2017. Under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention, they alleged that domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the violent, hate-motivated attack they experienced. The Ukrainian Government was formally notified of the complaints under Articles 8 and 14. Both the applicants and the Government submitted written observations regarding the merits and admissibility of the application to the Court.

case_name: CASE OF MUSINA AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicants are four Ukrainian nationals: the parents, sister, and daughter of the deceased, A.M. The respondent State is Ukraine. ### Key Factual Circumstances
In April 2014, forty-year-old A.M. was mobilized for military service. Medical examinations confirmed he was in good health. Although his formal discharge order was dated 25 March 2015, A.M. remained at his military unit for a few additional days to finalize administrative formalities. At approximately 11:00 p.m. on 27 March 2015, a military patrol discovered a heavily intoxicated soldier, V.S., tied up and gagged near a tent inside the military unit. The patrol freed him and let him return to the barracks. At approximately 6:10 a.m. the following morning, 28 March 2015, the patrol found A.M. dead inside the same tent. His wrists were bound behind his back with plastic hose clamps, his feet were tied to a tent pole with an electric cable, and a textile gag was secured in his mouth with adhesive tape. A forensic medical examination report from April 2015, supplemented by an additional report in November 2015, concluded that A.M.’s death was caused by acute coronary insufficiency exacerbated by heavy alcohol intoxication. The experts noted minor facial bruises and sores but concluded there was no causal link between the physical restraint (the tying of his hands and feet) and his death. ### Domestic Investigation and Procedural History
On 28 March 2015, authorities opened a criminal investigation into murder, though the initial registry entry noted there was no indication of a violent death. The military command asserted it lacked jurisdiction to investigate because A.M. had already been discharged; consequently, the case was transferred to the Novomoskovsk city police. A separate military inquiry into potential security and access control omissions at the unit was discontinued in June 2015 due to a lack of evidence of a criminal offence. The police investigation encountered several difficulties:
* The military unit’s management initially refused to provide information regarding who was present on the territory during the incident. * A January 2016 forensic cytological examination of the bindings, gag, and tape yielded no usable DNA. Although blood was found on the gag and tape, experts could not match it because investigators failed to provide blood samples for comparison. * The acting commander of the military unit, questioned in June 2016, maintained that the unit was a secure facility with strict access controls, ruling out unauthorized intruders. The Novomoskovsk police discontinued the investigation on three separate occasions (27 June 2015, 30 November 2016, and 30 March 2017), concluding each time that A.M. died of natural causes with no evidence of a violent death. The first two closure decisions were quashed by local prosecutors, who labeled them premature and unlawful, citing serious omissions, unfulfilled investigative instructions, and a poorly conducted inquiry. The investigator in charge was disciplined multiple times for the poor quality of the investigation. ### Applicants' Allegations and Government Position
The first and second applicants were granted victim status in the domestic proceedings on 6 July 2015. On 9 August 2016, the applicants lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. Under Article 2 of the Convention, the applicants alleged that the State was responsible for the death of their relative while he was under its control, and that the domestic authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of his death. The Ukrainian Government was formally notified of the application, and both the Government and the applicants subsequently submitted observations to the Court.

case_name: CASE OF SIMONCINI v. SAN MARINO
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Simoncini v. San Marino* (Application no. 3106/24)

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **The Applicant:** Mr. Massimiliano Simoncini, a San Marinese national born in 1963, who lives in Montegiardino. He is a member of the San Marino judiciary and is represented by Mr. A. Masiello, a lawyer practicing in Borgo Maggiore. *   **The Respondent State:** The Republic of San Marino, represented by its Agent, Ms. S. Bernardi. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Domestic Procedural History
The case arises from disciplinary proceedings initiated against the applicant, a sitting judge, for misconduct allegedly committed in February 2023. On 13 July 2023, the Judicial Council (*Consiglio Giudiziario*), acting as a court of first instance, established the applicant’s disciplinary liability under section 12 of Constitutional Law no. 1/2021. The Council imposed a disciplinary sanction of a warning (*ammonimento*). On 4 September 2023, the applicant lodged an appeal against this decision with the Constitutional Court (*Collegio garante della costituzionalità delle norme*) under section 16(10) of Constitutional Law no. 1/2021. On 12 September 2023, the President of the Constitutional Court issued a decree declaring the appeal inadmissible because the applicant had filed it without being represented by a lawyer. This was deemed a violation of section 9(1) of Qualified Law no. 55/2003 and section 12(1) of the Internal Regulations of the Constitutional Court, which mandate legal representation. On 15 September 2023, a lawyer appointed by the applicant submitted a brief formally ratifying the initial appeal to remedy the lack of representation. The lawyer argued that the applicant had filed the appeal himself due to the difficulty of securing counsel during the summer holidays. He further argued that under certain provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure—which also applied to disciplinary proceedings—the applicant was entitled to lodge the appeal directly. On 22 September 2023, the President of the Constitutional Court issued a second decree declaring the appeal inadmissible. The President reiterated that legal representation was mandatory and ruled that the lawyer’s ratifying brief had been submitted after the expiration of the 30-day statutory time-limit for filing an appeal. Following this, the applicant filed a plea of nullity (*querela nullitatis*) seeking the annulment of both presidential decrees, alongside a constitutional complaint challenging several statutory provisions regulating disciplinary proceedings. No domestic decisions had been delivered regarding these subsequent challenges at the time the applicant petitioned the European Court of Human Rights. #### 3. The Applicant’s Allegations
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 January 2024. He alleges violations of his rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, his complaints concern:
*   The right to a tribunal established by law. *   The right to a reasoned decision. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The San Marinese Government was formally notified of the applicant's complaints under Article 6 § 1. In accordance with the Court's procedures, the Government submitted observations addressing the applicant's allegations and the admissibility of the case. #### 5. Procedural History before the European Court of Human Rights
Following the lodging of the application, the Court decided to give notice to the San Marinese Government of the complaints raised under Article 6 § 1 concerning the right to a tribunal established by law and the right to a reasoned decision. The remainder of the applicant's complaints were declared inadmissible. Both the applicant and the Government subsequently submitted their observations to the Court.

case_name: CASE OF VYKHOR v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Pavlo Oleksandrovych Vykhor, a Ukrainian national and lawyer born in 1978, who lives in Kostyantynivka. The respondent state is Ukraine, represented before the Court by its Agent, Mrs. M. Sokorenko. ### Key Factual Circumstances
In May 2013, criminal proceedings were initiated against the applicant. He was charged with defrauding his client, V.O., by allegedly inciting him to hand over money that was purportedly demanded by police and judicial authorities to secure favorable treatment in V.O.’s own criminal case. On 23 May 2013, an investigating judge of the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal issued two orders authorizing the police to tap the applicant’s two mobile telephones and to carry out audio and video monitoring. The judge stated that there were sufficient grounds to believe these covert measures would yield information of fundamental importance for the prevention, detection, and cessation of criminal offences, and noted the police's assertion that this information could not be obtained by other means. On 31 May 2013, a prosecutor authorized a "controlled transaction" involving marked bills. By November 2013, the applicant learned that transcripts of his intercepted telephone conversations and a recorded meeting with V.O. had been included as key evidence in his prosecution file. ### The Applicant's Allegations
The applicant raised complaints under Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention. He alleged that the covert investigative measures used against him were incompatible with his right to respect for his private life and correspondence. Specifically, he argued that the surveillance authorizations were granted unlawfully without any assessment of whether there was a reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence. He further alleged that he lacked an effective domestic remedy to challenge these measures and complained that the criminal proceedings against him were excessively long. ### The Government's Position
The Ukrainian Government was formally notified of the applicant's complaints under Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention and subsequently submitted written observations in response to the application. ### Procedural History
On 28 February 2014, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to consider the applicant's appeals against the surveillance authorizations of 23 May 2013, finding that they were not subject to appeal under domestic law. The applicant subsequently lodged numerous criminal, disciplinary, and civil complaints challenging the covert measures. In March 2017, he filed an application with the Kostyantynivka City District Court seeking the exclusion of the surveillance evidence from his criminal file. As of January 2024, the criminal proceedings against the applicant were still at the trial stage, and no domestic decision had been reached regarding his complaints about the covert measures. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 April 2014. On 3 November 2021, a single-judge formation declared several of the applicant's other complaints under Articles 3, 5, 6, and 13 inadmissible. Additionally, the Court noted that new complaints raised in the applicant's observations—concerning the attachment of his property and its destruction by a missile in 2022—fell outside the initial scope of the case.

case_name: CASE OF R.E. AND OTHERS v. ICELAND
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case *R.E. and Others v. Iceland* concerns four applications lodged against the Republic of Iceland by four female Icelandic nationals: R.E., X, Y, and S.O. (the applicants). Two of the applicants, X and Y, were minors at the time of the material events. ### Factual Circumstances
Each applicant alleged they were victims of sexual assault and filed criminal complaints with the domestic police:
1. **R.E.** alleged she was raped by a co-worker in October 2017 while she was highly intoxicated. The police discontinued the investigation in January 2019, citing conflicting accounts regarding consent, the applicant's limited recollection, and a lack of corroborating evidence. 2. **X** (aged 17 at the time) alleged she was raped by an adult co-worker in July 2017. The suspect maintained the encounter was consensual. The District Prosecutor discontinued the case in May 2019, concluding the evidence was insufficient to secure a conviction. 3. **Y** (a minor at the time) alleged she was sexually assaulted by an acquaintance at a campsite in July 2018 while heavily intoxicated. The police discontinued the investigation in June 2019, finding insufficient evidence to prove non-consensual activity or that the suspect should have realized Y was unable to consent. 4. **S.O.** alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men in June 2012. She filed her complaint six years later, in May 2018. The suspects claimed the encounter was consensual. The District Prosecutor discontinued the case in June 2019 due to the lack of contemporaneous evidence and the passage of time. In all four cases, the applicants appealed the decisions to discontinue the investigations to the State Prosecutor, who subsequently upheld the discontinuances between May and October 2019, finding that the available evidence was insufficient to meet the burden of proof required for criminal prosecution. ### Applicants' Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. They alleged that the Icelandic authorities failed to conduct effective, thorough, and prompt investigations into their complaints of sexual violence. They argued that significant delays in questioning suspects (ranging from several months to nearly a year) allowed suspects to coordinate accounts and led to the deterioration of evidence. Furthermore, they asserted that the domestic authorities suffered from systemic, gender-based discrimination, arguing that the legal framework and prosecutorial practices placed an impossibly high evidentiary burden on victims of sexual offences, resulting in disproportionately low prosecution and conviction rates for crimes that predominantly affect women. ### Government's Position
The Icelandic Government contested these allegations. They maintained that the domestic legal framework provided comprehensive protection, with a consent-based definition of rape consistently applied by domestic courts. They argued that investigations into sexual offences were prioritized, thoroughly conducted, and subject to specialized procedures. While acknowledging some delays due to resource constraints and high caseloads, the Government asserted these did not prejudice the investigations. They argued that the decisions to discontinue the proceedings were based strictly on objective assessments of evidentiary sufficiency, in line with the presumption of innocence, and did not reflect any structural or gender-based bias. ### Procedural History
Following the State Prosecutor's decisions upholding the discontinuance of the investigations, the applicants lodged their applications with the European Court of Human Rights between October 2019 and March 2020. The Court subsequently decided to give notice of the applications to the Icelandic Government. Both parties submitted written observations, and the AIRE Centre was granted leave to intervene as a third-party commenter.

case_name: CASE OF BEGIĆ v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 5067/23)

#### 1. The Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Mr. Zlatan Begić, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1975 and living in Tuzla. He is a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front political party. * **Respondent State:** Bosnia and Herzegovina, represented by its acting Agent, Ms. H. Bačvić. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is an annex to the 1995 Dayton Agreement, establishes a power-sharing governance structure. It draws a distinction between the "constituent peoples" (Bosniacs, Croats, and Serbs) and "Others and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina" (those who do not declare an affiliation with any of the three constituent groups). Under Article IV § 3 (b) of the Constitution, the House of Representatives (the first chamber of the State Parliament) must select from its members one Serb, one Bosniac, and one Croat to serve as its Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the leadership rotating among them. Consequently, individuals who do not declare an affiliation with one of the three "constituent peoples" are constitutionally ineligible to hold these leadership positions. The applicant does not declare an affiliation with any of the constituent peoples and is thus categorized under the constitutional designation of "Others." On December 1, 2022, two members of the House of Representatives nominated the applicant for the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. However, his nomination was not put to a vote because it did not comply with the chamber's Rules of Procedure, which implement the constitutional ethnic requirements. #### 3. The Applicant's Main Allegations
The applicant complained about his ineligibility to stand for election to the position of Chair or Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives. He alleged that this restriction violated his rights under:
* **Article 14** of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of discrimination);
* **Article 17** of the Convention (prohibition of abuse of rights);
* **Article 3 of Protocol No. 1** to the Convention (right to free elections); and
* **Article 1 of Protocol No. 12** to the Convention (general prohibition of discrimination). #### 4. The Government's Position
The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina participated in the proceedings and submitted written observations in response to the applicant's complaints. The domestic legal framework notes that the power-sharing arrangements and ethnic requirements were originally accepted by international mediators during the Dayton peace negotiations to secure a ceasefire and end the conflict, with the understanding that the Constitution would remain a dynamic instrument. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
At the domestic level, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina had previously addressed the relationship between the Constitution and the European Convention in decisions nos. U 5/04 and U 13/05. In those cases, the Constitutional Court held that the European Convention does not have a superior status to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It concluded that it lacked the jurisdiction to rule on whether the Constitution itself was in conformity with the Convention, as its constitutional mandate is to uphold the domestic Constitution. Mr. Begić lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on January 20, 2023. The Court subsequently gave notice of the application to the respondent Government regarding the complaints under Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention, Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible. Both parties submitted their respective observations. Because the elected judge in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina was unable to sit in the case, the President of the Chamber appointed an *ad hoc* judge to the panel. The Chamber deliberated on the case in private on January 27, 2026.

case_name: CASE OF NOVÁK v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
step1_summary:
**Case Summary: Novák v. the Czech Republic**

The case of *Novák v. the Czech Republic* (application no. 6656/24) concerns a dispute between Mr. Stanislav Novák, a Czech national, and the Czech Republic regarding child custody and contact arrangements following the unilateral relocation of his children. **Key Factual Circumstances**
The applicant is the father of two daughters, born in 2014 and 2018. Following his separation from the children's mother in April 2021, the parents initially agreed to shared custody. However, the mother subsequently sought sole custody, leading to legal proceedings. In July 2022, the Brno Municipal Court awarded the parents shared custody on a weekly basis. The mother appealed this decision. In August 2022, while the appeal was pending, the mother unilaterally relocated with the children from Brno to Prague—a distance of approximately 200 kilometers—and enrolled them in a new school without the applicant's consent. **Procedural History**
In September 2022, the applicant applied for interim measures to compel the mother to return the children to Brno and to grant him temporary custody. The domestic courts dismissed these applications, finding no urgent need to alter the children's situation on an interim basis and leaving the residence issue to be decided in the main proceedings. In April 2023, the Brno Regional Court overturned the first-instance shared custody judgment, granting sole custody to the mother and awarding the applicant contact rights on alternate weekends and during holidays. The court reasoned that the children had adapted well to Prague over the preceding eight months and that the distance between the parents' homes made shared custody impractical. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's subsequent constitutional appeals. Following the custody ruling, the mother repeatedly refused to hand over the children for visits. This led to numerous enforcement proceedings in which the mother was fined. In February 2025, the mother was criminally convicted and given a suspended sentence for obstructing the enforcement of the contact decision. The applicant subsequently lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights. **The Applicant's Allegations**
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life). He alleged that the domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance between the competing interests. Specifically, he argued that by rejecting his applications for interim measures, the courts allowed the passage of time to consolidate an unlawful situation created by the mother's unilateral relocation. He further contended that the final custody decision effectively legitimized the mother's wrongful conduct and that the courts failed to properly ascertain the children's genuine views. **The Government's Position**
The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies regarding the length of the proceedings. On the merits, they maintained that the domestic courts' decisions were lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the children's best interests, and struck a fair balance. They asserted that the Regional Court was best placed to evaluate the family situation and had properly prioritized the children's need for stability, while also ensuring the applicant's continued involvement through contact rights.

case_name: CASE OF MOGYLA AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Mogyla and Others v. Ukraine*

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves several individual applicants, led by the applicant in application no. 1129/18 (Mogyla), along with two other applicants who lodged separate applications. The respondent party is the State of Ukraine, represented by its Government. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applications arise from domestic civil disputes within Ukraine. The applicants attempted to initiate civil proceedings before the Ukrainian domestic courts to resolve their legal disputes. However, during the initiation phase, they encountered procedural or financial limitations imposed by domestic law or court decisions. These limitations effectively restricted their ability to have their civil claims heard by a court. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants complained primarily under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to a fair trial. Specifically, they alleged that the domestic authorities had restricted their right of access to a court. They argued that the limitations imposed on them to institute civil proceedings were disproportionate and impaired the very essence of their right to judicial protection. Additionally, the applicant in application no. 1129/18 raised other complaints under different provisions of the Convention. #### 4. The Government's Position
Following the receipt of the applications, the European Court of Human Rights gave formal notice of the complaints to the Ukrainian Government. This procedural step provided the Government with the opportunity to submit its observations regarding the admissibility and merits of the applicants' allegations. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicants lodged their respective applications against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on the various dates indicated in the case files. Upon reviewing the incoming applications, the Court noted that application no. 1129/18 and the two other applications shared a similar subject matter, as they all concerned restrictions on the right of access to a court in Ukraine. Consequently, the Court decided to join the applications to examine them jointly in a single proceeding. The case was assigned to the Fifth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of three judges, to deliberate on the admissibility and merits of the joined complaints.

case_name: CASE OF ROMANI AND CANCELLI v. ITALY
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Romani and Cancelli v. Italy* (Applications nos. 54213/19 and 61041/19) involves individual applicants (as listed in the application details) and the respondent State, the Italian Republic, represented by its Agent, Mr. L. D’Ascia. ### Key Factual Circumstances and Domestic Procedural History
The case joins two separate applications concerning domestic civil proceedings initiated by the applicants following the deaths of their next of kin under medical care. *   **Application no. 54213/19:** The applicants’ mother was hospitalised from 2 to 17 January 2004 and passed away on 18 January 2004. On 29 April 2005, the applicants initiated a civil action against the hospital, seeking compensation for damages resulting from their mother's death, which they alleged was caused by the negligence of the medical staff. These civil proceedings spanned three levels of jurisdiction over a total of 14 years, concluding with a judgment delivered by the Court of Cassation on 15 April 2019. *   **Application no. 61041/19:** The applicant’s daughter, who had been affected by congenital heart problems since birth, was hospitalised from 12 to 20 December 1999. On 29 December 1999, the hospital decided not to readmit her, and she died later that day. On 18 January 2001, the applicant brought a civil action against the hospital, seeking compensation for damages sustained due to alleged medical negligence in his child's treatment. The resulting proceedings lasted 16 years and 7 months across four levels of jurisdiction. This included a decision by the Court of Cassation on 10 January 2017 to remit the case back to the Court of Appeal, which ultimately delivered its judgment on 14 May 2019. In parallel, the applicant sought remedy for the length of the proceedings under Law no. 89 of 24 March 2001 (the "Pinto Act") and was awarded 3,660 euros in compensation in 2020. ### The Applicants’ Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants relied on Articles 2 (right to life) and 6 (right to a fair trial) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. They complained about the overall ineffectiveness and excessive duration of the domestic civil proceedings they had pursued to establish liability and obtain compensation for the alleged medical negligence that resulted in the deaths of their family members. ### Government's Position and Procedural History before the ECtHR
The applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights in late 2019. The Court subsequently decided to give notice to the Italian Government of the complaint concerning the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention. At the same time, the Court declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible. The Italian Government, represented by Mr. L. D’Ascia, and the applicants both submitted written observations regarding the notified complaint. Following these submissions, the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, deliberated on the case in private on 2 April 2026.

case_name: CASE OF USATYUK v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Usatyuk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 1902/25)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves the applicant, Mr. Usatyuk, a Ukrainian national. Throughout the proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant was represented by Ms. K.O. Chuyeva, a legal practitioner based in Odesa, Ukraine. The respondent party is the Government of Ukraine. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The application arises from domestic criminal proceedings initiated against the applicant by Ukrainian law enforcement authorities. In connection with these proceedings, the applicant was placed into custody. The central factual background of the case concerns the period during which the applicant was held in pre-trial detention pending the final determination of the criminal charges against him. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant’s primary legal grievance concerns the duration of his confinement prior to trial. He alleged that the total length of his pre-trial detention was unreasonable and excessive. In making this claim, the applicant relied principally on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which protects the right to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. Under this provision, the applicant argued that the domestic authorities failed to justify his continued deprivation of liberty with relevant and sufficient reasons, and that the domestic proceedings were not conducted with the necessary expedition. In addition to the main complaint under Article 5 § 3, the applicant submitted several other complaints alleging further violations of his rights under other provisions of the Convention. #### 4. The Government’s Position
Following the receipt of the application, the European Court of Human Rights gave formal notice of the case to the Ukrainian Government. The provided procedural text does not detail the specific factual or legal arguments raised by the Government in response to the applicant's allegations, noting only that they were notified of the application in accordance with the Court's standard procedures. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the Court's Judgment
The application was officially lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 December 2024 under Article 34 of the Convention, which allows individuals to claim violations of their Convention rights by a contracting state. After the Government was given notice of the application, the case was assigned to the Fifth Section of the Court. The matter was subsequently referred to a Committee for examination. The Committee was composed of three judges: Andreas Zünd (serving as President), Diana Sârcu, and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina acting as the Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee met to deliberate on the admissibility and merits of the application in private on 9 April 2026.

case_name: CASE OF ISMAYILOVA v. AZERBAIJAN
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Ismayilova v. Azerbaijan* (Applications nos. 44031/17 and 41494/20)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Ms. Khadija Rovshan gizi Ismayilova, a well-known investigative journalist and Azerbaijani national residing in Baku. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Azerbaijan, represented by its Agent, Mr. Ç. Əsgərov. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 1 September 2015, the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted the applicant of large-scale misappropriation, illegal entrepreneurship, tax evasion, and abuse of power, sentencing her to seven years and six months’ imprisonment. Following an unsuccessful appeal, the Supreme Court on 25 May 2016 partially quashed her convictions, upholding only the charges of tax evasion and illegal entrepreneurship. The Supreme Court reduced her sentence to three years and six months’ imprisonment, suspended on probation for five years. Her release was conditioned on her not changing her permanent residence without notifying the Binagadi District Enforcement Department. In June 2016, the applicant was informed that a travel ban had been imposed on her for the duration of her probation. On 19 June 2016, she petitioned the Binagadi District Court to lift the ban, arguing that international travel was essential for her professional work as an investigative journalist and that she needed to accompany her mother to Türkiye for heart surgery. On 28 June 2016, the court dismissed her request, ruling that allowing her to travel would hinder the authorities' ability to monitor her behavior and that there were no guarantees of her return. On 7 July 2019, after more than half of her probation period had elapsed, the applicant requested the Binagadi District Court to revoke her suspended sentence, remove her conviction, and lift the travel ban. The court dismissed her request on 9 August 2019, finding insufficient evidence of her rehabilitation and noting the absence of an assessment from the bailiff. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
The applicant challenged the travel ban and the subsequent refusal to lift her probation through multiple levels of the domestic judiciary:
*   **Regarding the initial travel ban:** The applicant appealed the Binagadi District Court’s dismissal of 28 June 2016. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 15 August 2016, and the Supreme Court rejected her final domestic appeal on 8 December 2016. *   **Regarding the 2019 request for revocation:** The applicant appealed the Binagadi District Court’s dismissal of 9 August 2019, specifically requesting the court to find violations of Article 18 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 20 September 2019, and the Supreme Court upheld this decision on 6 February 2020. #### 4. Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that:
*   The travel ban violated her right to leave the country under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention, and that she lacked an effective domestic remedy in this regard, contrary to Article 13. *   The restriction interfered with her right to respect for private and family life (Article 8) and her freedom of expression (Article 10). *   Under Article 18 taken in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, the restrictions on her freedom of movement were applied for purposes other than those prescribed by the Convention. #### 5. Government’s Position and Proceedings before the ECtHR
The Azerbaijani Government submitted written observations in response to the applicant's complaints. Additionally, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the non-governmental organization Article 19 were granted leave to intervene as third parties and submitted comments on application no. 44031/17. The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, deliberated on the applications in private on 17 March 2026.

case_name: CASE OF GAZIN v. UKRAINE
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case involves the applicant, Mr. Andriy Yuriyovych Gazin, a Ukrainian national born in 1967, and the respondent State, the Government of Ukraine. ### Factual Circumstances
On August 3, 2012, the applicant was admitted to Dnipro Municipal Clinic no. 4 with acute flank pain, where he was diagnosed with a ureteral stone and renal colic. In the early hours of August 4, 2012, the duty doctor, M.P., performed a urinary catheterisation on him. Following the procedure, the applicant’s condition deteriorated, and he developed a fever, lower abdominal pain, and increased urinary frequency, leading to a diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis. He was discharged on August 17, 2012. In October 2012, the applicant was readmitted to the clinic with blood in his urine and frequent urination. Subsequent medical tests revealed chronic cystitis and a urethral stricture (narrowing of the urethra). ### Domestic Procedural History
Following a complaint by the applicant, the police initiated criminal medical malpractice proceedings on June 6, 2013. A forensic report completed in December 2015 concluded that the applicant's injuries resulted from an improperly performed catheterisation. Within these criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim against the clinic and M.P., seeking over 3 million Ukrainian hryvnias (equivalent to more than 100,000 euros at the time) in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. On September 28, 2016, M.P. was formally notified of suspicion of medical negligence. On December 5, 2016, the criminal case and the civil claim were referred to the Leninskyi District Court of Dnipro for trial. During the trial, conflicting forensic evidence was submitted: M.P. relied on a report stating his actions met medical standards, while the applicant submitted a report indicating the opposite. As of October 2025, the trial remained pending at first instance with no decision rendered on either the criminal charges or the civil claim. ### Applicant's Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under the procedural limb of Article 8 of the Convention (originally also relying on Articles 3, 6, and 13) that the domestic proceedings concerning his medical malpractice allegations had been excessively lengthy and ineffective. He argued that lodging a civil claim within the criminal proceedings was an appropriate remedy, but that it had ceased to be effective over time due to systemic delays and frequent postponements. ### Government's Position
The Government raised preliminary objections, arguing that the application was premature because the domestic proceedings were still pending. They also asserted that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he had not filed a separate civil action seeking compensation from the State for the excessive length of the pre-trial investigation. On the merits, the Government maintained that the authorities had proceeded without unjustified inactivity. They argued that the duration of the proceedings was due to the complexity of the case, the need for multiple forensic examinations, and the conduct of the applicant, whose representatives had requested 25 of the 98 scheduled postponements. ### Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his application on August 10, 2019. The Court decided to characterize the complaints under the procedural limb of Article 8 of the Convention. It joined the Government's preliminary objections regarding the exhaustion of domestic remedies to the merits of the case and declared the application admissible.

case_name: CASE OF NIKITIN v. ESTONIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: Nikitin v. Estonia

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Vladimir Nikitin, an Estonian national born in 1968, who is currently serving a life sentence in Viru Prison. He is represented in these proceedings by Mr. J. Valdma, a lawyer practicing in Tallinn. The respondent party is the Republic of Estonia, represented by its Agent, Mr. Tim Kolk. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The case concerns eight short-term visits that the applicant had with his wife and her son between June 2, 2018, and December 19, 2019, while detained at Viru Prison. During these visits, the applicant was physically separated from his family members by a glass partition, meaning they could only communicate via an intercom system. In November 2020, the applicant applied to the Viru Prison authorities for monetary compensation, arguing that the physical separation during these visits violated his rights. The prison authorities rejected the application. They pointed out that the applicant had never formally requested to have the meetings conducted without the glass partition, which they argued was a necessary primary remedy under the State Liability Act. The authorities also cited general security considerations for short-term visits and noted that alternative communication methods were available to him. Although the Internal Prison Rules allowed for discretionary exceptions to the glass partition requirement under specific circumstances, the prison authorities later asserted that the applicant’s situation did not meet any of those exceptions. #### 3. Procedural History
Following the rejection of his administrative claim, the applicant appealed to the Tartu Administrative Court. On May 31, 2021, the court dismissed the appeal. It determined that the use of the glass partition was a proportionate security measure under the Internal Prison Rules and that the overall interference with the applicant's rights was not severe enough to justify compensation, especially given the alternative communication channels available. The applicant appealed this decision to the Tartu Court of Appeal. On February 28, 2022, the appellate court upheld the lower court's judgment. It emphasized the applicant's passivity, noting he had never requested a partition-free meeting room, thereby failing to exhaust the primary domestic remedy of seeking an administrative order to oblige the prison to take such measures. On June 7, 2022, the Supreme Court of Estonia refused to grant leave to appeal. #### 4. Applicant's Allegations and Government's Position
The applicant subsequently lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. He alleges a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life) due to the domestic authorities' refusal to allow him short-term visits without a glass partition. The Estonian Government, having been given notice of the complaint, submitted its observations on the matter.

case_name: CASE OF GAZSÓ v. HUNGARY
step1_summary:
### Summary of the Case

#### 1. The Parties
The case of *Gazsó v. Hungary* (Application no. 48322/12) involves Mr. György Gazsó, a Hungarian national born in 1963 and residing in Telki, as the applicant. He was represented by Mr. D. Karsai, a lawyer practicing in Budapest. The respondent party is the Government of Hungary, represented by Mr. Z. Tallódi, Agent from the Ministry of Justice. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Domestic Procedural History
The case arose from a labor dispute between the applicant and his former employer. An initial round of litigation took place between 25 February 2002 and 18 May 2005, resulting in a court order requiring the employer to re-employ the applicant. The applicant did not accept the specific position offered to him under the re-employment order, which led to a second set of legal proceedings commencing on 5 January 2006. The domestic procedural history of this second dispute progressed as follows:
* **18 November 2008:** The Budapest Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s action. * **9 July 2010:** On appeal, the Budapest Regional Court reversed the first-instance decision and ruled in favor of the applicant. * **29 February 2012:** Following a petition for review filed by the employer, the Kúria (the Supreme Court of Hungary) reversed the appeal judgment and ruled in favor of the employer. In total, this second set of proceedings lasted from 5 January 2006 to 29 February 2012, spanning approximately six years and two months across three levels of jurisdiction. #### 3. Procedural History Before the European Court of Human Rights
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 July 2012. On 13 November 2014, the Court communicated the application to the Hungarian Government. At the time of communication, the Court proposed the application of the pilot judgment procedure (under Rule 61 of the Rules of Court) to both parties, who subsequently submitted their comments on the matter. The Court later examined the admissibility of the application and declared the complaints under both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 admissible, finding them not to be manifestly ill-founded or otherwise inadmissible. #### 4. The Applicant’s Allegations
The applicant raised two main complaints before the Court:
* **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a fair trial within a reasonable time):** The applicant alleged that the duration of the domestic labor proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement, particularly given the requirement of special diligence in employment-related disputes. * **Article 13 (Right to an effective remedy):** The applicant alleged that there was no effective domestic remedy available in Hungary through which he could accelerate the protracted proceedings or obtain adequate redress. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Hungarian Government contested the applicant's allegations:
* Regarding the Article 6 § 1 complaint, the Government disputed the assertion that the length of the proceedings was unreasonable under the specific circumstances of the case. * Regarding the Article 13 complaint, the Government contested the applicant’s arguments in general terms, disputing the claim that Hungarian law lacked effective domestic remedies to address the length of civil proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF MICLEA v. ROMANIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Miclea v. Romania* (Application no. 69582/12)

#### 1. Main Parties
* **Applicant:** Mr. Alexandru Miclea, a Romanian national born in 1989 and residing in Arad, Romania. * **Respondent State:** The Government of Romania. * **Other Key Actors:** Police officers D.C.I. and M.C., who were the subjects of the applicant's domestic criminal complaints. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Applicant’s Allegations
The case arises from an incident on August 8, 2010. According to the applicant, he and his friends were involved in a street fight outside a bar in Arad at approximately 4:00 a.m. After police arrived, the applicant and his friends were taken to the local police station to give statements. While waiting inside the station, the applicant allegedly witnessed a police officer behaving roughly with another arrestee and commented aloud on the behavior. In response, officers D.C.I. and M.C. allegedly took him to a back office, handcuffed him to a radiator, and repeatedly punched and kicked him until another officer intervened. Later that day, the applicant visited the emergency unit of Arad County Hospital, where he was diagnosed with maxillofacial trauma and contusions. On August 9, 2010, a forensic medical certificate was issued, noting a cut lip, bruising on his chest and face, and excoriations on both wrists, which the applicant asserted were consistent with being handcuffed. The certificate estimated that his injuries required nine days of medical treatment. The applicant alleged that this physical abuse constituted a violation of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and that the subsequent domestic investigation into the incident was ineffective. #### 3. Government’s Position
The Romanian Government disputed the applicant's account of the events. They maintained that the applicant and his friends had already been injured and had their clothes torn during the street fight before the police arrived. They asserted that the applicant was escorted home by police solely to prevent further conflict and did not report any police abuse at the time. Regarding the domestic investigation, the Government argued it was thorough and effective. They stated that the prosecutor had interviewed all relevant parties and witnesses, and that a requested witness, K.A., could not be summoned because the applicant had provided incorrect contact details and because records showed K.A. had not accompanied the applicant to the station. #### 4. Procedural History
On September 15, 2010, the applicant filed a criminal complaint against officers D.C.I. and M.C. for abusive investigative conduct and bodily harm. The case was eventually handled by the Prosecutor’s Office of the Arad District Court. During the investigation, the prosecutor took statements from the applicant and two of his friends, S.L. and S.N., who supported the applicant's claims. However, the accused officers and three other police officers present on the night of the incident denied any abuse, asserting the applicant's injuries resulted from the street fight. On January 12, 2012, the prosecutor decided not to initiate criminal proceedings, concluding that the allegations of police assault could not be established beyond doubt. The applicant’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the head prosecutor on February 7, 2012. The applicant then contested the decision before the Arad District Court, arguing that the prosecutor had ignored the medical evidence of wrist excoriations and relied unfairly on the testimony of biased police officers. On April 18, 2012, the Arad District Court rejected the applicant's complaint as manifestly ill-founded, ruling that the evidence did not prove the officers' guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and pointing to discrepancies between the statements of the applicant and his witnesses. Following this final domestic decision, the applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on October 11, 2012.

case_name: CASE OF PSMA, SPOL. S R.O. v. SLOVAKIA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *PSMA, spol. s r.o. v. Slovakia* (Application no. 42533/11)

#### 1. Main Parties
* **Applicant:** PSMA, spol. s r.o., a private limited company established under Slovak law. * **Respondent State:** The Slovak Republic (represented by its Government Agent). * **Domestic Counterparty:** Slovak Radio (*Slovenský rozhlas*), Slovakia’s national public-service radio broadcaster. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In March 1995, the applicant company entered into a contract with Slovak Radio to act as its exclusive agent for selling advertising broadcasting time. The contractual relationship proceeded successfully and was amended multiple times to extend its validity through December 2007. However, in 2004, relations deteriorated. Slovak Radio expressed dissatisfaction with the volume of business generated and billed the applicant company for the difference between estimated and actual profits. When the applicant company did not pay, Slovak Radio served a notice of contract termination, which took effect in September 2005. In June 2006, the applicant company sued Slovak Radio, demanding an indemnity of approximately EUR 693,000 for the termination of the contract. This sum was calculated based on average yearly commissions, which factored in both financial and non-financial (barter) transactions. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
* **First-Instance Judgment:** The Bratislava I District Court served the lawsuit on Slovak Radio, but the broadcaster failed to submit written observations or attend any scheduled hearings. In May 2007, the District Court granted the applicant company’s action in full, determining the case on the available evidence. * **Appellate Judgment:** Slovak Radio appealed to the Bratislava Regional Court, disputing the inclusion of barter transactions in the indemnity calculation and challenging its exclusion from the first-instance hearings. In November 2007, the Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. The decision became final and binding on January 9, 2008. * **First Constitutional Complaint:** In March 2008, Slovak Radio filed a constitutional complaint. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible in July 2008, ruling that Slovak Radio had failed to exhaust ordinary appeals on points of law. * **Extraordinary Appeal:** In April 2008, Slovak Radio petitioned the Prosecutor General to lodge an extraordinary appeal on points of law. The Prosecutor General complied in October 2008, arguing to the Supreme Court that the lower courts had failed to independently and properly examine the validity of the contract and its termination. In August 2009, the Supreme Court allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed the final judgments of both lower courts, and remitted the case to the first-instance court. * **Second Constitutional Complaint:** The applicant company challenged the Supreme Court's decision before the Constitutional Court. In November 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the applicant's complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. #### 4. The Applicant's Allegations before the ECHR
The applicant company lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) of the Convention. Specifically, the applicant argued that:
* The quashing of a final, binding, and enforceable judgment in its favor via an extraordinary appeal violated the principle of legal certainty. * The extraordinary appeal mechanism operated as an ordinary appeal in disguise, allowing a passive party to bypass standard procedural requirements. * The proceedings lacked equality of arms and adversarial fairness, particularly as the Supreme Court did not address the applicant's submitted observations. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Slovak Government contested the application on both procedural and substantive grounds:
* **Prematurity:** The Government argued the application was premature because, following the Supreme Court's remittal, the domestic proceedings on the merits of the compensation claim were still actively pending before the first-instance court. * **Merits:** Substantively, the Government maintained that the extraordinary appeal was justified to correct a fundamental error, asserting that the lower courts had failed to properly examine the validity of the contract termination notice, which undermined the substantive correctness of the original judgments.

case_name: CASE OF KOVÁROVÁ v. SLOVAKIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Kovárová v. Slovakia* (Application no. 46564/10)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Ms. Eva Kovárová, a Slovak national born in 1947 and residing in Bratislava. *   **Respondent State:** The Slovak Republic, represented by its Agent, Ms. M. Pirošíková. *   **Domestic Defendant:** A community of owners of residential and non-residential premises in Bratislava (a registered legal entity). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 9 May 2007, the applicant initiated civil proceedings before the Bratislava V District Court against the community of flat owners (the defendant). She sought a ruling to declare a flat owners' meeting held on 24 April 2007 unlawful and its decisions void. While the lawsuit was pending, the defendant was struck out of the official register on 14 December 2007 because the administration of the building was transferred to a specialized agency. On 3 March 2008, the District Court discontinued the proceedings on the grounds that the defendant had ceased to exist and had no legal successor. The applicant appealed, arguing that the new administration agency was the legal successor, or alternatively, that the court should have stayed the proceedings pending the outcome of another lawsuit challenging the validity of the decision to wind up the defendant. On 30 May 2008, the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the discontinuance, noting that the defendant had lost its capacity to be a party to the proceedings. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
Following the Regional Court's decision, the applicant filed an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, arguing that she had been prevented from pursuing her case and that the appellate court had failed to provide adequate legal or factual reasoning. On 7 May 2009, the Supreme Court declared her appeal inadmissible, finding that the alleged shortcomings did not meet the statutory criteria for an appeal on points of law and that staying proceedings was a discretionary option rather than a mandatory duty of the lower courts. On 17 August 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 127 of the Slovak Constitution against the decisions of all three levels of ordinary courts. On 16 December 2009, the Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible. It rejected the complaint against the Regional Court as belated (filed outside the two-month statutory limit) and concluded that the Supreme Court's decision on the admissibility of her appeal on points of law was sufficiently reasoned and non-arbitrary. #### 4. Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of her rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (access to court and a fair hearing). Specifically, she complained that:
*   The ordinary courts' decisions to discontinue the proceedings on her civil claim were arbitrary. *   The Constitutional Court breached her right of access to a court by rejecting her complaint against the Regional Court's decision as belated. #### 5. Government’s Position
The Government argued that the application should be distinguished from previous similar cases. They contended that the Constitutional Court had actually reviewed the substance of the applicant's arguments regarding the ordinary courts' refusal to stay the proceedings and had found the approach compatible with her fundamental rights. Furthermore, the Government maintained that the defendant had been wound up without a universal legal successor, and that the applicant had failed to submit timely arguments to the first-instance court to justify continuing the proceedings before they were discontinued. #### 6. Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights
The application was lodged with the Court on 3 August 2010 and was communicated to the Slovak Government on 2 April 2014. The Court examined the admissibility of the applicant's complaints regarding the fairness of the proceedings and her access to the Constitutional Court together, declaring the application admissible.

case_name: CASE OF K.F. v. CYPRUS
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *K.F. v. Cyprus* (Application no. 41858/10) involves Mr. K.F., a Syrian national of Kurdish origin, and the Republic of Cyprus. ### Factual Circumstances
Mr. K.F. entered Cyprus illegally in February 2005 and applied for asylum. The Asylum Service rejected his application in August 2008, citing contradictions in his account of why he fled Syria. His subsequent appeal to the Reviewing Authority for Refugees was dismissed in June 2009. In August 2009, deportation and detention orders were issued against him, and he was detained until December 2009, when the orders were revoked. In May 2010, he requested the reopening of his asylum file, presenting a document allegedly showing he was wanted by Syrian authorities; this request was ultimately rejected in May 2011. In May 2010, Mr. K.F. participated in a continuous protest with other Syrian Kurds in Nicosia against Cypriot asylum policies. On June 11, 2010, police conducted an early-morning operation, transferring the protesters, including Mr. K.F., to the Emergency Response Unit (ERU) headquarters for identification. Mr. K.F. was arrested, charged with unlawful stay, and detained under new deportation and detention orders. In March 2011, he briefly escaped detention, was injured, hospitalized, and returned to custody. He was released on April 20, 2011. In mid-2012, Mr. K.F. voluntarily left Cyprus and relocated to Northern Iraq. ### Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that his deportation to Syria would violate Article 3 of the Convention, exposing him to torture or inhuman treatment due to his Kurdish origin, political activities, and past detention. Under Article 13, he argued he lacked an effective domestic remedy to challenge his deportation. Under Article 5 § 1, he claimed his transfer to the ERU and subsequent detention were unlawful. Under Article 5 § 4, he argued that domestic law did not provide a speedy judicial remedy to challenge his detention. ### Government’s Position
The Cypriot Government contended that the applicant’s asylum claims were not credible. Regarding the June 2010 police operation, they argued the protest encampment posed a public health and safety hazard, and the transfer to the ERU was a brief, necessary measure for identification rather than an unlawful deprivation of liberty. Regarding Article 5 § 4, they maintained that the domestic habeas corpus proceedings were conducted as speedily as possible under the circumstances. Finally, they argued that because the applicant had voluntarily relocated to Iraq, he was no longer at risk of deportation to Syria, making his Article 3 and 13 complaints inadmissible. ### Procedural History
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on June 14, 2010. On the same day, the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39, directing Cyprus not to deport him. Domestically, the applicant filed a habeas corpus application in January 2011, which the Supreme Court of Cyprus dismissed in March 2011. His subsequent appeal was dismissed by the appellate court in October 2012 as moot because he had already been released. Additionally, the Supreme Court dismissed his main asylum-related recourse in January 2012. Following the applicant's relocation to Iraq, the European Court lifted the Rule 39 interim measure in June 2012.

case_name: AFFAIRE SANTOS SILVA c. PORTUGAL
step1_summary:
### Summary: *Santos Silva v. Portugal* (Application no. 52246/12)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves the applicant, Mr. José António Oliveira Santos Silva, a Portuguese national born in 1957 and residing in Louredo, Santa Maria da Feira. He was represented by Mr. J. J. Ferreira Alves, a lawyer practicing in Matosinhos. The respondent party is the Republic of Portugal, represented by its Agent, Mrs. M. F. da Graça Carvalho, Deputy-Attorney General. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The dispute originated on December 19, 2005, when the applicant filed a civil lawsuit in the Santa Maria da Feira Court against multiple defendants to assert his right to use a water channel. The proceedings faced immediate procedural complications:
*   In February 2006, one defendant (I.) informed the court that her husband (defendant A.) had died in May 2005. Another defendant (J.) informed the court that defendant A. J. had died in 1973, and his heirs were living in Brazil. *   On May 5, 2006, the court stayed the proceedings pending the outcome of inheritance proceedings, directing the applicant to submit the deceased defendants' death certificates. *   The applicant applied to continue the proceedings against the heirs on November 27, 2006, and submitted the required documentation on January 9, 2007. The court admitted the heirs as parties on July 2, 2007, and subsequently resumed the main proceedings. *   On April 23, 2008, the applicant was notified that the court had failed to summon one of the defendants (A. G.). *   On January 27, 2010, the court interrupted the proceedings, citing a lack of action by the parties. *   The applicant provided a new address for defendant A.’s heir on January 26, 2011, and the proceedings were resumed. *   On November 24, 2011, the Santa Maria da Feira Court dismissed the applicant’s claim on the grounds that it was time-barred. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
Following the first-instance dismissal, the applicant appealed to the Porto Court of Appeal (*Tribunal da Relação do Porto*) on December 6, 2011. On June 4, 2013, the Porto Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision and ordered a new trial. The case was sent back to the first-instance court, where the proceedings remained pending. By the time the matter was examined internationally, the domestic proceedings had been active for over nine years across two levels of jurisdiction. #### 4. The Applicant's Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant raised two primary complaints:
*   **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** He alleged that the length of the domestic civil proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement. *   **Article 13 (Right to an Effective Remedy):** He alleged that Portuguese law did not provide an effective domestic remedy through which he could challenge or expedite the excessive length of the proceedings. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Portuguese Government contested the applicant's allegations. While they acknowledged that the domestic proceedings had experienced delays exceeding what would normally be expected, they argued that the responsibility for the protracted timeline lay with the applicant's own procedural conduct rather than with the domestic judicial authorities.

case_name: CASE OF PENTIKÄINEN v. FINLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Pentikäinen v. Finland* (Application no. 11882/10)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicant is Markus Veikko Pentikäinen, a Finnish photographer and journalist employed by the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*. The respondent party is the Republic of Finland. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On September 9, 2006, the applicant was sent by his employer to take photographs of the "Smash ASEM" demonstration in Helsinki. Prior to the event, police risk assessments indicated a high likelihood of violence. After the demonstration turned violent, the police cordoned off the area, stopped the demonstration from marching, and repeatedly broadcasted orders for the crowd to disperse. While hundreds of people left through designated checkpoints, a core group of protesters and the applicant remained inside the cordon. The applicant, who was dressed in dark clothing and did not have his press badge visibly displayed, stayed to document the event. At approximately 9:00 p.m., a police officer personally ordered him to leave. The applicant refused, stating he was a journalist covering the event. Shortly thereafter, the police apprehended the remaining individuals, including the applicant. He was detained for seventeen and a half hours before being interrogated and released. His camera equipment was held during his detention but was not confiscated, and he was permitted to keep and use all of his photographs.
