The case of *Korošec v. Slovenia* (Application no. 77212/12) involves the applicant, Mr. Tadej Korošec, a Slovenian national born in 1980, and the respondent state, the Republic of Slovenia. ### Factual Circumstances
Mr. Korošec suffers from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and requires 24-hour assistance with his daily activities. In 2006, the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of the Republic of Slovenia ("the Institute") awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance at 70% of the reference amount. In May 2009, the applicant’s general practitioner applied for an increase in this allowance to 100%, citing a deterioration in the applicant's respiratory functions and stating that he required permanent professional medical assistance alongside family care. In July 2009, the Institute’s first-instance disability commission, composed of two medical specialists, examined the applicant and his medical files, concluding that he did not require permanent professional medical assistance. Based on this opinion, the Institute dismissed the request for an increase. The applicant appealed, but in September 2009, the Institute’s second-instance disability commission reached the same conclusion. Consequently, the Institute dismissed the applicant's appeal. ### Domestic Procedural History
In October 2009, the applicant filed a lawsuit against the Institute before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court, requesting that the court appoint an independent medical expert to assess his condition. In September 2010, the court dismissed his claim and rejected the request for an independent expert, ruling that the opinions of the Institute's own first- and second-instance disability commissions, alongside other evidence, were sufficient. The applicant appealed to the Higher Labour and Social Court, arguing that the first-instance court lacked the medical expertise to make such a determination without an independent expert. In January 2011, the Higher Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the lower court had properly relied on the expertise of the Institute's commissions. The applicant then applied for leave to appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the lower courts' reliance on the Institute's commissions contradicted established Supreme Court case-law (specifically decision no. VIII Ips 3/2006), which dictated that the Institute's disability commissions could not be treated as independent experts in judicial proceedings where the Institute itself was a party. In May 2011, the Supreme Court dismissed his application. The applicant subsequently lodged a constitutional complaint, which the Constitutional Court dismissed in June 2012. ### Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights and Allegations
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on November 29, 2012. The application was officially communicated to the Slovenian Government on October 2, 2014. Under Article 6 of the Convention, the applicant alleged that the domestic court proceedings had been unfair. He specifically contended that the domestic courts' refusal to appoint an independent medical expert, and their reliance instead on the opinions of the disability commissions—which were appointed by and operated within the respondent party (the Institute)—violated his right to a fair hearing. The Slovenian Government was represented in these proceedings by their Agent, Ms. J. Morela.

case_name: CASE OF KRISTIANSEN v. NORWAY
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicant is Mr. Jørgen Kristiansen, a Norwegian national. The respondent state is the Kingdom of Norway. The case also involves the complainant, Ms. A, and a juror, referred to as "J."

### Key Factual Circumstances
The case originates from criminal proceedings against the applicant. On 9 March 2008, the applicant (then 23 years old) and Ms. A (then 17 years old) left a party in a borrowed car. The car’s battery failed, and they waited inside the vehicle for a taxi. Ms. A subsequently accused the applicant of attempting to rape her during this time. The applicant denied the charge, maintaining that their physical contact had been voluntary. During the appeal trial before the High Court, Juror J disclosed to the presiding judge during a recess that she had prior contact with Ms. A. J was the foster mother of a child who had been in the same school class as Ms. A, and she had interacted with Ms. A at birthday parties and class outings several years prior. J stated that she recalled Ms. A from that time as a "quiet and calm girl." 

Following this disclosure, the applicant’s defense counsel requested J’s disqualification on the grounds of lack of impartiality. Ms. A’s assistant advocate supported the motion, and the public prosecutor expressed understanding of it. The High Court rejected the motion, finding J’s prior contact sporadic and remote, and concluded that her recollection was not capable of influencing her assessment of the case. J subsequently participated in the full trial, the jury's deliberations, and the sentencing. ### Procedural History
On 18 September 2008, the Sarpsborg City Court convicted the applicant of attempted rape. On appeal, the Borgarting High Court, sitting with a jury, upheld the conviction on 5 February 2009, sentencing the applicant to one year's imprisonment and ordering him to pay compensation to Ms. A. The applicant appealed the High Court's procedure to the Supreme Court of Norway, challenging J's impartiality. On 26 June 2009, the Supreme Court rejected the appeal by a 3-to-2 majority. The majority held that J's sporadic, historical contact did not undermine her impartiality and that her description of Ms. A was a neutral observation of childhood behavior rather than an assessment of credibility. The minority dissented, arguing that because the case turned entirely on the credibility of the victim versus the applicant, J's positive characterization of Ms. A—made right after hearing the testimonies—could easily be perceived as favoring the victim's credibility. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 23 December 2009. ### Applicant's Allegations
Before the European Court, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arguing he was denied a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal. He contended that J's prior relationship with the victim and her description of Ms. A as "quiet and calm" created an objectively justified fear of bias. He emphasized the timing of J's statement, the decisive nature of the victim's credibility to the outcome of the case, and the fact that all legal representatives at the trial had supported or expressed understanding of the disqualification motion. ### Government's Position
The Government contested the applicant's allegations, arguing that J's prior acquaintance with Ms. A was remote and typical of a classmate's parent. They maintained that J's statement was a neutral recollection of past behavior, not an opinion on her current credibility. Furthermore, they highlighted domestic procedural safeguards, such as the professional judges' power to overturn jury verdicts and the High Court's reasoned decision on the impartiality motion, arguing these measures satisfied the requirements of Article 6 § 1.

case_name: CASE OF MYUMYUN v. BULGARIA
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: *Myumyun v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 67258/13)

**1. The Main Parties**
The case was brought by Mr. Nuray Bayramali Myumyun, a Bulgarian national born in 1979, against the Republic of Bulgaria. The key domestic actors involved were three officers of the Pavel Banya police force: Mr. N.K., Mr. I.K., and Mr. T.A. **2. Key Factual Circumstances**
On 20 February 2012, Mr. Myumyun went to the Pavel Banya police station in response to an inquiry regarding a burglary. While at the station, he was taken into a room where officers N.K., I.K., and T.A. subjected him to physical violence to extract information. The applicant was repeatedly hit with a wooden bat and a rubber truncheon, kicked, and subjected to electric shocks administered via an electroshock prod. The beating stopped after he began bleeding from his nose. He was released later that afternoon after signing a statement. A forensic medical examination the following day documented numerous haematomas and bruises across his face, shoulder, back, and torso. **3. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment**
*   **Criminal Proceedings:** Following a complaint, the Kazanlak District Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal proceedings against the three officers, charging them with causing minor bodily harm in the performance of their duties. The applicant requested that the officers be charged with more severe offences, such as coercing a confession (Article 287 of the Criminal Code) or abuse of office (Article 282). The prosecution and the court rejected these requests, noting that Article 287 strictly applied only to individuals who already held the formal status of an accused or witness in an active criminal investigation. Because the charged offence carried a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment and the officers had no prior convictions, domestic law (Article 78a of the Criminal Code) required the court to waive criminal liability and replace it with administrative penalties. On 12 December 2013, the Kazanlak District Court convicted the officers, waived their criminal liability, and fined each BGN 2,000 (approximately EUR 1,023). The court chose not to disqualify them from police work. This decision was upheld on appeal by the Stara Zagora Regional Court on 25 April 2014. *   **Disciplinary Proceedings:** An internal police inquiry resulted in Mr. N.K. and Mr. I.K. being barred from promotion competitions for three years for unlawful detention. The disciplinary commission concluded that no physical ill-treatment had occurred. *   **Civil Proceedings:** The applicant filed a civil claim for damages. On 19 January 2015, the Stara Zagora Administrative Court found the regional police directorate liable for the officers' actions and awarded the applicant BGN 4,000 (approximately EUR 2,045) in non-pecuniary damages. **4. The Applicant’s Allegations**
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the domestic authorities' procedural response to his ill-treatment fell short of the requirements of Article 3 of the Convention. He argued that the administrative fines were excessively lenient and disproportionate to the gravity of the abuse, which he asserted amounted to torture. He also contended that the domestic legal framework was deficient because it failed to properly criminalize torture or allow for the prosecution of coercing a confession in pre-investigation phases. **5. The Government’s Position**
The Bulgarian Government maintained that the domestic response was adequate and compliant with Article 3. They argued that the authorities had carried out a prompt and effective investigation, and that the domestic courts had carefully weighed mitigating and aggravating factors. They asserted that the combination of criminal fines, disciplinary sanctions, and civil damages ensured that the officers were held accountable and did not act with impunity.

case_name: CASE OF KIIVERI v. FINLAND
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Kiiveri v. Finland* involves the applicant, Mr. Timo Veikko Kiiveri, a Finnish national who owns 90% of the shares in a construction and decoration company, and the respondent State, the Republic of Finland. ### Factual Circumstances
In 2005, Finnish tax authorities conducted an inspection of the applicant’s company, concluding that it had failed to declare taxes, paid off-the-books salaries, and engaged in fraudulent activities. On September 8, 2008, the tax authorities imposed additional income taxes and tax surcharges on both the company and the applicant personally for the tax years 2002, 2003, 2005, and 2006. The applicant did not appeal these administrative decisions. Under domestic law, the five-year appeal period elapsed, making the tax decisions final on December 31 of 2008 (for the tax year 2002), 2009 (for 2003), 2011 (for 2005), and 2012 (for 2006). ### Domestic Procedural History
Parallel to the tax proceedings, the police initiated a criminal investigation in June 2007. On March 6, 2009, the prosecutor charged the applicant with accounting offences and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. The first count concerned the company's taxes (years 2000–2006) and the second concerned his personal income taxes (years 2000–2003 and 2005–2006). On September 9, 2009, the District Court of Tampere convicted the applicant, sentencing him to three years' imprisonment, ordering him to pay EUR 685,080.66 in compensation, and imposing a six-year business ban. The Court of Appeal of Turku largely upheld this judgment on September 15, 2010, rejecting the applicant’s *ne bis in idem* argument. On February 27, 2012, the Supreme Court of Finland partially altered the judgment. It dismissed the criminal charge concerning the tax year 2002 without examining the merits, ruling that because the tax surcharges for 2002 had become final before the criminal charges were brought in 2009, the *ne bis in idem* principle barred prosecution for that year. The Supreme Court upheld the remaining convictions but reduced the applicant's prison sentence to two years and ten months. An extraordinary appeal by the applicant was refused by the Supreme Court in March 2013. ### Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. He argued that he had been tried and punished twice for the same offence, having been subjected to both administrative tax surcharges and subsequent criminal prosecution and imprisonment based on the same underlying facts. ### Government’s Position
The Finnish Government contested the allegations. They argued that the applicant lost his victim status regarding the tax year 2002 because the Supreme Court had already dismissed that charge. They also contended that the *ne bis in idem* principle did not apply to the company-related offences, as the applicant was not personally liable for the company's tax surcharges and the underlying facts were distinct. Finally, they argued that Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 did not apply to parallel proceedings, noting that for the tax year 2006, the tax decision only became final after the criminal proceedings had concluded.

case_name: CASE OF NALBANDYAN v. ARMENIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: Nalbandyan v. Armenia (Applications nos. 9935/06 and 23339/06)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicants:** Mr. Bagrat Nalbandyan (first applicant), his wife Ms. Narine Nalbandyan (second applicant), and their daughter Ms. Arevik Nalbandyan (third applicant), all Armenian nationals. *   **Respondent State:** The Republic of Armenia. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In June 2004, Armenian law-enforcement authorities initiated a murder investigation following the discovery of a local girl's body near the applicants' home in Vardenis. The first applicant was taken into custody on 8 June 2004 and was subsequently sentenced to fifteen days of administrative imprisonment for allegedly disobeying police orders. On 9 July 2004, the first and second applicants were formally arrested on murder charges. During their detention, medical examinations recorded physical injuries. Upon her transfer to a detention facility on 14 July 2004, the second applicant was found to have bruised and swollen feet. On 16 July 2004, a medical examination of the third applicant (who was a minor at the time) revealed a suspected concussion along with bruising on her head, back, and left arm. #### 3. The Applicants' Main Allegations
The applicants alleged that they were subjected to systematic physical and psychological ill-treatment by police officers and prosecutors to coerce confessions. *   The first applicant alleged that his administrative detention was a pretext to keep him in custody unlawfully, during which he was repeatedly beaten. *   The second applicant alleged that on 8 July 2004, she was beaten on the soles of her feet with rubber batons by police officers and a regional deputy prosecutor until she fainted. She further alleged that officers locked her daughter in a nearby rat-infested room and threatened her with rape, which coerced both her and her husband into confessing. *   The third applicant alleged that she was repeatedly detained, threatened with rape, locked in a dark cell, and physically assaulted by the deputy prosecutor and other officers. *   The applicants also alleged that they were deprived of effective legal assistance, asserting that their lawyer was forced to miss trial hearings due to safety fears from courtroom disorder, and that the court falsely recorded that they had voluntarily waived their right to counsel. #### 4. The Government's Position
The Armenian Government contested the allegations of ill-treatment, arguing that the applicants failed to produce credible evidence. They asserted that:
*   No injuries were recorded on the first applicant upon his admission to the detention facility. *   The second applicant's foot swelling and bruising were caused by high blood pressure rather than physical abuse, and video footage from 10 July 2004 showed her walking freely without signs of injury. *   The third applicant's medical report did not specify the cause of her injuries, and she had failed to complain immediately after her release. *   The domestic authorities had thoroughly investigated the complaints and found them to be unsubstantiated. #### 5. Domestic Procedural History
On 31 August 2004, a regional prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the accused police officers, relying on the officers' denials and the medical explanation regarding the second applicant's high blood pressure. On 4 February 2005, the Gegharkunik Regional Court convicted the first and second applicants of murder, sentencing them to nine and fourteen years’ imprisonment, respectively. The court dismissed their allegations of ill-treatment. The applicants appealed, but on 2 July 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld the convictions. During these proceedings, the court ruled that the applicants had dispensed with their lawyer's services, a claim the applicants disputed. On 12 August 2005, the Court of Cassation dismissed the second applicant's appeal and left the lawyer's appeal unexamined. In parallel, the applicants challenged the prosecutor's refusal to investigate their ill-treatment. After several appeals regarding the failure of the authorities to formally serve the refusal decision on them, the Court of Appeal ultimately dismissed their challenge on 10 November 2005, ruling that the allegations had already been examined and resolved within the main criminal trial. The applicants subsequently lodged their applications with the European Court of Human Rights in February and May 2006, alleging violations of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and lack of effective investigation) and Article 6 (right to a fair trial and legal assistance) of the Convention.

case_name: CASE OF TATAR v. SWITZERLAND
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Tatar v. Switzerland* (Application no. 65692/12)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Mehmet Ali Tatar, a Turkish national born in 1950. *   **Respondent State:** The Swiss Confederation (Switzerland). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant arrived in Switzerland in June 1988. Following claims of past detention and torture in Turkey due to his membership in the Turkish Communist Party (TCP), Swiss authorities recognized him as a refugee and granted him asylum in 1994. His family subsequently joined him in Switzerland. In 1990, the applicant suffered a severe workplace injury and was subsequently granted an invalidity pension. In 2001, the applicant killed his wife during a dispute. In 2003, he was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. During the criminal proceedings, he was diagnosed with a recurrent depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms (schizophrenic disease syndrome). Consequently, the court accepted a plea of diminished responsibility and suspended his prison sentence to allow for treatment in a closed psychiatric facility. In March 2009, the Federal Office for Migration revoked the applicant's asylum status because he had committed a serious crime, though his status as a refugee under the 1951 Refugee Convention was maintained. In April 2010, the applicant was paroled on the condition that he reside in an open facility with continuous psychiatric care and supervision. Medical expert reports indicated that the applicant was unable to live independently, required ongoing psychotropic medication, and would suffer a severe mental health deterioration and potential psychotic relapses if expelled. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
In June 2010, the Migration Office of the Canton of Zurich revoked the applicant’s residence permit and ordered him to leave Switzerland. The applicant appealed the decision through the domestic courts. On August 2, 2012, the Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland dismissed his appeal. The court ruled that the applicant could be expelled despite his refugee status because of his conviction for a serious crime. It concluded that adequate psychiatric facilities were available in Turkey, that the applicant had not substantiated a real threat of a blood feud by his deceased wife's relatives, and that his past political activities did not pose a current threat of persecution. The expulsion order remained in force, though its execution was subsequently postponed. #### 4. Applicant's Allegations and Government's Position before the ECtHR

*   **Articles 2 and 3 (Right to Life / Prohibition of Inhuman or Degrading Treatment):** 
    *   *The Applicant Alleged:* His expulsion to Turkey would cause a rapid and life-threatening deterioration of his mental health due to the lack of adequate, affordable psychiatric care in Turkey and the separation from his supportive family in Switzerland. He also claimed he faced a real risk of being killed in a blood feud by his wife's relatives and of being arrested and tortured by Turkish authorities due to his past TCP membership. *   *The Government Contested:* They argued that adequate psychiatric treatment was available in Turkey and that, prior to any removal, they would assess the applicant's fitness to travel, provide medical escorts if necessary, and coordinate his medical needs with the receiving Turkish authorities. They further maintained that the risks of a blood feud and political persecution were unsubstantiated. *   **Article 8 (Right to Respect for Private and Family Life):**
    *   *The Applicant Alleged:* His deportation would violate his right to respect for his private and family life, as his children and grandchildren reside in Switzerland. *   *The Government Contested:* They argued that this complaint was inadmissible because the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, having not raised this specific claim before the Federal Supreme Court. *   **Article 6 (Right to a Fair Trial):**
    *   *The Applicant Alleged:* The refusal of the domestic courts to hold public hearings violated his right to a fair trial. *   *The Government Contested:* They argued that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention is not applicable to decisions regarding the entry, stay, and deportation of foreign nationals.

case_name: CASE OF A.T. v. LUXEMBOURG
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *A.T. v. Luxembourg* (Application no. 30460/13)

#### 1. Main Parties
The case involves Mr. A.T., a British national (the applicant), and the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg (the respondent Government). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In October 2009, Luxembourg authorities initiated a criminal investigation against the applicant on charges of rape and indecent assault of a minor under his authority. On December 4, 2009, the applicant was arrested in the United Kingdom under a European Arrest Warrant (EAW) and was surrendered to Luxembourg on December 17, 2009. Upon his arrival at Luxembourg airport, the applicant was served with the EAW and immediately taken to a police station for questioning. According to the police report, the applicant initially refused to make a statement and requested legal assistance, referencing British law. After police officers explained the applicable Luxembourgish procedures, the applicant agreed to proceed with the interrogation without a lawyer. He denied all allegations. At the end of the session, he requested legal assistance for the following day. On the morning of December 18, 2009, the applicant was brought before an investigating judge. He was informed of his right to counsel and was assigned an officially appointed lawyer, Mr. W. The applicant was then interrogated in the presence of his lawyer and an interpreter, during which he confirmed the statements he had previously made to the police. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
On March 31, 2011, the District Court of Luxembourg convicted the applicant and sentenced him to a seven-year prison term (with three years suspended). The court's judgment noted that the applicant had repeatedly changed his "version of events" during the investigations. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on February 7, 2012. Addressing the applicant’s complaint regarding the lack of counsel during his initial police questioning, the appellate court concluded that the applicant had voluntarily agreed to make statements without a lawyer after the procedure was explained to him. The court also noted inconsistencies between the applicant's police statements and his subsequent trial testimony. On November 22, 2012, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law, finding no violation of his defense rights because he had recorded his agreement to be questioned without counsel. #### 4. The Applicant’s Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained of violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention. He alleged that:
* He was denied the assistance of a lawyer during his police questioning on December 17, 2009, arguing that his subsequent agreement to speak did not constitute a voluntary or fully informed waiver. * He did not receive effective legal assistance during his interrogation by the investigating judge on December 18, 2009. He argued that under Luxembourg law, his lawyer was systematically denied access to the case file prior to the first interrogation, and that domestic law did not permit any prior private communication between an accused and an officially appointed lawyer, rendering the lawyer's presence purely passive. * The domestic appellate and cassation courts failed to remedy these violations and instead used his unrepresented police statements to undermine his credibility and secure his conviction. #### 5. The Government’s Position
The Government contested these allegations, arguing that:
* The applicant’s waiver of counsel during the police interview was unequivocal, voluntary, and accompanied by the necessary procedural safeguards. * The applicant's conviction was not based on his initial police statements but on other independent evidence, including witness testimonies and medical reports. * The legal assistance provided before the investigating judge was effective. The Government maintained that the lawyer was free to intervene and ask questions, and that domestic practice allowed for unrestricted communication between defendants and their lawyers upon request. They further argued that postponing access to the case file until after the first interrogation was a justified measure to protect the integrity of the investigation.

case_name: CASE OF A.K. v. LIECHTENSTEIN
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *A.K. v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 38191/12) was lodged by Mr. A.K., a German national residing in Switzerland, against the Principality of Liechtenstein. The domestic dispute also involved a private counterparty, F.H. ### Key Factual Circumstances
Beginning in 2004, the applicant and F.H. were locked in legal disputes over the ownership of 75% of the bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In December 2009, the Regional Court granted an interim injunction requested by F.H. to prevent the registration of corporate changes decided during an extraordinary shareholders' meeting in July 2004. These changes would have removed F.H. from the supervisory board and established the applicant as the sole managing director. Following appeals and a remittal, the Regional Court issued a fresh, identical interim injunction in July 2010. The court reasoned that the injunction was necessary to preserve the status quo and prevent irreversible damage to F.H. pending the outcome of the main proceedings. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal against this decision in September 2010. In October 2010, the applicant filed a constitutional complaint. In November 2011, the Constitutional Court notified him of the five judges (B., Bu., S., V., and W.) assigned to deliberate on his case. The applicant subsequently filed motions for bias against all five judges and the court secretary. He argued that the court had repeatedly ruled to his disadvantage, discriminated against German nationals, and delayed his case. He also cited close professional and personal ties between the assigned judges and judge H., who was the vice-president of the Constitutional Court and the brother of F.H. Additionally, he raised individual challenges, such as judges performing work for the government, holding corporate board seats, or having conflicts of interest through their private law firms. On 28 November 2011, the Constitutional Court dismissed the motions for bias. To do so, the court adopted a procedure where each challenged judge abstained from the deliberation and decision regarding the motion against themselves, leaving the remaining four judges to decide on that specific challenge. In December 2011, the Constitutional Court allowed the applicant's complaint in part regarding the unreasonable length of the proceedings but dismissed the remainder of his claims. ### Procedural History and Parties' Positions before the ECtHR
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 May 2012. The complaint concerning the alleged lack of impartiality of the Constitutional Court was communicated to the Government, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal). He argued that the Constitutional Court judges were not impartial, particularly because of the procedure used to decide the bias motions, which he claimed violated the principle that no one should be a judge in their own cause (*nemo iudex in sua causa*). He asserted that the court should have instead appointed substitute judges as provided for under the Constitutional Court Act. The Government contested the applicability of Article 6 § 1, arguing that the interim injunction did not effectively determine civil rights. On the merits, they maintained that the Constitutional Court was impartial. While they conceded that the procedure technically breached the *nemo iudex in sua causa* principle, they argued it was justified to prevent judicial paralysis, especially given the time constraints and the small size of Liechtenstein's jurisdiction. The Court declared the application admissible, finding Article 6 § 1 applicable under the *Micallef v. Malta* criteria because the interim order effectively determined the civil right to manage and represent the corporation while it remained in force.

case_name: CASE OF BERLAND v. FRANCE
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: Berland v. France (Application no. 42875/10)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Daniel Berland, a French national born in 1987. The respondent party is the Government of France. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On September 12, 2007, the twenty-year-old applicant stabbed his former girlfriend to death and wounded two other individuals at her workplace. Following his arrest, he was placed under judicial investigation for premeditated murder and intentional wounding. Psychiatric evaluations conducted by two separate expert boards concluded that, at the time of the events, the applicant suffered from a mental disorder that severely impaired his discernment and control over his actions. Consequently, he was admitted to a specialized hospital center. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
While the investigation was ongoing, France enacted the Act of 25 February 2008, which introduced new procedures regarding preventive detention and declarations of criminal insanity. Under this new framework, the public prosecutor requested a ruling on the applicant's lack of criminal liability. In February 2009, the Investigation Division of the Dijon Court of Appeal determined that there was sufficient evidence that the applicant had committed the physical acts of the offenses, but declared him to lack criminal liability due to his mental state. Utilizing the provisions of the newly enacted 2008 Act, the court ordered his compulsory hospitalization, citing the ongoing risk he posed to public safety. Additionally, the court imposed preventive measures for a twenty-year period, which included prohibiting him from contacting the victims' families and from carrying weapons. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, arguing that applying the 2008 Act to actions committed in 2007 violated the constitutional and international principle of the non-retroactivity of harsher criminal laws. In April 2010, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, ruling that the measures imposed under the 2008 Act were preventive and protective rather than punitive, meaning the rule against retroactivity did not apply. Subsequently, in February 2011, the local Prefect denied the applicant's request for unescorted rehabilitation leave, citing the court-ordered contact prohibitions. #### 4. Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 7 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits the retrospective application of a heavier penalty than the one applicable at the time of the offense. He argued that the 2008 Act's procedures—specifically the formal judicial declaration of his actions and the accompanying long-term compulsory hospitalisation and prohibitions—amounted to a criminal conviction and "penalties" in practice. Because these measures did not exist in this form at the time of the offense, he contended their retrospective application was unlawful. #### 5. Government’s Position
The French Government contested the applicability of Article 7. They argued that the measures did not constitute "penalties" because they did not stem from a criminal conviction or a finding of guilt. Instead, they characterized the measures as purely preventive, therapeutic, and protective, designed to treat the applicant's mental illness and safeguard society. They emphasized that the measures were flexible, subject to medical review, and lacked any punitive intent. #### 6. European Court Proceedings
The application was lodged on July 21, 2010. The Court subsequently declared the application admissible, deciding to join the Government's objection regarding the applicability of Article 7 to the merits of the case.

case_name: CASE OF ELBERTE v. LATVIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Elberte v. Latvia* (Application no. 61243/08)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The applicant is Ms. Dzintra Elberte, a Latvian national residing in Sigulda. She is the widow of Mr. Egils Elberts. The respondent party is the Government of the Republic of Latvia. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On May 19, 2001, the applicant’s husband died from injuries sustained in a car accident. His body was taken to the State Centre for Forensic Medical Examination (the Forensic Centre) in Riga for an autopsy. Following the autopsy, a forensic medical expert removed a portion of dura mater (brain membrane) from the deceased's body. The removal was conducted under a 1994 cooperation agreement between the Forensic Centre and a German pharmaceutical company. Under this agreement, the Forensic Centre supplied human tissues to the company, which processed them into bio-implants. Some of these implants were returned to Latvia for medical use, while others were used elsewhere. In return, the German company funded medical equipment and computers for Latvian medical institutions. The applicant was not informed of the tissue removal at the time of her husband's death. She only discovered that tissue had been removed approximately two years later, in 2003, when the Latvian security police contacted her during a criminal inquiry into the potentially illegal removal of organs and tissues at the Forensic Centre. Additionally, when the applicant first saw her deceased husband's body prior to his funeral on May 26, 2001, she observed that his legs had been tied together, and he was buried in this state. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that the removal of tissue from her deceased husband’s body without her prior knowledge or consent violated her right to respect for her private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention. She argued that Latvian law at the material time was neither clear nor foreseeable, as it failed to define a clear procedure for experts to ascertain the wishes of a deceased person's next of kin. She further alleged under Article 3 of the Convention that the unauthorized tissue removal, combined with the state in which her husband's body was returned for burial (with his legs tied), caused her severe mental suffering amounting to degrading treatment. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government contested the applicant's claims. First, they argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because she had not filed a constitutional complaint, submitted a complaint to the medical inspectorate (MADEKKI), or pursued a civil claim for damages under the Civil Law. On the merits, the Government maintained that the tissue removal was "in accordance with the law" under a domestic system of "presumed consent." They asserted that the forensic expert had verified that the deceased’s passport did not contain a stamp objecting to tissue donation. The Government argued that domestic law did not impose an active obligation on medical experts to contact relatives or inform them of their right to object; rather, it was the responsibility of the relatives to express any objection proactively. They concluded that the practice pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the health and rights of others by securing bio-implants to save or improve lives. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
In March 2003, the security police opened a criminal inquiry into the Forensic Centre's tissue removal practices. Over several years, prosecutors repeatedly discontinued and reopened the investigation due to differing interpretations of whether Latvian law established an "informed consent" or "presumed consent" system. On June 26, 2008, the Riga City Vidzeme District Court quashed a previous decision to discontinue the case on statute-of-limitation grounds. Instead, the court ordered the proceedings discontinued on exonerating grounds (the absence of a crime). The court ruled that domestic law did not obligate forensic experts to inform relatives of their right to object or to seek their consent. Consequently, the court found that the experts had not committed a criminal offense. A superior prosecutor issued a final decision upholding this outcome on October 23, 2008. Ms. Elberte lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on December 5, 2008. On April 27, 2010, the Court gave notice of the application to the Latvian Government. On July 9, 2013, the Court decided to examine the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.

case_name: CASE OF SATAKUNNAN MARKKINAPORSSI OY AND SATAMEDIA OY v. FINLAND
step1_summary:
### Parties
The applicants are two Finnish limited liability companies, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy. The respondent party is the Republic of Finland. ### Factual Circumstances
Starting in 1994, the first applicant company published *Veropörssi*, a magazine containing public information regarding natural persons’ annual taxable income and assets. In 2002, the magazine published taxation data on 1.2 million individuals, which comprised approximately one-third of all taxable persons in Finland at the time. In 2003, the second applicant company, which shared ownership with the first, partnered with a telecommunications operator to launch an SMS-based service. This service allowed users to send a person's name to a designated number to retrieve their taxation information, utilizing a database compiled from the data published in the magazine. ### Procedural History
In 2003, the Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman requested the Data Protection Board to forbid the applicant companies from processing taxation data to the extent they had in 2002 and from transferring such data to the SMS service, arguing these activities did not fall under the "journalistic purposes" derogation of the Personal Data Act. The Data Protection Board and, subsequently, the Helsinki Administrative Court rejected the Ombudsman's request, ruling that the publication had a journalistic purpose and served the public interest. The Ombudsman appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which in 2007 requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) regarding the interpretation of Directive 95/46/EC. In December 2008, the CJEU ruled that while "journalism" should be interpreted broadly, derogations for data protection must apply only where strictly necessary to balance the right to privacy with freedom of expression. In September 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the lower decisions and referred the case back to the Data Protection Board. It found that the wholesale publication of the database did not constitute journalistic activity and that the public interest did not require the disclosure of personal data to such an extent. Consequently, in November 2009, the Data Protection Board issued an injunction prohibiting the applicants from processing the taxation data in the manner done in 2002 and from forwarding it to the SMS service. The applicants appealed this decision, but their challenges were rejected by the Turku Administrative Court in 2010 and ultimately by the Supreme Administrative Court in June 2012. ### Applicants' Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that:
1. **Article 10 (Freedom of Expression):** The domestic decisions constituted prior censorship and a de facto ban on publishing public information, which was not "necessary in a democratic society."
2. **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial):** The total length of the administrative proceedings, which spanned more than eight years, was excessive. 3. **Article 14 (Prohibition of Discrimination):** They were discriminated against compared to other media outlets that were permitted to continue publishing taxation data. ### Government's Position
The Finnish Government contested the applicants' claims, arguing that:
1. **Article 10:** The measures did not ban publication itself but regulated the processing of personal data to protect the right to privacy. Any resulting interference was prescribed by law and necessary to protect the rights of others. 2. **Article 6 § 1:** The duration of the proceedings was reasonable given the legal complexity of the case, the necessity of obtaining a preliminary ruling from the CJEU, and the absence of significant periods of inactivity by the domestic authorities. 3. **Article 14:** The applicants were not in a comparable situation to other newspapers, as no other media outlet published personal taxation data on such an unprecedented scale.

case_name: CASE OF GASIMLI AND OTHERS v. AZERBAIJAN
step1_summary:
### Main Parties
The case concerns five Azerbaijani nationals: Mr. Ali Salah oglu Gasimli, Mr. Tazakhan Maharram oglu Miralamli, Mr. Parviz Kamran oglu Hashimov, Mr. Natig Mehman oglu Jafarov, and Mr. Eyyub Umud oglu Umudov (the applicants). The respondent party is the Government of the Republic of Azerbaijan. ### Key Factual Circumstances
The applicants stood as candidates in the Azerbaijani parliamentary elections of 7 November 2010, either as self-nominated candidates or nominated by an opposition party coalition. Under the domestic Electoral Code, candidates were required to collect and submit at least 450 valid voter signatures to their respective Constituency Electoral Commissions (ConECs) to secure registration. Each applicant submitted signature sheets containing more than 450 signatures. These sheets were verified by special working groups established by the ConECs. The applicants were not invited to participate in these verification processes. Subsequently, the ConECs refused to register the applicants, ruling that numerous signatures were invalid on various grounds—including incorrect voter information, expired identity documents, and suspected repeat or falsified signatures. This left each applicant with fewer than the required 450 valid signatures. The applicants were not invited to the ConEC meetings where these decisions were made, and the relevant working group documents and decisions were only provided to them after the refusal decisions had been finalized. ### The Applicants’ Allegations
The applicants alleged a violation of their right to stand for election under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. They argued that the electoral commissions' decisions to invalidate their signatures were factually incorrect, subjective, and arbitrary, particularly because the working groups lacked qualified handwriting experts. They also claimed several procedural violations of the Electoral Code, including:
* A failure to notify them of the signature examinations or allow them to attend;
* A failure to provide working group documents 24 hours prior to the ConEC meetings;
* A failure to allow them to correct rectifiable errors on the signature sheets; and
* The unlawful invalidation of signatures on grounds not prescribed by law (such as recently expired identity cards). Additionally, four of the applicants complained under Article 14 of the Convention, alleging that they had faced discrimination and systematic electoral barriers as members of the political opposition. ### The Government’s Position
The Government argued that the requirement to collect 450 signatures pursued the legitimate aim of preventing overcrowded candidate lists and avoiding voter confusion. They maintained that domestic law provided sufficient safeguards against arbitrary decisions, pointing out that the working groups consisted of trained experts from state forensic and interior departments, meetings were legally open to candidates, and candidates had access to multiple levels of appeal. The Government asserted that the registration refusals were justified because the applicants had failed to produce the minimum number of valid signatures, and noted that the applicants had not requested a graphological expert examination during their appeals before the domestic courts. ### Procedural History
Following the ConECs' decisions, the applicants filed complaints with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC). The CEC conducted its own reviews of the signature sheets without the applicants' presence, found different numbers of invalid signatures, and rejected the complaints. The applicants then appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal, which dismissed their claims as unsubstantiated. Subsequent cassation appeals to the Supreme Court of Azerbaijan were also dismissed, with the court finding no grounds to challenge the findings of the electoral commissions or the lower court. The applicants lodged their applications with the European Court of Human Rights in 2011. In September 2014, the Government submitted unilateral declarations requesting the Court to strike the applications out of its list of cases under Article 37 of the Convention. The applicants objected, and the Court rejected the Government's request, deciding to proceed with its examination of the admissibility and merits of the applications.

case_name: CASE OF BLESA RODRÍGUEZ v. SPAIN
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Blesa Rodríguez v. Spain* (Application no. 61131/12)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Antonio Carlos Blesa Rodríguez, a Spanish national born in 1931 and a former professor at the Faculty of Pharmacy of La Laguna University. *   **Respondent State:** The Kingdom of Spain. *   **Other Involved Party:** La Laguna University, which acted as the private prosecutor in the domestic criminal proceedings against the applicant. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In May 2003, La Laguna University filed a criminal complaint against the applicant, accusing him of forgery for allegedly submitting a falsified curriculum vitae in a public tender for pharmaceutical establishment licences. An investigating judge initially suspended the investigation in 2004, finding no objective reasons to believe a crime had been committed. However, in May 2006, the Santa Cruz de Tenerife *Audiencia Provincial* (composed of Judges A., S., and C.) quashed the suspension and ordered further investigation. In June 2010, the *Audiencia Provincial* scheduled the trial, initially indicating the bench would consist of Judges A., S., and G. At the preliminary hearing on July 1, 2010, the defense was informed that the bench had been modified to Judges A., G., and Sa. (the latter acting as a substitute judge). Following a trial in July 2010, this bench convicted the applicant of forgery, sentencing him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, suspension from office, and a fine. #### 3. Procedural History (Domestic)
The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, alleging a lack of impartiality regarding Judges A. and Sa. He argued that Judge A. had previously participated in quashing the suspension of the investigation, and that Judge Sa. was an associate professor and administrative employee at La Laguna University, the prosecuting institution. In May 2011, the Supreme Court rejected these challenges. It ruled that the applicant had failed to challenge Judge A. in a timely manner and that Judge A.'s prior decision did not undermine his objective impartiality. Regarding Judge Sa., the Supreme Court found that his part-time academic role did not constitute a conflict of interest under domestic law, nor was there evidence of any personal interest in the outcome. However, the Supreme Court reduced the applicant's sentence to one year and six months due to the excessive duration of the domestic proceedings, which had lasted over seven years. The applicant subsequently filed an *amparo* appeal, which the Constitutional Court declared inadmissible in March 2012 on the grounds of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, finding he had failed to raise the impartiality complaints properly in the earlier stages. #### 4. The Applicant's Allegations before the ECtHR
The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on September 7, 2012, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal). He maintained that Judge A. lacked objective impartiality due to his prior involvement in the investigation stage. He further argued that Judge Sa.’s professional and financial relationship with La Laguna University created a dependency incompatible with his role as an impartial judge. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Spanish Government contested the allegations. On admissibility, they argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he did not formally challenge either judge during the trial stage despite being notified of the bench's composition. On the merits concerning Judge Sa., the Government contended that the judge's part-time, non-exclusive academic duties were entirely unrelated to the criminal dispute and did not create any financial or personal interest in the outcome of the trial, meaning there was no objective basis to doubt his impartiality. #### 6. Admissibility Decision of the European Court
The European Court declared the complaint concerning Judge A. inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies, as the applicant had not challenged him before the trial. However, the Court declared the complaint regarding Judge Sa. admissible, finding that the applicant had raised the issue as soon as practically possible given the late notification of the bench's composition.

case_name: CASE OF FURMAN v. SLOVENIA AND AUSTRIA
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Furman v. Slovenia and Austria* (Application no. 16608/09)

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Andrej Furman, a Slovenian national born in 1955 and residing in Maribor, Slovenia. *   **Respondent States:** The Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Austria. *   **Other Key Individuals:** M.P. (the applicant’s former extramarital partner) and P. (their daughter, born on December 14, 1993). #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
The applicant and M.P. lived in an extramarital relationship from 1991 to 1997. Following their separation in 1997, they concluded agreements through the Maribor Social Work Centre ("the Centre") regarding child maintenance and a provisional contact schedule for their daughter, P., covering the period from February 24 to April 13, 1998. After this provisional period expired, M.P. allegedly stopped allowing the applicant to have contact with P. Having failed to reach a permanent agreement with M.P., the applicant applied to the Centre on February 24, 1998, for an order determining his contact rights. He sought contact with his daughter on designated weekdays, alternate weekends, and during winter and summer holidays. In June 1998, M.P. informed the Centre that she would be living in Graz, Austria, from July 1, 1998, to August 31, 1999, for doctoral studies, and requested that the contact proceedings be suspended. The Centre attempted to establish her whereabouts and schedule hearings, but faced difficulties serving her with summonses. On October 29, 1998, the Centre issued an interim order establishing a provisional contact schedule (one weekend per month and one week during winter and summer holidays). M.P. appealed this order, arguing it could not be implemented because she and P. were living in Austria. In April and June 1999, the applicant requested the enforcement of the interim order. Although the Maribor Administrative Unit granted the enforcement requests in August 1999, M.P. appealed, claiming improper service and objecting to the order's contents. On September 27, 1999, the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs upheld M.P.’s appeal, quashed the interim order, and remitted the matter to the Centre. The Ministry determined that the service of the interim order and summonses had not complied with administrative procedures, noting that parties residing abroad must be invited to appoint a representative authorized to receive official mail. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
The applicant alleged that he was unable to enjoy family life with his daughter. He asserted that this situation arose due to a lack of diligence and responsiveness on the part of both the Slovenian and Austrian authorities in regulating and enforcing his contact rights. #### 4. The Governments' Positions
The Slovenian Government was represented by its Agent, Mrs. B. Jovin Hrastnik, and the Austrian Government was represented by its Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy. The specific arguments and substantive positions of the respondent Governments regarding the merits of the applicant's allegations are not detailed in the provided introductory text. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
*   **Domestic Level:** The proceedings took place before the Maribor Social Work Centre, the Maribor Administrative Unit, and the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs, culminating in the Ministry's September 1999 decision to quash the interim contact order and remit the case. *   **European Court Level:** The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on March 23, 2009. On July 3, 2012, the application was officially communicated to the Governments of Slovenia and Austria. The Chamber of the Fifth Section of the Court subsequently deliberated on the case in private on January 13, 2015.

case_name: CASE OF CARAIAN v. ROMANIA
step1_summary:
### Case Briefing: *Caraian v. Romania* (Application no. 34456/07)

#### 1. The Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Mr. Vasile Caraian, a Romanian national born in 1940 and residing in Bucharest. *   **Respondent State:** Romania, represented by Agents from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances and Procedural History
The case arose from criminal proceedings initiated against the applicant in 1996. *   **First Round of Proceedings:** In August 1996, the applicant was detained on suspicion of intellectual forgery and using forged documents. In September 1997, he was indicted for bribery, influence peddling, complicity in fraud, intellectual forgery, and use of forged documents. In June 2000, the Sibiu County Court acquitted him. On appeal by the prosecution, the Alba Iulia Court of Appeal quashed the acquittal in December 2000, convicting the applicant and sentencing him to three years’ imprisonment. In March 2002, the Court of Cassation quashed this conviction and referred the case back to the prosecutor’s office, citing serious procedural defects and an inadequate investigation. *   **Second Round of Proceedings:** In June 2003, the National Anticorruption Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the bribery and influence peddling charges. The remaining charges of complicity in fraud and forgery were referred to the Sibiu Prosecutor’s Office, which discontinued the investigation in July 2003 because the prosecution was time-barred, though it noted the applicant's criminal liability was "undeniable." Seeking to establish his innocence, the applicant requested the continuation of the proceedings under domestic law. The investigation was reopened but discontinued again on the same time-barred grounds in November 2003, with the prosecutor asserting the applicant's guilt was proven. Following an appeal, the Sibiu District Court ordered the case reopened in July 2004 because the investigation had been conducted by the same prosecutor who originally indicted him. *   **Third Round of Proceedings:** In March 2005, a different prosecutor again discontinued the investigation as time-barred, explicitly stating in the order that the applicant was guilty of the offences. The applicant appealed to the Sibiu District Court, requesting that the court quash the prosecutor's decision, retain the case, and acquit him on the merits. In February 2006, the District Court dismissed his appeal, upholding the prosecutor's decision and finding that the applicant had committed the acts. In March 2007, the Bacău County Court dismissed the applicant's final appeal on points of law, confirming the prosecutor's finding of guilt while upholding the discontinuation of the case due to the statute of limitations. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the criminal proceedings against him had been excessively lengthy. He further alleged a violation of his right to the presumption of innocence and his right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2. Specifically, he argued that the prosecutor’s office and the domestic courts had declared him guilty of the offences in decisions that discontinued the proceedings as time-barred. He contended that the domestic courts endorsed his guilt by relying solely on the existing file, without formally retaining the case for a trial on the merits, hearing him, or adducing additional evidence. #### 4. The Government’s Position
*   **Length of Proceedings:** The Government submitted a unilateral declaration acknowledging a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the excessive length of the proceedings and offered a financial sum in just satisfaction, requesting the Court to strike this part of the application from its list. *   **Presumption of Innocence and Fair Trial:** The Government argued that the applicant had been given ample opportunity to present his case and request evidence. They noted that after the reopening of the investigation, the applicant explicitly stated he had no further evidence to submit, believing the existing file proved his innocence. The Government contended that the prosecutor's office and the domestic courts had carried out a full assessment of the available evidence to establish the applicant's guilt before discontinuing the case as time-barred. Consequently, they maintained that no issue arose regarding the applicant's right to be presumed innocent.

case_name: CASE OF TOLMACHEV v. ESTONIA
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case of *Tolmachev v. Estonia* (Application no. 73748/13) was lodged against the Republic of Estonia by Mr. Kirill Tolmachev, an Estonian national born in 1990. ### Factual Background
On 17 September 2012, a police officer fined the applicant 80 euros (EUR) for a misdemeanour involving a breach of public order, specifically for breaking a glass panel of a bus shelter. The applicant contested this decision before the Viru County Court. He argued that he had not committed the act, challenged the assessment of witness statements, and complained that the police had failed to present him to a witness for identification. The County Court scheduled a hearing for 21 March 2013. The summons sent to the applicant indicated that his participation was mandatory and warned that, pursuant to Article 126 § 2 of the Code of Misdemeanour Procedure, the court would refuse to examine the complaint if he failed to appear. While the applicant's counsel received the summons, the court's security officer was unable to serve it to the applicant personally; his mother refused to accept it, stating he was living abroad. At the hearing, the applicant did not appear. His counsel requested that the court examine the complaint in the applicant's absence because he was abroad. The applicant's father, who was present in the courtroom as a spectator, stated that the applicant would not return to Estonia for five years. ### Domestic Procedural History
On 2 April 2013, the County Court issued a decision refusing to examine the applicant's complaint. The court concluded that the applicant was aware of the hearing but had failed to notify the authorities of his change of address. It found that the case could not be examined without his participation because his own complaints—such as the police's failure to present him to a witness for identification—required his physical presence to resolve. Furthermore, the court noted that adjournment was futile since the applicant would not return within the statutory one-month limit. The applicant's counsel appealed, invoking the right to defend oneself through legal assistance under Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention. On 23 May 2013, the Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the County Court's ruling, confirming that the first-instance court had properly justified the necessity of the applicant's presence. No further domestic appeal was available. ### Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights and Parties' Submissions
The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of his right to a fair trial and his right to defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention. He argued that he had a right, rather than an obligation, to attend the hearing and that the court should have proceeded with his counsel present or adjourned the hearing. The Estonian Government contested the application. They first requested the Court to declare it inadmissible, arguing that the applicant had not suffered a significant disadvantage. On the merits, the Government maintained that the applicant's presence was necessary for the domestic court to thoroughly examine the factual circumstances of the misdemeanour. They argued that the applicant was fully aware of the mandatory nature of the hearing and that his failure to appear, without requesting an adjournment, amounted to an obstruction of the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF OLIARI AND OTHERS v. ITALY
step1_summary:
### Parties
The case *Oliari and Others v. Italy* originated from two joined applications lodged against the Italian Republic by six Italian nationals: Mr. Enrico Oliari, Mr. A., Mr. Gian Mario Felicetti, Mr. Riccardo Perelli Cippo, Mr. Roberto Zaccheo, and Mr. Riccardo Zappa. ### Factual Circumstances
The applicants are three same-sex couples living in stable, committed relationships. Between 2008 and 2011, each couple requested their local civil status offices to issue marriage banns. All of these requests were rejected by the municipal authorities on the ground that, under the Italian Civil Code, marriage requires the spouses to be of opposite sexes. At the time of the applications, Italian law did not provide same-sex couples with any alternative legal framework, such as civil unions or registered partnerships, to obtain formal legal recognition and protection. ### Domestic Procedural History
The applicants pursued different paths within the domestic legal system:
*   **Mr. Oliari and Mr. A.** challenged the administrative rejection before the Trent Tribunal, which dismissed their claim. On appeal, the Trent Court of Appeal referred the question of the law's constitutionality to the Constitutional Court. In Judgment No. 138 of 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the challenge inadmissible. It held that while same-sex couples possess a fundamental right to obtain legal recognition of their union under Article 2 of the Italian Constitution, the specific method and timing of providing such recognition fell within the legislative discretion of Parliament. Consequently, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants' claims in September 2010. *   **Mr. Perelli Cippo and Mr. Zaccheo** challenged their rejection before the Milan Tribunal, which dismissed their claim in July 2010, citing the Constitutional Court’s precedent. They did not appeal further. *   **Mr. Felicetti and Mr. Zappa** did not seek judicial remedies, asserting that doing so would be ineffective following the Constitutional Court’s 2010 ruling. ### Applicants' Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (respect for private and family life), Article 12 (right to marry), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. They argued that the complete lack of a legal framework to recognize their relationships discriminated against them based on sexual orientation. They asserted that this legal vacuum caused daily practical difficulties and legal uncertainty regarding essential rights—such as inheritance, mutual assistance, maintenance, and tax benefits—which could not be adequately resolved through private cohabitation agreements. ### Government's Position
The Italian Government raised preliminary objections, arguing that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because they did not appeal their cases to the Court of Cassation. On the merits, the Government contended that the regulation of same-sex unions falls within the State's wide margin of appreciation, given the lack of a European consensus and the sensitive moral, social, and religious issues involved. They argued that Italian jurisprudence already provided de facto protection for same-sex couples on a case-by-case basis, that private cohabitation agreements were available, and that Parliament was actively debating several bills on civil unions. ### Procedural History before the European Court
The applications were lodged in March and June 2011 and subsequently joined. The Chamber declared the complaints under Articles 8 and 14 admissible. Several non-governmental organizations, including FIDH, ILGA-Europe, and the European Centre for Law and Justice, intervened as third parties. On June 30, 2015, the Chamber decided that an oral hearing was unnecessary.

case_name: CASE OF ROHLENA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Rohlena v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 59552/08)

#### 1. The Main Parties
The case involves the applicant, Mr. Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966, and the respondent State, the Czech Republic. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
In May 2006, the applicant was indicted for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk between 2000 and February 2006. On June 1, 2004, a new provision—Article 215a of the Criminal Code—was introduced, specifically criminalizing the abuse of a person living under the same roof. Prior to this amendment, domestic violence was prosecuted under general provisions, such as violence against an individual (Article 197a) or assault occasioning bodily harm (Article 221). In April 2007, the Brno Municipal Court found the applicant guilty of the continuous offense of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a, applying the classification to his conduct spanning the entire period from 2000 to 2006. He was sentenced to a suspended term of two and a half years' imprisonment and placed on probation. The applicant’s subsequent appeals were dismissed by the Brno Regional Court, the Supreme Court, and the Constitutional Court. The Supreme Court clarified that under Czech law, a "continuous criminal offense" is treated as a single legal act. Consequently, its legal classification must be assessed under the law in force at the time the final act is completed (in this case, February 2006), provided that the acts committed prior to the legislative change were also punishable under the older law. The domestic courts concluded that the applicant's conduct prior to June 2004 met the criteria for offenses under Articles 197a and 221. #### 3. The Applicant’s Main Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 7 of the Convention (no punishment without law). He argued that the domestic courts had retroactively applied Article 215a to his conduct prior to June 1, 2004, to his detriment. He contended that his earlier actions did not constitute criminal offenses at the time but were merely regulatory infractions. Furthermore, he argued that his actions did not meet the domestic criteria for a "continuous offense" because they lacked a single intent and were not closely connected in time. Finally, he claimed that this retroactive application subjected him to a heavier penalty than what would have been possible had the individual acts been prosecuted separately. #### 4. The Government’s Position
The Government contested these allegations, maintaining that the legal framework was sufficiently clear and foreseeable. They argued that the concept of a continuous offense was well-established in Czech jurisprudence before the applicant completed his conduct in 2006. The Government asserted that the applicant's actions prior to June 2004 were clearly criminal under Articles 197a and 221 of the Criminal Code. They also argued that classifying the conduct as a single continuous offense did not disadvantage the applicant; rather, prosecuting the acts separately would have resulted in a concurrent sentence that could have been equally or more severe. #### 5. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on December 4, 2008. It was allocated to the Fifth Section, which subsequently declared the complaint under Article 7 of the Convention admissible and the remainder of the application inadmissible. Following a request by the applicant, a panel of the Grand Chamber referred the case to the Grand Chamber on September 9, 2013. Both the applicant and the Government subsequently filed written observations on the merits and replied to specific questions put to them by the Grand Chamber.

case_name: CASE OF LHERMITTE v. BELGIUM
step1_summary:
### Case Brief: *Lhermitte v. Belgium* (Application no. 34238/09)

#### 1. Main Parties
*   **Applicant:** Ms. Geneviève Lhermitte, a Belgian national. *   **Respondent State:** The Kingdom of Belgium. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 28 February 2007, the applicant killed her five children and attempted suicide. She was subsequently committed to stand trial for premeditated intentional homicide. During the pre-trial investigation, several psychological and psychiatric assessments were ordered. An initial psychiatric report from October 2007 concluded that while the applicant suffered from severe anxiety and depression, she did not have a mental disorder that rendered her incapable of controlling her actions. However, during her trial in December 2008, new evidence emerged in the form of letters she had written to her psychiatrist prior to the incident. A supplementary psychiatric report was ordered, which unanimously concluded that at the time of the events, the applicant was suffering from a severe mental disturbance making her incapable of controlling her actions. #### 3. Domestic Procedural History
The trial took place in the Assize Court of Walloon Brabant. At the close of proceedings, the jury was asked five questions concerning the applicant's guilt, premeditation, and mental capacity. The jury answered "yes" to the questions of guilt and premeditation, but "no" to the question of whether she suffered from a mental disorder making her incapable of controlling her actions. On 19 December 2008, the Assize Court sentenced her to life imprisonment. In its sentencing judgment, the court noted that her mental fragility and personal difficulties did not constitute mitigating factors given the extreme violence of her actions. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, which dismissed her appeal on 6 May 2009. The Court of Cassation ruled that the jury's simple "yes/no" verdict was legally prescribed and that the Assize Court had sufficiently explained why her mental state did not preclude criminal responsibility. #### 4. Proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights and the Applicant's Allegations
The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 June 2009, and the complaint was subsequently declared admissible. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial), asserting that both the jury's verdict and the Assize Court's sentencing judgment lacked adequate reasoning. She argued that the questions put to the jury were ambiguous and failed to explain why the jury chose to disregard the unanimous psychiatric reports concluding she lacked criminal responsibility. Furthermore, she contended that the Assize Court's sentencing judgment was contradictory and failed to justify the lack of mitigating circumstances. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Belgian Government contested these allegations. They argued that the detailed indictment and trial proceedings provided the applicant with a clear understanding of the charges and evidence. They maintained that psychiatric reports represent professional opinions rather than absolute scientific truths, and that the Assize Court's sentencing judgment sufficiently detailed why her claim of mental incapacity was rejected, ensuring adequate safeguards against arbitrariness.

case_name: CASE OF FERREIRA ALVES v. PORTUGAL
step1_summary:
### Case Summary: Ferreira Alves v. Portugal (Application no. 78165/12)

#### 1. Main Parties
The applicant is Mr. Jorge de Jesus Ferreira Alves, a Portuguese national born in 1953 who resides in Matosinhos and works as a lawyer. The respondent party is the Republic of Portugal, represented before the Court by its Agent, Mrs. M. F. da Graça Carvalho, Deputy-Attorney General. #### 2. Key Factual Circumstances
On 22 February 2008, the Porto Ethics Council of the Portuguese Bar Association initiated disciplinary proceedings (no. 100/2008) against the applicant. These proceedings were triggered by a complaint lodged by the Administrative Central Court of the North. The complaint arose from the applicant’s conduct as a legal representative in four separate tort actions against the State, during which he requested that a judgment from the European Court of Human Rights be translated and paid for by the domestic court. Under Article 125 of the Statute of the Portuguese Bar Association, disciplinary offenses can carry severe penalties, including suspension from practice for up to ten years or complete expulsion from the Bar. On 9 November 2012, the Porto Ethics Council dismissed the disciplinary proceedings against the applicant on the grounds that the action had become time-barred. #### 3. Procedural History Up to the European Court's Judgment
The applicant was officially notified of the disciplinary proceedings on 10 March 2008 and submitted his defense on 13 March 2008. Following the dismissal of the case by the Porto Ethics Council on 9 November 2012, the domestic proceedings concluded, having lasted a total of four years and eight months for a single level of jurisdiction. On 23 November 2012, the applicant lodged his application against the Portuguese Republic with the European Court of Human Rights. The application was subsequently communicated to the Portuguese Government on 4 March 2014. #### 4. The Applicant's Allegations
Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the duration of the disciplinary proceedings against him was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement stipulated under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Additionally, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 13 of the Convention, arguing that he did not have access to an effective domestic remedy within the Portuguese legal system to challenge or obtain redress for the protracted length of the disciplinary proceedings. #### 5. The Government's Position
The Portuguese Government contested the applicant's allegations on multiple grounds. First, they argued that Article 6 § 1 was inapplicable to the case, asserting that the applicant's civil right to practice law was not genuinely at stake during the disciplinary process. Second, the Government contended that the applicant had not suffered any "significant disadvantage" under the terms of the Convention. They pointed out that the applicant was never suspended or prevented from practicing his profession while the proceedings were pending. Furthermore, they argued that the applicant had actually benefited from the delay, as it ultimately resulted in the disciplinary charges being dropped as time-barred. Finally, the Government opposed the applicant's Article 13 claim, maintaining that the domestic framework was sufficient.

case_name: CASE OF LJAJIĆ v. SERBIA
step1_summary:
